Enhancing decision support system by prioritising critical areas in landslide disaster management of Kinnaur District, Himachal Pradesh
papers.summary: Abstract The Himalayan region is highly susceptible to landslides and has witnessed several fatal incidents in recent years. Implementing a priority-based ranking system for landslide management is essential to help decision-makers identify the most vulnerable or high-risk zones. This approach ensures that limited resources—such as funding, manpower, and technical expertise—are allocated efficiently. The prioritization process involves systematically evaluating and categorizing areas or projects based on the severity of risk, potential impact, and urgency of required interventions. By focusing on mitigation efforts, emergency preparedness, and infrastructure enhancement in the most at-risk zones, authorities can significantly reduce the likelihood of landslide-related disasters and strengthen community resilience. In this study, we propose a priority score ranking system for the Kinnaur district of Himachal Pradesh, based on the assessment of exposure levels of individual elements at risk, both in terms of landslide initiation and runout paths, along with their strategic importance. The resulting individual priority score maps and the integrated priority map are intended to support decision-making for a landslide early warning system and the effective allocation of resources for disaster risk reduction. Our findings indicate that approximately 5% area of the Kinnaur district should be prioritized for resource allocation to implement targeted mitigation strategies. This framework can be readily adapted on a regional scale for use in other landslide-prone regions to support focused planning and execution of disaster risk reduction initiatives.

papers.title: The rise and fall of a volcanic plateau: Landscape evolution at the fringes of the former Patagonian Ice Sheet, Meseta Chile Chico, central Patagonian Andes
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Understanding Earth‐surface processes along the fringes of large ice sheets is integral to deciphering cold‐region environmental variability and anticipating slope instability under climate change. We investigate the Meseta Chile Chico, a volcanic plateau in the central Patagonian Andes, located at the eastern margin of the former Patagonian Ice Sheet. Here, glacier retreat patterns are well‐constrained, while the influence of periglacial, paraglacial, and postglacial processes is not. We employ geomorphological mapping integrated with geological and palaeoclimate reconstructions to provide a spatio‐temporal model of landscape evolution. Enhanced erosion since the late Pliocene, caused by differential tectonic uplift and glacial isostatic rebound, produced the rugged morphology that characterizes the Meseta Chile Chico. During the Last Glacial Maximum, glaciers occupied surrounding valleys, while the surface of the plateau was reshaped by long‐lasting periglacial freeze‐thaw cycles and nivation. Postglacial landscape adjustment included intensified landslide activity along the edges of the plateau (linked to paraglacial de‐buttressing at its bordering valleys) and regional base‐level changes. During the Holocene, flow‐type landslides became increasingly controlled by climatic variability. The geomorphology of the Meseta Chile Chico reflects an interplay between inherited geology, (de)glaciation, and climate, highlighting the importance of an interdisciplinary approach for understanding recent landscape dynamics in deglaciating mountain regions.

papers.title: Largely Automated Regional Screening of Candidate Active-Slope Units Integrating InSAR and Topographic Constraints
papers.summary: Landslides are among the most serious geohazards worldwide, and accurately identifying their locations is a prerequisite for effective risk prevention and mitigation. However, regional-scale screening of candidate active-slope units from InSAR observations is still hindered by subjective manual interpretation, inconsistent deformation-rate thresholds, and insufficient topographic constraints. To address these limitations, this study proposes a largely automated terrain-constrained framework for candidate active-slope screening by integrating InSAR observations, slope units, and screening based on slope-unit bootstrap intervals and a regional two-standard-deviation background envelope. First, surface deformation rates are derived from InSAR measurements and post-processed to reduce the influence of identifiable artifacts before slope-unit analysis. Then, a clustering-based method is introduced to delineate topographically constrained slope units in alpine canyon regions, whose visual terrain correspondence is examined qualitatively using terrain information and optical imagery. Next, rather than applying a fixed site-specific deformation-rate cutoff in mm/yr, data-dependent bootstrap confidence-interval comparisons are used to determine whether the deformation interval of each slope unit extends beyond the regional deformation-background interval, thereby enabling rule-based screening of candidate active-slope units. This confidence-interval screening rule provides a quantitative criterion for regional screening but requires further calibration across additional geomorphic and deformation settings. Finally, the proposed method is applied to two landslide-prone regions in western China, located in sections of the Upper Yellow River and Upper Jinsha River, where final inventories containing 92 and 25 candidate active-slope units are produced, respectively. papers.title: Finite Element Greenfield Modelling for building damage assessment under groundwater-induced slope movements
papers.summary: This study presents a numerical investigation of ground movements induced by groundwater rise in slopes using a plane strain finite element model with a Mohr–Coulomb constitutive law under drained, steady-state seepage conditions. The main methodological contribution is the definition of a Greenfield Slope Analysis framework, which adapts the Limiting Tensile Strain Method (LTSM) to assess potential damage in shallow-founded buildings affected by slow-moving landslides. Finite element analyses are used to evaluate displacement and strain fields across the slope from which maximum tensile strains are derived, together with the corresponding changes in slope stability. Groundwater rise leads to progressive increase in ground displacements, whereas the spatial distribution of strain is primarily controlled by slope kinematics. For the selected idealised slopes with a layer of uniform thickness, the central portion shows predominantly translational behaviour, while rotation-like components develop near the crest and toe. The crest is mainly associated with tensile horizontal strains, whereas the toe is mainly associated with compressive horizontal strains, resulting in different damage potential depending on the adopted structural idealisation. Sensitivity and parametric analyses indicate that normalised slope-parallel displacement may be used as a proxy for greenfield deformation levels, supporting preliminary damage assessment and interpretation of in-situ monitoring data.

papers.title: Integrating social vulnerability and landslide susceptibility for spatial risk assessment in the Langat basin, Malaysia
papers.summary: Landslides are among the most significant natural hazards in Malaysia, threatening human lives, infrastructure, and socioeconomic development. This study developed an integrated landslide risk assessment framework by combining landslide susceptibility modelling and social vulnerability analysis in the Langat Basin, Malaysia. Landslide susceptibility was modelled using the Frequency Ratio (FR) approach based on six conditioning factors: elevation, slope, aspect, geology, land use, and distance to river. Social vulnerability was quantified using eight demographic and socioeconomic indicators to construct a Social Vulnerability Index (SoVI) at the level of the 14 spatial units. The SoVI results revealed considerable spatial variation, with Lenggeng (0.597), Nilai (0.586), and Putrajaya (0.475) exhibiting the highest vulnerability, whereas Morib (0.202), Sungai Pelek (0.206), and Sijangkang (0.216) showed the lowest. ROC analysis yielded an Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.800 for distinguishing the sampled landslide locations from randomly generated background points. Because the same landslide inventory was used to calculate the Frequency Ratio weights, this result should not be interpreted as independent validation of predictive performance. Integrating the SoVI and susceptibility maps in a Geographic Information System (GIS) produced a relative Landslide Risk Index (LRI) map, in which 38.91% of the basin was classified as Very Low risk and 13.64% as High to Very High risk. High-risk zones were concentrated where elevated landslide susceptibility coincided with socially vulnerable communities. The proposed framework provides a practical approach for supporting disaster risk reduction, sustainable land use planning, and community resilience in line with the Sendai Framework and Sustainable Development Goal 11.

papers.title: Antecedent rainfall patterns and situational vulnerability of victims of rainfall-induced fatal landslides in Pakistan
papers.summary: Abstract. Fatalities from rainfall-induced landslides depend not only on rainfall conditions but also on the time of occurrence, the exposure setting and demographic vulnerability. In data-scarce mountain regions such as Pakistan, event-scale rainfall histories and individual casualty records have long been disconnected. This study places event-scale rainfall and individual victim circumstances within a single event catalogue, characterises antecedent rainfall patterns and tests whether they explain fatality magnitude, in order to inform scenario-based early warning in data-scarce mountains. Based on a 2004–2024 catalogue of rainfall-induced fatal landslides in Pakistan (positioned as a lower-bound estimate because flood–landslide–debris-flow–building-collapse cascades mask landslide-attributed deaths), 213 of 250 events with spatial accuracy levels I–II were matched to CHIRPS 0.05° daily rainfall, and individual attributes of 309 fatalities during 2018–2024 were compiled. Results show that 53.5 % of events have zero event-day rainfall in CHIRPS; among four antecedent-rainfall types defined by event-day and 7-day antecedent rainfall, the low-event-day-rainfall types C and D together account for 86.4 %, and sensitivity tests using 15/40, 20/50 and 25/60 mm boundaries give 81.2–89.7 %, indicating robustness to the classification boundaries. The intensity–duration quantile relations share a common exponent of −0.59, yet no rainfall metric correlates significantly with per-event fatality. Victim records show that 66.0 % of deaths with known setting occurred indoors and 74.5 % of those with known timing occurred at night, making the night–indoor combination the most concentrated exposure; both gender and age are significantly associated with exposure setting (χ² = 28.61, Cramér's V = 0.367; χ² = 35.34, V = 0.362; p < 0.001), and the setting–timing association is also significant (χ² = 70.87, df = 2, p < 0.001, V = 0.594). papers.title: Biopolymer-based sustainable stabilization using xanthan gum–cement composite for slope soil from Lohaghat, India
papers.summary: Climate change intensifies rainfall-induced landslides, necessitating sustainable ground improvement alternatives to carbon-intensive cement. This study innovatively employs the biopolymer xanthan gum to stabilize soil from a vulnerable slope in Lohaghat, India. A comprehensive evaluation of mechanical, durability and microstructural properties was conducted. Xanthan gum was added at dosages from 0.25% to 2.5% by soil weight, with 1% xanthan gum selected as the engineering optimum because it provided the most balanced overall engineering performance. Durability testing through six wetting–drying cycles showed moderate mass loss but maintained a substantial proportion of its initial strength and remained stronger than the untreated soil. Scanning electron microscopy and X-ray diffraction analyses confirmed a physical stabilization mechanism. To further enhance the performance, a novel composite was created by adding low cement content (2–6%) to the optimal biopolymer mix. This xanthan-cement combined effect increased unconfined compressive strength and cohesion. The findings demonstrate that xanthan gum and its hybrid composite provide an effective, eco-friendly slope stabilization solution. The proposed xanthan gum–cement composite demonstrated enhanced mechanical performance under the investigated laboratory conditions and contributes to the growing body of research on biopolymer-based stabilization for more sustainable geotechnical applications.

papers.title: Ensemble frequency ratio-maximum entropy landslide susceptibility modelling for climate‑resilient road corridors in Bocas del Toro and Chiriquí, Panama
papers.summary: Landslides are a major rainfall-triggered hazard affecting road infrastructure across the mountainous terrain of western Panama. This study develops an ensemble Frequency Ratio (FR)-Maximum Entropy (MaxEnt) modelling framework to assess landslide susceptibility, identify critical management zones, and determine key drivers of slope failure along road corridors in the mainland districts of Bocas del Toro and along the Rambala-Hornito-David route. Within a 1,000 m corridor buffer, 87 mapped landslides (63 for training and 24 for validation) and 15 environmental conditioning factors were used to develop and validate the FR and MaxEnt models. An AUC-weighted linear combination of the independently calibrated FR and MaxEnt models was used to generate the ensemble susceptibility map. The ensemble delineated 9.67% and 3.99% of the corridor as high and very high susceptibility, respectively, achieving the highest predictive performance (AUC = 0.945) and outperforming the FR (0.873) and MaxEnt (0.943) models. Sensitivity analyses based on alternative training-validation partitions (57:30 and 70:17) produced consistently good performance (prediction-rate AUC > 0.88), indicating that the principal findings were not strongly influenced by the inventory allocation. Hotspot analysis identified three major clusters of elevated susceptibility and confirmed statistically significant spatial clustering at the 95% and 99% confidence levels. More than 71 km of primary roads intersect high-susceptibility zones, with Hornito, Bajo Cedro, and Valle de Agua Arriba exhibiting the greatest exposure. Slope gradient and NDVI were identified as the most influential predictors. These findings provide a practical basis for prioritising monitoring, slope stabilisation, drainage improvement, and ecosystem-based interventions to strengthen the resilience of road infrastructure in tropical mountain environments. Future work should incorporate larger landslide inventories, event-based rainfall informa

papers.title: Chemical weathering progress and whole-rock mineral assemblage changes associated with slope geo-hazards in Guangdong, China
papers.summary: The geochemical and mineralogical processes underlying the mechanical weakening of rock and soil in subtropical South China remain insufficiently quantified. We evaluated lithology-dependent chemical weathering as an intrinsic background for collapses and landslides in northern and eastern Guangdong, China, coupling 6,841 mapped hazard sites with X-ray fluorescence and whole-rock X-ray diffraction (XRD) analyses of 40 samples from 11 sites. Igneous-rock areas show higher total hazard density (13.58 vs. 9.49 sites/100 km²) and 1.9-fold higher collapse density than sedimentary-rock areas. After correction for silicate CaO (CaO*) using measured P₂O₅, igneous products have site-balanced means (site means averaged equally) of 88.3 for the chemical index of alteration (CIA) and 71.9 for parent-rock-normalized CIA-rate, versus 85.0 and 21.7 for sedimentary products. CIA distributions overlap despite a modest sample-level difference (exact p = 0.043), whereas CIA-rate separates the product groups completely (exact p = 1.0 × 10⁻⁷). Whole-rock assemblages show feldspar depletion, quartz persistence and kaolinite enrichment in igneous products. Sedimentary products, with each subtype represented by one site, remain heterogeneous because of inherited 2:1 clay minerals and framework grains. Mineral-ratio differences within the conservative XRD sensitivity envelopes are not interpreted. These patterns characterize lithology-specific weathered materials associated with regional hazards; the observational design does not establish independent causal contributions. CIA-rate expresses normalized differences from selected lithology-specific parent-material baselines. Mineral ratios support interpretation of relative weathering intensity in the sampled igneous rocks. In sedimentary rocks, they serve only as lithology-sensitive descriptors of mineral assemblages.

papers.title: Brief communication: Landsifier 2 – Python-based Software for Automated Landslide Type Classification
papers.summary: Abstract. Most mapped landslide inventories lack movement-type and trigger information, limiting their value for process-based research and hazard assessment. Here, we present Landsifier 2, an open-source Python library that enriches polygon inventories using three-dimensional geometry, topological descriptors, and configurable classification. Building on our existing trigger identification, this revamped library adds movement-type prediction, customizable classes, and geospatial outputs with class probabilities. Applications to independently labelled and previously undocumented inventories demonstrate its flexibility. Landsifier 2 provides a reproducible means of transforming landslide inventories into informative datasets for comparative geomorphology and hazard assessment.

papers.title: Physics-Informed Multimodal Graph-Temporal Network with Closed-Loop Hydro-Mechanical Equilibrium Correction for Dynamic Slope Stability Prediction under Rainfall-Vegetation-Soil Coupling
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Overview Rainfall-induced shallow landslides on vegetated hillslopes are governed by nonlinear feedbacks among canopy interception, root water uptake, capillary hysteresis, and moisture-dependent root reinforcement. Purely data-driven sequence models frequently violate water mass conservation and wetting suction monotonicity during intense rainstorms. Conversely, open-loop soft-penalty physics-informed networks overlook scanning-curve hysteresis, near-saturation root slippage, and preferential macropore bypass. We present PIM-RVSNet, a Physics-Informed Multimodal (PIM) graph-temporal network with closed-loop hydro-mechanical equilibrium correction for dynamic Factor of Safety (F_s) and instability lead-time forecasting. PIM-RVSNet integrates three coupled stages: (1) a Multimodal Cross-Scale Eco-Hydrological Encoder (MC-EHE) using Depth-Directed Eco-Hydrological Cross-Attention (DEH-CA) and vertical graph-recurrent message passing to align atmospheric forcing, canopy-root traits, and four-layer soil profiles; (2) a Differentiable Richards-Wu-Mohr-Coulomb Coupled Operator (RWMC-Op) embedding van Genuchten scanning hysteresis and saturation-attenuated root cohesion; and (3) a Closed-Loop Hydro-Mechanical Equilibrium Correction (HMEC) module combining Mass-Balance Projection, Macropore Bypass Gating, and Suction-Equilibrium Calibration over three damped proximal steps. Evaluated on a calibrated two-dimensional multi-slice coupled seepage and limit-equilibrium hillslope benchmark (48 slope units, 240 storm episodes, and 2,880 states across four eco-geomorphic zones), PIM-RVSNet achieves test R^2 = 0.9856 ± 0.0001, RMSE_F_s = 0.0533 ± 0.0001, F1_crit = 0.9381 ± 0.0026, 1.71 h pre-onset warning lead time, and 2.08% Physical Consistency Violation Rate (PVR), outperforming eight baselines under slope-unit cluster inference. Contents This record contains 16 files. The table lists every data table in the archive with its row count. FileRowsSize (KB)data/benchmark/episode_time

papers.title: Shear Strength of Unsaturated Organic Clay across Natural Dry-Density Gradients from Landslide Sites in Bogor, Indonesia
papers.summary: Rainfall-induced landslides in tropical regions are closely linked to the loss of apparent cohesion as unsaturated soils approach saturation. This study examines how the apparent cohesion (c′) and internal friction angle (φ′) of unsaturated organic clay respond to variations in natural dry density (γd) across a range of degrees of saturation (Sr), using natural dry density values obtained from three actual landslide sites in Bogor, Indonesia, rather than from laboratory-compacted specimens. A total of 231 direct shear tests (3 sites × 7 specimens × 3 normal-stress levels × 3–4 repetitions) and 42 filter-paper tests (3 sites × 7 specimens × 2 repetitions) were performed on remolded specimens reconstituted to in-situ γd values at seven Sr levels. The results reveal four main findings. The three soils have very low and uniform air-entry values (1.52–2.09 kPa), so the suction contribution is lost soon after infiltration. Apparent cohesion does not decrease monotonically but peaks at intermediate saturation (44–56%), with peak values tiered according to density (10.60; 6.30; 4.69 kPa). c′ and φ′ respond to Sr through different mechanisms: c′ peaks while φ′ decreases monotonically. The cohesion advantage of the densest soil, prominent under moist conditions, vanishes near saturation, where the cohesion of the three densities converges to a nearly identical low value. A multiple linear regression model, c′ = 16.162·γd − 0.089·Sr − 5.076, is proposed as a practical estimator. These findings imply that initial density alone does not guarantee slope stability under heavy rainfall.

papers.title: Reproducibility archive for "Rain-gauge quality and record continuity as limits on rainfall inputs for landslide early warning"
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Code and derived data that reproduce the landslide analyses, sensitivity tests and figures of a manuscript under review in Landslides. The archive contains hourly dual-gauge (tipping-bucket and weighing) classes for the AMOS mountain network, hourly weather-radar rainfall at stations and landslide cells, and the analysis scripts (Python). run_all.py reruns all steps and writes a verification report. Raw 10-min records and raw radar composites are not redistributed. Access to the files is restricted during peer review. Code: PolyForm Noncommercial License 1.0.0. Derived data: CC BY 4.0. papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: This repository provides the reference PyTorch implementation, training pipelines, and deterministic evaluation scripts for PIM-RVSNet (Physics-Informed Multimodal Graph-Temporal Network with Closed-Loop Hydro-Mechanical Equilibrium Correction for Dynamic Slope Stability Prediction under Rainfall–Vegetation–Soil Coupling). Core Modules pim_rvsnet/model.py: Multimodal Cross-Scale Eco-Hydrological Encoder (MC-EHE, Stage 1) with Depth-Directed Eco-Hydrological Cross-Attention (DEH-CA), vertical HorizonGraphTemporalBackbone, and full PIMRVSNet architecture. pim_rvsnet/physics_operators.py: Differentiable Richards–Wu–Mohr–Coulomb Coupled Operator (RWMC-Op, Stage 2) embedding van Genuchten scanning hysteresis, Janbu obliquity-corrected column equilibrium, and moisture-attenuated Wu–Waldron root cohesion. pim_rvsnet/agent_verifier.py: Closed-Loop Hydro-Mechanical Equilibrium Correction (HMEC, Stage 3) incorporating Mass-Balance Projection, Macropore Bypass Gating, and Suction-Equilibrium Calibration along a damped proximal trajectory. pim_rvsnet/baselines.py: Competing baseline architectures (PIDL-Landslide, PGNN-3DSlope, PIML-Suscept, ST-GNN-Trans, Backbone-Only, XGB-HydroMech, Persistence-HYDRUS1D, and Naive-Persistence). pim_rvsnet/metrics.py: Evaluation metrics ($R^2$, RMSE, MAE, F1_crit, AUROC, failure warning lead time, physical consistency violation rate, mass balance error, and cluster-bootstrap statistics). Execution and Reproduction reproduce.py: Deterministic evaluation script computing all derived summary tables in data/derived/ directly from benchmark observations and model predictions. scripts/train_and_evaluate.py: End-to-end training, hyperparameter validation grid search, multi-seed evaluation, and autoregressive rollout pipeline. scripts/make_figures.py: Deterministic plotting script generating all publication figures (Figure 2 through Figure 8). tests/test_suite.py: Unit verification test suite covering gradients, flux conservation, and deterministic rep

papers.title: Unreported mass movement cascades and future Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) hazard in Jammu and Kashmir, Western Himalaya
papers.source: Natural hazards and earth system sciences
papers.summary: Abstract. The Warwan sub-basin in Jammu and Kashmir is a remote glaciated region containing several glacial lakes and has recently experienced population growth and infrastructure development. Due to inaccessibility and geomorphic masking, multiple mass movement events including avalanches and Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs) have remained largely unreported. This study analyzes three major avalanche events from the past two decades. The September 2005 and September 2020 avalanches originated from glaciers GL-B and GL-A within the same glacier complex, while the March 2020 rock–ice avalanche initiated from the headwall of glacier GL-F in an adjacent valley and terminated before reaching its ablation zone. Runout mapping shows that the September 2020 avalanche descended from the headwall of GL-A and impacted its proglacial lake, triggering a GLOF. In contrast, the September 2005 event terminated before reaching the glacial lake that began forming in 1999 at the terminus of GL-B. Geomorphic analysis indicates persistent sediment influx from meltwater streams of GL-D and GL-E into the lake associated with GL-A, progressively infilling the basin. Continued glacier retreat caused meltwater to accumulate behind the sediment infill, dividing the basin into two disconnected lakes. Impact from the September 2020 avalanche led to complete drainage of stored water and sediment, generating a downstream debris flow. Pre- and post-GLOF imagery reveals breaching and widening of the outflow channel and deposition of a debris fan downstream. The repeated history of mass movements and continued growth of glacial lakes raise serious hazard concerns in the Warwan sub-basin. GLOF modeling identifies Lake-B as potentially hazardous lake at the present condition posing significant downstream risk. Settlements such as Youdu and Qaderna, along with bridges, roads, and residential structures, lie within potential GLOF inundation zones. High sediment availability from past mobilization an

papers.title: MPM modelling of impact-loading shallow flow-like landslides in unsaturated slopes
papers.summary: Debris avalanches (DA) pose severe hazards in urbanized piedmont areas due to their large runout and potential for progressive volume increase through bed entrainment. Impact-loading mechanisms at bedrock outcrops can trigger cascading slope failures, yet the conditions controlling whether a small initial instability arrests or evolves into a catastrophic debris avalanche remain poorly understood.,This study proposes a hydro-mechanical framework for impact-induced debris avalanche inception, integrating an energy-based interpretation of the interaction between a moving saturated mass and a downslope unsaturated deposit. An advanced Material Point Method (MPM) model is developed to simulate the coupled evolution of stresses, pore water pressures, and deformations during the impact and afterwards. The simulations reproduce the loading exerted by the incoming mass and capture the progressive response of the impacted slope. Results show that the abrupt deceleration of the impacting mass leads to rapid pore pressure buildup in the impact zone and stress redistribution in successive downslope volumes. The evolution of kinetic energy reveals progressive energy transfer from the moving mass to the impacted soil, governing whether the instability is arrested or propagates downslope.,The parametric analysis demonstrates that initial soil suction in the impacted slope is the most important parameter controlling debris avalanche inception. Cases with low initial suction exhibit sustained energy transfer, progressive volume mobilization, and debris avalanche development with large volume amplification factors. In contrast, cases with higher suction dissipate kinetic energy rapidly after impact, arresting the cascading process with limited volume growth. Variations in basal friction angle, deposit thickness, and initial mass size have secondary effects. These findings provide an interpretation of impact-induced debris avalanche inception in unsaturated pyroclastic slopes, with im

papers.title: Multi-hazard assessment of the eastern slope of the Sistema de Famatina, La Rioja province (Argentina)
papers.summary: Abstract In the eastern sector of the Sistema de Famatina, both natural processes and anthropogenic activities pose considerable risks to the landscape and its inhabitants. This study investigates the geohazards and environmental agents that have historically affected the region, with a focus on their implications for local communities and territories. The analysis integrates case studies of documented natural events, identification of mitigation strategies, satellite imagery interpretation, landform recognition, and direct field observations. In addition, meteorological, hydrological, seismic, and demographic data were compiled to identify previously undocumented events with the potential to generate significant socio-environmental impacts. The study area is subject to a range of natural hazards, including those originated by meteorological events (e.g., intense precipitation and strong winds), fluvial processes (e.g., avulsion, gully erosion, and flooding), mass movement processes (e.g., landslides and rockfalls), and seismic activity. Our results reveal the recurrent nature of these hazards; in general, their consequences are compounded by anthropogenic pressures, including land-use changes, variations in land cover, and environmental pollution. Collectively, these factors intensify existing socio-environmental issues. This research contributes to sustainable environmental management by considering plausible future scenarios and hazard interactions. Our findings are intended to inform local and regional socio-economic development strategies and to serve as a scientific resource for policymakers and planners. Furthermore, by enhancing awareness of ongoing and recurring hazards, the study supports community resilience building and the reduction of adverse impacts at the local level.

papers.title: Time-Lapse Three-Dimensional TEM Imaging and Damage Evolution of Hydraulic Fracturing in Landslide Fracture Zones
papers.summary: Landslide fracture zones play a critical role in slope instability, yet their hydraulic fracturing processes remain difficult to monitor using conventional geophysical methods. This study proposes a time‐lapse three‐dimensional transient electromagnetic (TEM) imaging approach to characterize fracture damage evolution in the Xiaolongdong–Xiahaizi landslide, Zhaotong City, China. Repeated TEM observations, integrated with GNSS displacement monitoring and environmental measurements, were used to reconstruct dynamic resistivity fields through three‐dimensional inversion. The method achieved localization accuracies better than 1 m horizontally and 2 m vertically and detected water‐filled fractures wider than 0.3 mm. Distinct resistivity precursor anomalies, characterized by a 3%–8% increase followed by a rapid decrease, occurred 2–5 min before fracture propagation. During hydraulic fracturing, resistivity decreased from 30–50 Ω·m to 8–15 Ω·m, reflecting progressive fracture connectivity. Rainy‐season permeability coefficients reached 10⁻⁴–10⁻³ m/s, one to two orders of magnitude higher than those during the dry season. Freeze–thaw processes and rainfall infiltration jointly contributed 25%–35% of slope displacement. The proposed framework provides quantitative visualization of fracture evolution and effective geophysical constraints for landslide stability assessment and early warning.

papers.title: Early warning system for non-seismic gravity driven tsunamis
papers.summary: Gravity-driven mass flows represent a significant near-field hazard in volcanic environments and, increasingly, in coastal regions affected by climate-driven slope instability. Despite their destructive potential, quantitative assessments of real-time detection systems operating under natural conditions remain scarce. Here we present the performance and sensitivity of the tsunami early-warning system currently operating at Stromboli Volcano (Italy), based on offshore pressure gauges and a real-time detection algorithm. Sixteen years of sea-level records (2010–2026), including 63 tsunamis events ranging from 0.02 to 2 m height, show that the system issues alert within less than 22 s from the tsunami onset and tens of seconds before its maximum amplitude, with no false alarms. A sensitivity analysis, based on Peak-Over-Threshold statistics and extreme wave modeling, demonstrates that the detection capability remains effective even under extreme sea state conditions also for tsunami with height as low as 4 m. To support regional tsunami warning and reduce the alerts for tsunami with no inundation effects on a distant (> 10 km) coasts, we apply real-time Ensemble Empirical Mode Decomposition (EEMD), which successfully extracts tsunami signals and preserves waveform characteristics. EEMD also isolates longer period sea level oscillations associated with atmospheric pressure waves within the meteotsunami frequency band, demonstrating the applicability of the method to multiple classes of non-seismic tsunamis. This work provides the first long-term quantitative evaluation of an operational near-field early-warning system for volcanogenic tsunamis and proposes a transferable multi-tier framework for landslide-tsunami and meteotsunami hazard mitigation for coastal environments worldwide.

papers.title: Role of Reforestation in Reducing Landslide Risk in Galyat, Pakistan: A Remote Sensing and GIS-Based Temporal Analysis (2011–2025)
papers.summary: Landslides are among the most common natural hazards in mountainous regions, often resulting in loss of life, damage to infrastructure, and destruction of agricultural land. Forest cover plays an important role in slope stabilization, soil erosion control, and landslide-risk reduction; however, empirical evidence regarding this relationship in specific mountainous landscapes remains limited. This study investigates the relationship between vegetation change and landslide occurrence in the Galyat region of Pakistan from 2011 to 2025. Remote sensing and Geographic Information System (GIS) techniques were used to derive the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) from Landsat 5, 8, and 9 imagery for 2011, 2017, and 2025. These data were compared with a landslide inventory digitised from high?resolution Google Earth Pro imagery for the corresponding years. Mean NDVI decreased from 0.355 in 2011 to 0.181 in 2017 before increasing slightly to 0.197 in 2025. Landslide frequency decreased from 125 events in 2011 to 52 in 2017 and then increased to 76 in 2025. In contrast, total landslide-affected area increased from 55.78 ha in 2011 to 93.26 ha in 2017 and 98.38 ha in 2025. These contrasting trends indicate that vegetation condition alone does not explain changes in landslide activity in Galyat. Reforestation should therefore be considered alongside rainfall, slope characteristics, geology, and land-use change within an integrated landslide-risk reduction strategy. The study also demonstrates the usefulness of remote sensing and GIS for monitoring vegetation and landslide dynamics in data-scarce mountainous regions.

papers.title: Creep deformation until failure under constant water content in sandy model slope
papers.summary: The measurement of displacement on slopes under excavation or rainfall revealed that the displacement increased not only during excavation or rainfall but also afterward. The increase in displacement after stress loading can be identified as creep displacement under constant stress. However, the conditions for the generation of creep displacements are still unknown. To this end, inclined direct shear tests were conducted under constant stress and rainfall infiltration, and the measured data were analyzed to examine the conditions for creep displacement generation under rainfall infiltration. In some cases, shear displacement grew under constant volumetric water content (VWC) just prior to failure, but not in other cases. In the latter cases, shear displacement grew with increasing VWC. An accelerating increase in shear displacement just prior to failure—referred to as tertiary creep—could be observed in all cases in which shear displacement increased under constant VWC; meanwhile, a decelerating increase in shear displacement just after the start of the constant VWC duration—referred to as primary creep—could not be observed in some cases. The creep displacement normalized by all shear displacements until failure was larger when the increase in VWC corresponding to the shear displacement during soil absorption was greater. Thus, a larger increase in VWC corresponding to shear displacement during the absorption process is a condition for the generation of creep displacement under constant VWC. Primary creep displacement developed under the condition of no normal displacement, indicating a steady state in the shear zone. The primary creep displacement was greater for cases with a higher initial velocity at the start of the constant VWC duration. Thus, the absence of an increase in normal displacement under constant VWC may be a condition for the generation of primary creep, and a larger primary creep might be generated with a larger initial displacement velocity at th

papers.title: LGSTNet: Efficient Local–Global Collaboration for Heterogeneous Remote-Sensing Landslide Segmentation
papers.summary: Purpose: Landslide segmentation from remote sensing imagery is challenged by scale variation, irregular morphology, blurred boundaries, and confusion with spectrally similar backgrounds. This study aims to develop an efficient framework that coordinates heterogeneous input regulation, local structural preservation, and hierarchical semantic modeling. Methods: LGSTNet is organized around two coupled design principles. An input-configuration-oriented local–global encoder combines input recalibration, a shallow Ghost branch, and a compact three-stage Swin Transformer. An accuracy–efficiency-oriented compressed context-fusion strategy enhances the deepest Transformer feature through compressed multi-scale, directional, and global context branches and integrates multi-level representations using a lightweight projection–fusion decoder. Results: Experiments were conducted on the Jiuzhai Valley, HR-GLDD, and Landslide4Sense datasets. On Landslide4Sense, LGSTNet achieved the best F1-score, foreground intersection over union (IoU), mean IoU (mIoU), and Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) among the seven evaluated models, reaching 64.01%, 47.07%, 72.81%, and 63.39%, respectively, with 3.79 M parameters, 2.39 G FLOPs, and 63.93 frames per second. On HR-GLDD and Jiuzhai Valley, it provided competitive segmentation performance with favorable inference efficiency, although it did not outperform every baseline. A within-dataset input-configuration experiment on Landslide4Sense further showed that the F1-score of LGSTNet increased from 42.87% with RGB input to 64.01% with the full fourteen-channel input; SegFormer exhibited the same overall trend, increasing from 42.50% to 61.56%. Conclusions: LGSTNet provides a favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-off across the three evaluated remote-sensing configurations. The within-dataset input-configuration results provide additional evidence that the complete system can benefit from the information available in the full multi-channel inpu

papers.title: Spatiotemporal Evolution, Co-Sensitivity Hotspots, and Robustness of Multi-Process Composite Ecological Sensitivity in an Alpine Mountain Region: A Case Study of Aba Prefecture, China
papers.summary: Alpine mountain regions are shaped by interacting ecological processes. Using Aba Prefecture on the eastern Qinghai–Tibet Plateau as a case study, we derived sensitivity indices for desertification, soil erosion, landslide disaster, freeze–thaw erosion, and habitat quality for six selected study years between 2000 and 2024, and integrated them into a composite ecological sensitivity index (CESI) using the spatial distance index. We assessed class transitions, trajectories, multiscale clustering, co-sensitivity hotspots, county-level and elevation-stratified patterns, and robustness. The results showed that: (1) mean CESI rose slightly from 1.483 to 1.487, indicating marginally weaker sensitivity, but fell to 1.427 in 2020; (2) 75.86% of the area retained its initial class, with persistent low, stable moderate, and persistent high trajectories covering 48.65%, 9.29%, and 15.37%, respectively, while spatial clustering weakened at coarser scales; (3) persistent co-sensitivity hotspots covered 2900.93 km2, the dominant 2024 combination was desertification–soil erosion–freeze–thaw erosion, and over 97% of highly and extremely sensitive areas and hotspots occurred above 4000 m, indicating a pronounced concentration of ecological sensitivity and co-sensitivity hotspots in high-elevation areas; and (4) continuous sensitivity gradients were robust, whereas class assignments and high-sensitivity boundaries were more responsive to factor composition, aggregation, and scale. The findings can inform spatial planning, the prioritization of environmental monitoring and field assessment, and differentiated ecological management in alpine mountain regions.

papers.title: Case studies on IoT monitoring of debris flow and landslides
papers.summary: Aiming at the critical demand for real-time monitoring of slope disasters in mountainous and urbanized regions, this study develops Internet of Things (IoT)-based real-time monitoring systems to resolve the issues of data delay and fragmentation in conventional manual monitoring. Through three engineering cases conducted by the authors, we demonstrate the adaptability of IoT technology in slope disaster monitoring under different instability mechanisms (debris flows and landslides) and geological conditions (artificial-reinforced and semi-natural slopes). Specifically, in Case 1, a novel IoT monitoring system for debris flows integrated with the structural characteristics of rigid barriers is proposed. In Cases 2 and 3, multi-type monitoring sensors and equipment are deployed, including deformation sensors, rainfall gauges and video surveillance devices, to achieve accurate early warnings of rainfall-induced landslides. The novelty of this work lies in proposing a unified IoT architecture scheme applicable to different types of slope disasters. This scheme systematically integrates physico-mechanical sensing devices, a solar-battery collaborative power supply system, video monitoring equipment, data transmission methods, early warning modes, and a cloud-based processing module. Furthermore, the effectiveness of the proposed scheme is validated via successful early warning cases, and this scheme provides an effective technical framework for slope disaster prevention and control.

papers.title: Donald Trump’s Republicans suffer landslide defeat – what this means for the world
When Geology Behaves Badly, Big Fixes Are Needed: Part 1
papers.summary: The Pipestem Dam spillway, located near Jamestown, North Dakota, was undergoing a spillway rehabilitation to address the risk driving failure mode of spillway erosion starting in 2023. The design included approach channel excavation, approach channel armouring, labyrinth weir control structure, and roller compact concrete (RCC) terminal structure and stilling basin. In the spring of 2024, final excavation for the RCC terminal structure resumed. Immediately following excavation to near final grade, a landslide occurred on the right side of the terminal structure. After rigorous analysis, geologic conditions were identified which led to the landslide. The root causes for the landslide were isolated to the right side of the terminal structure excavation. Construction continued on the weir control structure and left side of the terminal structure. This paper will discuss the investigations, geologic conditions, site characterization, observations before and during construction, along with dewatering, geologic conditions, root cause, and lessons learned related to the landslide. The paper will also address the complex geologic conditions and the theory that resulted in the geologic conditions. Part 2 of this paper will discuss the repair of the landslide and other associated construction sequencing modifications to reduce downstream life safety risk.

papers.title: Design and Construction of a Retaining Wall on the Miller Creek Landslide, I-70 West Vail Pass Auxiliary Lanes Project, Eagle County, Colorado
papers.summary: In 2021, design work began for a Colorado Department of Transportation project to improve a 10-mile stretch of Interstate 70 (I-70) from the Town of Vail to the summit of Vail Pass. The project included design and construction of a 1,150-ft-long, 5-tiered soil nail wall (CP3 Wall 1) located at the toe of the Miller Creek Landslide, a large landslide complex first investigated during initial construction of I-70 in the 1970s. The primary geotechnical challenge for the design and construction of CP3 Wall 1 was maintaining stability of the wall and landslide under elevated groundwater conditions. This paper will discuss the background of the project, stability and seepage analyses conducted during the design of the CP3 Wall 1, the use of temporary and permanent horizontal drains, and geotechnical instrumentation data used to evaluate conditions during construction.

papers.title: Interpretable Landslide Susceptibility Mapping in Pacitan, Indonesia Using Bayesian-Optimized XGBoost and SHAP Analysis
papers.summary: Background: Landslide susceptibility mapping is essential in areas with complex topographic and geological conditions, such as Pacitan Regency, Indonesia, to identify landslide-prone areas and assess the factors influencing landslide susceptibility. Objective: This study developed a landslide susceptibility mapping model using Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), optimized through Bayesian optimization and interpreted using the SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) method. Methods: The dataset consisted of 1,486 samples, comprising 743 landslide occurrence points and 743 non-landslide points. Eleven landslide conditioning factors were used as predictor variables: elevation, aspect, slope, geology, land use, profile curvature, plan curvature, distance to roads, distance to rivers, Stream Power Index (SPI), and Topographic Wetness Index (TWI). Model hyperparameter optimization was performed using Bayesian optimization with a Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE). Results: The optimized XGBoost model achieved an accuracy of 69.80%, a precision of 70.34%, a recall of 68.46%, an F1 score of 69.39%, and a receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC) of 0.7564 on the independent test set. The resulting susceptibility map classified the study area into five categories: very low, low, moderate, high, and very high susceptibility. SHAP analysis identified slope, aspect, plan curvature, geology, and distance to roads as the dominant factors influencing model predictions. Conclusion: Integrating Bayesian optimization, XGBoost, and SHAP provides an interpretable approach to landslide susceptibility mapping in Pacitan Regency. The resulting susceptibility map and feature-level explanations can support preliminary disaster risk assessment and spatial planning. However, residual classification errors and limitations associated with the use of static environmental predictors should be considered when interpreting the results.

papers.title: InSAR-based stability assessment of creep-type landslides: A case study in the Wudongde Reservoir area

papers.title: Quantifying spatiotemporal heterogeneity in landslide deformation using an improved graph deep learning framework for reliable displacement forecasting
LAND CARRYING CAPACITY, WATER SAFETY, AND COMMUNITY HEALTH UNDER POPULATION PRESSURE: A MULTIDISCIPLINARY ASSESSMENT OF HILLSIDE SETTLEMENT IN NEGERI BATU MERAH, AMBON, INDONESIA
papers.summary: Background Small island cities grow on scarce, steep, and hazard-prone land. Negeri Batu Merah, a customary village in Ambon City, is classified as a heavy slum area with 66,424 people on 911 ha. Its dense settlement relies on septic tanks and shallow wells, linking land limits to water safety, and maternal and child health. This study assesses Batu Merah’s land-carrying capacity, measures how existing settlements are distributed across it, and interprets the results for engineering, water safety, community health, access, and spatial governance. Methods Nine land capability units were analyzed following Minister of Public Works Regulation No. 20/PRT/M/2007 and converted into potential, limitation, and constraint zones. Settlement from the 2018 national land cover map is overlaid on these zones and each unit. Published water quality and health studies on Ambon were compiled, and the results were interpreted from eight disciplines, including chemistry, global health, and midwifery. Results The village had moderately high (56.14%), moderate (42.87%), and low land capability (0.99%). Settlement covers 600.61 ha at about 110 persons per settled hectare. The potential zone was 96.5% built-up, and the constraint zone was almost entirely. All 97.67 ha of settlement in the limitation zone stands on land with low foundation stability, moderate slope stability, and a moderately high hazard potential. The waste disposal capability was only moderate under 77.6% of settlement. The Wai Batu Merah River exceeds the national standard for ammonia and coliforms, and in Batu Merah, poor water, sanitation, and hygiene conditions increase the odds of stunting in children under two 2.7-fold. Conclusions Future growth will move onto land requiring specific technical measures. Controlling this requires explicit zoning requirements, communal wastewater treatment, monitoring of wells and refill depots, maternal and child health services that reach hillside neighborhoods, and the involvement

papers.title: Linking climate projections with farmer perspectives to inform agricultural adaptation in northern Tanzania
papers.summary: While there is growing evidence about how African farmers are adapting to climate change, there remains a lack of research highlighting direct linkages between future climate scenarios, impacts on agriculture, and viable adaptation strategies. To address this gap, our research objectives are to understand how farmers in Tanzania perceive (1) climate change-impacts, (2) current adaptation strategies and future adaptation options given climate scenarios. First, we modeled future climate scenarios with a focus on temperature and precipitation. Second, we directly integrated these scenarios into a survey of 125 farmers; eliciting crop-specific concerns and targeted adaptation options given future climate scenarios. Third, we conducted 12 qualitative farmer interviews to interpret the survey findings. Key study findings highlighted farmer concerns about high wind events, as well as excessive precipitation and drought. However, farmer concerns about future climate scenarios varied by crop type, with some impacts perceived as beneficial. Overall, 73.5% of survey respondents perceived not having implemented any climate change-specific adaptation strategies, and interviewees highlighted a lack of climate services, training, and extension staff as a major adaptation barrier. In the future, about 30% of respondents said they would like to implement soil and water conservation practices, such as berms and terraces, to avoid soil erosion during extreme precipitation events. Our findings suggest that increased access to context-specific climate information services, combined with agricultural extension programs, may have practical implications for effective, informed adaptation responses. Our study also provides an example of integrating climate modeling and social science research methods. Practical implications In this study, we integrate climate projections into an analysis of climate change impacts and adaptation options for farmers in Tanzania. In these efforts, we used clim

papers.title: Landslide Susceptibility Assessment of Lixian County, Gansu Province, China Using a Physics‐Integrated Multi‐Task Neural Network
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Landslide susceptibility assessment (LSA) is a critical strategy for disaster prevention and mitigation. However, current machine learning‐based LSA algorithms often exhibit instability under data‐sparse conditions and suffer from a lack of physical interpretability. To address these challenges, this study proposes a physics‐integrated multi‐task neural network (PIMTN). The proposed framework incorporates slope‐stability information derived from the infinite slope model into a multi‐task neural network through an auxiliary learning task. The model simultaneously performs landslide susceptibility classification and learns a physics‐derived diluted probability of failure (DPOF). Through joint optimization, the auxiliary DPOF task influences the shared representation and guides susceptibility prediction towards spatial patterns consistent with physics‐derived slope‐stability information. Comparative experiments demonstrate that the PIMTN outperforms benchmark models (Precision: 0.737, F 1‐Score: 0.754, AUC: 0.817). Furthermore, quantitative analysis confirms the superiority of the proposed model and the effectiveness of knowledge transfer from the physical domain. This framework presents a novel solution for enhancing model interpretability and improving predictive robustness under limited‐inventory conditions.

papers.title: Chapter 4: Glaciogenic sediments and structures in the Port Askaig Formation on the Garvellachs and Islay
papers.summary: In this Chapter, we conduct a thorough reappraisal of evidence for glaciation in the Port Askaig Formation (PAF) based on comprehensive documentation of all exposures on the Garvellachs and parts of Islay. Diamictites and associated facies record a range of terrestrial, lacustrine and marine environments. Most massive diamictites on the Garvellachs contain structures indicating shear beneath grounded ice, including ‘stoss-lee’ clasts, strong preferred a-axis orientations, glaciotectonism of subjacent sediments, and streamlined and folded rafts, and are interpreted as subglacial traction tills and glaciotectonites. The Great Breccia on the Garvellachs and the Persabus Complex on Islay consist of folded and thrust megablocks and diamictite, interpreted as the product of proglacial glaciotectonic deformation in which permafrozen foreland materials were excavated and upthrust before being over-ridden. The PAF also contains intervals of laminated mudstones with dropstones, stratified diamictites, and interbeds of sandstone and conglomerate, interpreted as the products of subaqueous deposition in glaciolacustrine and glaciomarine environments. Glaciomarine deposition is most spectacularly recorded in the ‘Disrupted Beds’, including subaqueous fans, submarine landslides, and rain-out of ice-rafted debris. Glaciogenic facies associations exhibit systematic evolution through time, revealing the interplay of climate, glacier advance-retreat cycles and sea-level change over the course of the Sturtian panglaciation.

papers.title: Technical validation of a regional landslide forecasting system in the Eastern Himalayas
papers.summary: Rainfall-induced landslides pose a recurrent threat in the Darjeeling–Kalimpong Himalaya, India. The Geological Survey of India developed a prototype Regional Landslide Forecasting System (RLFS) that issued daily experimental forecast bulletins during the 2020–2023 monsoon seasons. Here we present the first systematic evaluation of an Indian regional landslide early warning system using the EDuMaP framework. Performance was assessed over 2,316 block-days spanning 373 monsoon days across 11 administrative units. Of 521 landslides analysed, 96.50% of block-days recorded no or only minor activity. Aggregated validation yielded 361 correct predictions, 1,862 true negatives, 19 missed alerts, and 74 false alerts. Green and yellow grades together represented 95.60% of forecast–observation pairs, with a mean combined efficiency index of 0.86 across the nine non-overlapping forecast zones. The system’s error structure was dominated by overwarning rather than catastrophic missed events. A stakeholder-driven transition to finer administrative forecast zones improved skill scores. Because the forecasts combined an automated rainfall-threshold model with expert review, the reported skill reflects this hybrid system, not the model alone.

papers.title: Was the Nepal disaster caused by a Coulomb explosion?
papers.summary: Abstract On August 26, 2006, a huge mass of rock and glacier broke off from the parent body at an altitude of approximately 5,200 metres and collapsed 1,200 metres downward. The resulting mudflow destroyed roads and bridges and flooded downstream coastal settlements along the Lende-Khola and Trishuli-Khola rivers, covering almost 100 km. Members of the intergovernmental organization "International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development" (ICIMOD), based in Kathmandu, concluded that the cause of the powerful mudflow was an avalanche of ice and rocks, not a breakout of water from a glacial lake. USGS staff reported that at the point with coordinates 28.271° N, 85.515° E, 55 km NW of Kodari̇, Nepal, a glacier collapse occurred, triggering an M5.2 earthquake and a powerful avalanche. At present (September 4, 2026), the actual cause of the disaster is unknown, but judging by similar catastrophic landslides that occurred in the past, as well as the scale of the material involved and the energy of this seismic event, it can be assumed that the cause of the landslide was a Coulomb explosion in the rock massif that served as the underlying layer for the glacier located on it. This article reveals the possible mechanism of the Coulomb explosion in the rocks and the cause of the landslide.

papers.title: Time–Cost–Quality Impact Assessment and FMEA-Based Prioritization of Geological, Environmental, and Operational Risks in Road Infrastructure Projects
papers.source: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology
papers.summary: Road infrastructure projects are exposed to geological, environmental, and operational hazards that jointly determine delivery time, cost, and quality. Risk studies and guidance often address one hazard family at a time, and hazard lists are not always converted into ranked priorities that project managers can act on. This paper presents a structured, three-stage assessment of fifteen risk factors that commonly affect road projects. First, each factor is rated for its impact on project time, cost, and quality and aggregated into a composite impact index. Second, the factors are ranked using a probability–severity matrix. Third, seven critical failure modes are prioritized using Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) with the Risk Priority Number (RPN). The results show that geological factors have the highest composite impact (mean 8.2 out of a maximum of 9), followed by operational (7.3) and environmental factors (6.5). Slope failure, earthquakes, and safety incidents are the only factors rated High on all three performance dimensions, and ten of the fifteen factors fall in the High priority tier. In the FMEA, project mismanagement (RPN 252), flooding (240), and material shortage (210) rank highest and together account for 55.5% of the total RPN. The qualitative ranking and the RPN agree on the severity of geological hazards but diverge for material supply, which illustrates the value of including detectability in prioritization. Illustrative mitigation scenarios indicate that the aggregate RPN could be reduced by roughly two-thirds if targeted controls are implemented. The ratings are judgement-based and require field validation, as discussed in the limitations

Understanding Disaster Risk and Local Response: A Study of Chhatrakot, Gulmi, Nepal
papers.source: International Journal of Advanced Business Studies
papers.summary: Natural disasters such as earthquakes, floods, and landslides in Nepal continue to pose a significant threat to the lives of people in the rural hills and mountains. This study focuses on the vulnerability, preparedness, and mitigation measures of natural disasters among the inhabitants of Chhatrakot-4, Gulmi. The researchers adopted a mixed-methods research design by analyzing existing policies and field observations, and engaging local actors to generate findings on the general status of natural disasters, major causes, and mitigation measures in the area. It is found that Chhatrakot-4, Gulmi, is highly vulnerable to natural disasters due to poor infrastructure, ineffective early warning systems, insufficient disaster preparedness, lack of coordination among local agencies, and other human-related factors. This study recommends that community-based disaster management coupled with strengthening of institutional coordination, improvement in infrastructure, and community education should be prioritized in order to reduce the negative impacts of natural disasters. It was also found that active community participation and local initiative, as well as collaboration between government and non-governmental organizations, can lead to improved disaster preparedness and management capacity in the area. These results suggest that disaster risk reduction requires a comprehensive response that promotes community-based initiatives as well as effective coordination at the local institutional level. The study contributes to the existing body of knowledge on climate change adaptation and disaster risk reduction by providing policy recommendations for local government, development partners, and other stakeholders to consider.

papers.title: When Geology Behaves Badly, Big Fixes Are Needed: Part 2
papers.summary: In the spring of 2024, a landslide occurred in the roller compacted concrete (RCC) terminal structure excavation for the Pipestem Dam Spillway project. This paper will build upon and present the engineering and construction solutions to address the landslide presented in Part 1. The solutions not only needed to consider worker safety during repair of the landslide and long term performance of the repair, but also protection of completed construction work, incremental downstream life safety risk in its interim condition, and minimization of cost and schedule impacts. Topics related to the repair of the landslide will include investigations, analyses, contracting approach, design, and construction of a soldier pile lagging wall with tie backs. Evaluations were performed to confirm the repair would not adversely impact the performance of the completed terminal structure and associated drainage system.

papers.title: Peace Communication in the Transformation of Environmental Conflict: A Positive Peace Framework for a Just Transition at the Bantargebang Integrated Waste Processing Facility, Bekasi City
papers.summary: This article develops an evidence-sensitive framework for assessing how peace communication may contribute to environmental conflict transformation at the Bantargebang Integrated Waste Processing Facility in Bekasi City, Indonesia. The analysis addresses limits of compensation-centered responses by connecting communication practices with bargaining power, institutional accountability, and material remediation as criteria for positive peace. An integrative-critical review synthesizes 40 academic, legal, policy, and official sources considered through October 2026, using Galtung’s violence triangle and positive peace, Lederach’s conflict transformation, environmental justice, collaborative governance, and just transition perspectives. The contextual evidence concerns unequal participation, disputes over compensation classification, site-specific groundwater findings, and the 8 March 2026 waste landslide that killed seven people. Four proposed communication mechanisms are examined: rights-based reframing, democratization of evidence, inclusive negotiation, and traceable institutional commitments. These mechanisms are linked conceptually to bargaining influence and implementation capacity rather than treated as demonstrated causal effects. The resulting framework identifies six evaluation domains: recognition, meaningful participation, redistribution of risk, material remediation, accountability, and livelihood security for waste pickers. It also formulates four propositions to guide future field research and distinguish procedural settlement from substantive improvement. The synthesis argues that dialogue, consensus, and compensation alone cannot establish positive peace without verifiable changes in environmental protection and affected groups’ decision-making influence. Because the study collects no primary data and lacks a complete archived search record, the proposed relationships and their effectiveness remain empirically untested.

papers.title: The effect of flexural stiffness on the pipe responses to lateral ground movement
Fault Geometry and Tectonic Implications of the 2026 Jalalpur Sharif Earthquake, Pakistan
papers.summary: The moderate-magnitude (Mw 4.5) 26 May 2026 Jalalpur Sharif earthquake in northern Pakistan caused localized severe damage, one fatality, and a maximum Modified Mercalli Intensity (MMI) of VII. Field observations documented liquefaction-related ground deformation, transient groundwater turbidity, differential settlement, tilted utility poles, and earthquake-induced landslides in Quaternary deposits. Moment tensor inversion indicates shallow (~3 km) oblique-thrust faulting, with NE–SW strike direction (strike 217°, dip 55°, rake 46°). Gravity modeling reveals a ~20 mGal residual anomaly aligned with the Pabbi Anticline, supporting structural complexity and the presence of shallow faulting, although the causative fault cannot be uniquely resolved. Regional seismicity is concentrated at 10–15 km depth, with a peak near 12 km, indicating depth-dependent deformation within the sedimentary cover and deeper regional thrust system. Coulomb stress modeling shows negligible static stress changes (~0.001 bar) at Jalalpur Sharif from the 2019 Mw 5.8 Mirpur and 2024 Mw 5.0 Kharian earthquakes, providing little support for direct static triggering. The localized damage likely resulted from the combined effects of shallow faulting, potentially liquefiable sediments and vulnerable buildings. These findings highlight the importance of incorporating shallow seismogenic structures and local ground conditions into seismic hazard assessments across the eastern Potwar foreland.

papers.title: Suitability of Suction Stress–Based Rainfall Intensity–Duration Paradigm for Predicting Tropical Storm–Induced Multiple Slope Failures
papers.source: Journal of Geotechnical and Geoenvironmental Engineering
papers.summary: Abstract A case study analyzing three landslides in Pohang, South Korea, during tropical storm Typhoon Hinnamnor in September 2022 is conducted to assess the suitability of the recently developed suction stress–based rainfall intensity–duration (SS-ID) paradigm for predicting multiple slope instabilities. Postfailure field investigation and laboratory testing were carried out to determine field hydrologic and geotechnical settings and soil properties. This information was used to determine these slopes’ critical suction stress profiles where the effective stress reaches the failure state or the local factor of safety reaches unity. Hydromechanical numerical modeling was then conducted under various rainfall intensities to identify the slopes’ corresponding durations for slope failure and thus the rainfall intensity–duration (ID) threshold curves of the slopes. The precipitation records during and before Typhoon Hinnamnor at Pohang were used to determine rainfall episodes and slopes’ rainfall intensity–duration data. The determined rainfall intensity–duration data at the three sites for Typhoon Hinnamnor were all above the corresponding predetermined ID threshold curves, correctly and novelly predicting the occurrence of the observed landslides. Further independent physical simulations of transient two-dimensional hydromechanical processes at the three failed slopes were conducted for independent confirmation. Excellent matches in predictions of the slope failure locations and timings are demonstrated, further physically validating the suitability and effectiveness of the SS-ID paradigm for multiple slope instability prediction. Because the suction stress–based ID curves are characteristic of a given region and they can be determined a priori, the SS-ID paradigm provides a practical way to use live rainfall data to forecast multiple slope instability in a region.

papers.title: Preferential Freeze–Thaw Damage in Limestone Containing Stylolites and Calcite Veins from High-Altitude Mining Areas
papers.summary: Abstract Limestone slopes in high-altitude mining areas are subjected to strong diurnal temperature fluctuations and repeated freeze–thaw cycles, which can induce the development of internal pores and cracks and cause structural deterioration of the rock mass. However, where preferential damage occurs and how it affects the structural continuity of limestone remain unclear. To investigate how structural units, including stylolites, calcite veins, and the matrix, control the spatial distribution of freeze–thaw damage in natural limestone, this study examined limestone containing stylolites and calcite veins. The specimens were classified into sparse and dense structural-unit types according to the degree of structural-unit development. Low-field nuclear magnetic resonance T2 spectra, magnetic resonance imaging, scanning electron microscopy, energy-dispersive spectroscopy, and P-wave velocity tests were combined to reveal the evolution of the pore structure, microscopic damage, and structural continuity under freeze–thaw cycles. The results show that the dense structural-unit specimens exhibited a more pronounced increase in long-T2 components, clustering of high-signal MRI regions, and P-wave velocity attenuation. After 30 freeze–thaw cycles, the velocity attenuation rate of the dense specimens reached 28–30%, significantly higher than that of the sparse specimens, which was 10–12%. The absolute value of the fitted porosity–velocity slope for the dense specimens was approximately 2.17 times that of the sparse specimens. SEM-EDS results indicate that the matrix and calcite vein interiors showed limited changes, although localized crack-like features developed near some vein boundaries after 30 cycles, whereas stylolites gradually evolved into widened, deepened, and rough-bounded banded damage zones, accompanied by relative Ca depletion and local enrichment of Si and Al. These findings demonstrate that freeze–thaw damage in natural limestone is not a uniform accumulati

papers.title: Three-dimensional monitoring of non-rigid ground surface deformation based on time-series multi-view collaborative tracking
papers.summary: Abstract High spatiotemporal resolution surface deformation information offers the advantage of comprehensively, precisely, and rapidly revealing surface deformation characteristics, and is key data for early identification and dynamic warning of geological disasters such as landslides and ground subsidence. However, the vast majority of monitoring methods suffer from shortcomings such as low spatiotemporal resolution, and traditional feature tracking algorithms exhibit limited reliability in long-term, non-rigid deformation scenarios. To address these issues, a surface deformation tracking method based on Time-Series Multi-View Collaborative Tracking (TS-MVCT) was constructed. The TS-MVCT framework estimates the spatial positions of the initial point cloud after deformation by establishing 2D correspondences between temporally adjacent observations within consecutive short-term intervals, followed by reliability-weighted depth fusion for 3D position estimation. To validate the effectiveness of the constructed method, an indoor simulated surface deformation experiment was conducted. The experimental results demonstrate that, compared to the M3C2 algorithm, which primarily characterizes displacement along the local surface normal, TS-MVCT effectively reduces deformation underestimation and the loss of displacement components in different spatial directions, while enabling the estimation of 3D displacement vectors at a higher density than SIFT-FT. Quantitative validation under laboratory conditions indicates that the relative deviations of the retrieved 3D displacements—measured against manually annotated reference values—are generally within 2 mm. On markerless natural surfaces, the algorithm achieves PSR and reprojection-error values within a similar numerical range to those of artificial-target regions, indicating comparable internal matching and multi-view geometric consistency under the controlled experimental conditions. In summary, the TS-MVCT framework present

papers.title: Landslide inventory (1953-2014), Andrews Experimental Forest and Blue River Basin
papers.summary: Landslide inventory (1953-2014), Andrews Experimental Forest and Blue River Basin. This layer is a combination of data from five landslide inventory efforts that have been conducted in the area beginning in the late 1960's. Data represent landslide occurrences between 1953 and 2014. Data are in the UTM coordinate system; zone 10, NAD27. The data table that describes the characteristics of the landslides inventoried in the following: Individual layers tied to inventories by Ted Dyrness, Fred Swanson, Dan Marion, and Matt Wallenstein were appended and linked to the shape file. The location and attributes of the slides were verified and corrected in 2022 by Fred Swanson, Julia Jones, and Catalina Segura.
