Points have been screen digitized from field maps using streams, roads, contour lines, and harvest units as reference layers. Original file exists as a database table.

papers.title: PhysInSAR: Unwrapping-free ground motion from paired C- and L-band wrapped interferometric phase
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: # PhysInSAR v0.9.0 — Unwrapping-free ground motion from Sentinel-1 and NISAR PhysInSAR is a research project that rethinks how ground deformation is measured from satellite radar. Instead of unwrapping each interferogram and fusing the results of separate processing chains, it fits a single continuous, physics-informed neural model of three-dimensional ground motion directly to the wrapped interferometric phase of Sentinel-1 C-band and NISAR L-band at the same time. The two wavelengths constrain one shared description of how the ground moves, so the cycle ambiguity that limits each sensor on its own is resolved jointly rather than guessed separately. This is the first public release. The method is a research prototype, validated on a realistic synthetic benchmark and not yet applied to real NISAR acquisitions. Phase unwrapping is the weak point of InSAR time series. It fails where C-band decorrelates in vegetation, and over fast or sharply localised motion such as mining subsidence, groundwater extraction, landslides and volcanic unrest. These are often the places where reliable measurements matter most. Its errors are whole cycles: silent, spatially coherent, and carried into every product built on top of them. With NISAR now observing the same ground as Sentinel-1, two complementary wavelengths are available for the first time at global scale. C-band is precise but fragile; L-band is robust but coarse. PhysInSAR is designed to combine them where they complement each other most: in the raw phase, before any information is lost. At its core is a differentiable physics forward model that predicts each sensor's phase from its own viewing geometry, including atmospheric delay, dispersive ionosphere, orbit errors and DEM error. Predictions are compared with observations through a von Mises likelihood, a periodic noise model under which a prediction that is right modulo one cycle is right, weighted by bias-corrected coherence. Ground motion is represented as a neural fie

papers.title: Characterization of iron mining tailings for reuse in sustainable civil infrastructure
papers.summary: Iron ore production generates approximately 1.4 billion tonnes of tailings annually. Research worldwide has investigated the reuse and recycling of this material. In civil engineering applications, research has mostly focused on pavement construction and block manufacturing, both of which commonly require the addition of binders. This paper proposes the use of iron ore tailings from a large Brazilian iron ore production area as a sand substitute in general geotechnical applications, while also addressing the global scarcity of natural sand. A comprehensive geotechnical characterization was performed, including the determination of hydraulic conductivity, deformability, and shear strength at optimum compaction conditions and at 95% of maximum dry unit weight and water content deviations within ±2%. The results indicate that, without binders, the material is suitable for use as trench fill and backfill for containment structures, as a soft-soil replacement material, in geosynthetic-reinforced soil walls, and in geotextile-encased granular columns.

papers.title: A machine learning framework for predicting the unconfined compression index of nano-silica stabilized fine-grained soils using leave-one-soil-type-out validation
papers.summary: The Lesser Himalayan region presents significant challenges for infrastructure development due to weak, landslide-prone soils. This study evaluates nano-silica (NS) stabilization of three fine-grained soils and introduces the Unconfined Compression Index ( Ic ), defined as the axial strain at 50% of peak unconfined compressive strength ( qu ), as a measure of stabilized-soil deformability. Laboratory specimens were prepared with NS contents of 0–4% and cured for 3–90 days. Six machine-learning models Linear Regression, Random Forest, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGB), K-Nearest Neighbors, Support Vector Machine, and Lasso Regression—were trained to predict Ic from soil type, NS content, curing duration, and early-cure qu . To avoid interpolation bias inherent in random splitting of factorial data, a Leave-One-Soil-Type-Out Cross-Validation was adopted. XGB achieved the highest predictive accuracy ( R 2 = 0.961; MAE = 0.158), while multicollinearity among predictors was mitigated via regularization. The results demonstrate that Ic can be estimated from routine strength data, offering a practical tool for assessing strain compatibility in NS-stabilized Himalayan soils.

papers.title: Enhanced Shear Strength Reduction Method for Stability Analysis of High-Friction Slopes: Implementation, Verification, and Application
papers.summary: Abstract Over the last two decades, the shear strength reduction method (SRM) has emerged as a prominent alternative for slope stability analysis. However, existing studies reveal significant differences (16%–28%) between the factor of safety (FOS) achieved by the traditional SRM and the limit analysis method (LAM) for steep slopes with high friction. To address this limitation, this study proposes an enhanced shear strength reduction method (ESRM) that dynamically adjusts the dilation angle of geomaterials based on their stress states. Subsequently, the ESRM is comprehensively verified against the LAM analytical solution through extensive sensitivity analyses and a benchmark study, involving 201 sets of slope experimental groups with different geometric parameters and geomaterial parameters. The results show that the maximum error in the FOS achieved with the ESRM is only 8%, and the predicted distribution and development of the potential slip surface are also satisfactory, confirming the applicability of the ESRM for steep slopes with high friction. Simultaneously, considering that the LAM analytical solution cannot be used for engineering-level verification, the engineering-level comparison methods of the ESRM, namely, the Davis A approach and Davis B approach, are reproduced and verified within the same verification framework. Results demonstrate that only the Davis B approach achieves satisfactory accuracy. Finally, a case study of the ShaiKou landslide is conducted. The ESRM and Davis B approach achieve highly consistent FOS values of 1.259 and 1.258, respectively, along with comparable slip surface distribution and development, further evaluating the practical value of the ESRM in analyzing engineering problems involving with high-friction slopes.

papers.title: Databases of Daily and Monthly Turbidity Data from Bull Run Reservoir # 1 Turbidity Stations 59-0 and 59-1 (1965–2026), Bull Run Drainage Basin, Oregon, USA
papers.summary: Daily turbidity data from Reservoir # 1 in the Bull Run drainage basin, Oregon, were requested from the Portland Public Records Center (PPRC) to constrain estimates of elevated turbidity durations in Reservoir # 1 following 1) the 1964 flood, 2) the 972 North Fork landslide, (3) the 1996 flood, and 4) the cessation of clearcut harvesting in the Bull Run watershed. These data provide context for interpretations of gravity-cores collected in Reservoir # 1.

papers.title: Geography, geospatial analysis and artificial intelligence: between traditional methods and new spatial paradigms
papers.summary: In 1986, yes 1986, it is not a typographical error, Helen Couclelis, one of the pioneers of Geographic Information Science (GIScience) and an expert in urban and regional modelling and planning, spatial cognition, and the geography of the information society, indicated that artificial intelligence (AI) and geography were interconnected within a broad context that addressed fundamental issues of theory, epistemology, and scientific method. At the time, the still little-known logical-mathematical context of AI was explored, demonstrating substantial implications for modelling in general, prediction, the interpretation of theoretical structures, and, moreover, for our understanding of science as a process. These more abstract aspects of the 'computational revolution', of which AI is a product, could, according to the author, have far-reaching consequences for geographical research (Couclelis, 1986).Since then, AI has been profoundly transforming geography by providing advanced methods for analysing, modelling, and interpreting geospatial data. As a discipline concerned with spatial relations, places, environments and human-environment interactions, geography increasingly benefits from AI methods capable of processing large and complex spatio-temporal datasets (e.g., Big Data), generating new insights into territorial dynamics and complex geographical phenomena (Encalada-Abarca et al., 2023).AI has made significant contributions to geospatial data processing, extending existing capabilities for handling and analysing increasingly large and heterogeneous datasets (Mohamad Alshiha, 2024). Techniques based on machine learning, including deep learning, have become increasingly relevant for processing and interpreting geographic information. These methodologies enable the identification of patterns, the modelling of trends, and the development of new analytical approaches to urban, environmental, and social challenges. AI-based methodologies are now widely explored in geospa

papers.title: Landslide susceptibility probability tables and sample points from Reconstructability Analysis, Wilson-Trask-Nestucca and Siletz-Yaquina watersheds, Oregon Coast Range, USA
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Sample points and conditional landslide probability tables for the Wilson-Trask-Nestucca and Siletz-Yaquina (WTNSY) watersheds of the Oregon Coast Range, USA. The probability tables were produced with Reconstructability Analysis (RA), an information-theoretic modelling method that works directly on categorical data. The data accompany Percy et al., “Information-theoretic modeling of landslide susceptibility using mostly categorical spatial data”, submitted to Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences. The study area was stratified into volcanic and sedimentary lithologies and modelled separately. Each row of a probability table is one combination of predictor states (for example elevation bin, terrane group, landform, soil taxonomic subgroup and particle size class) with the model probability of landslide presence, P(LS=1), the predicted class, and the number of training samples (n) from which the probability was estimated. Landslide presence comes from the Statewide Landslide Information Database for Oregon (SLIDO-4.5, Oregon Department of Geology and Mineral Industries); predictor variables come from DOGAMI geologic mapping, the USDA-NRCS Soil Survey Geographic Database (SSURGO), NLCD 2021 land cover and terrain data. Categories below 1% of a stratum's sample count were collapsed into a single category labelled “(other/rare)”. All files are in WTNSY_landslide_RA_data_v1.0.zip, which unpacks to a single folder (README.txt is also provided separately): • volcanic_probability_table.csv and sedimentary_probability_table.csv: flat, human-readable tables covering the full state space (144 volcanic and 512 sedimentary predictor-state combinations). • landslide_probability_tables.sqlite: the same tables in normalized form (a value table for each predictor and a prediction table for each stratum, linked by integer keys), with views volcanic_readable and sedimentary_readable that rebuild readable tables for browsing; these views leave out the (other/rare) categories, so use

papers.title: Earthquake-driven influx of organic matter enhances authigenic carbonate formation in hadal trenches
papers.summary: Shallow marine carbonates are recognized as key agents in deep carbon cycling. However, the formation and burial of carbonates below the carbonate compensation depth still remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate carbonates from the > 7000 m water-depth Japan Trench hadal zone and find widespread authigenic calcium carbonate buried in these ultra-deep sediments. Stable and radiocarbon isotope depletions in the authigenic carbonates indicate an organic carbon (OC) source, likely primarily delivered by deep-sea landslides. Isotopic modeling suggests that subduction of these OC-derived carbonates can impart negative δ13C signatures to fluids released in the NE Japan subduction zone. The OC-derived carbonate flux in the Japan Trench is estimated to reach ~ 28.6 Tg C Myr–1. We propose that earthquake-driven organic matter influx into the hadal zone may have facilitated sustained carbonate production. Thus, OC-derived authigenic carbonates in hadal trenches represent an underappreciated carbon sink and a potential mechanism for transferring OC into the deep Earth. Earthquake-driven organic matter influx into hadal zones facilitates sustained organic carbon-derived carbonate production. The formation of these authigenic carbonates represents both an underappreciated carbon sink and a potential mechanism for transferring OC into the deep Earth.

papers.title: Integrated Geological and Geophysical Characterization of the 2024 Lernapat Landslide, Armenia: Slip-Surface Delineation and Stability Assessment
papers.summary: The May 2024 Lernapat landslide in northern Armenia occurred following rainfall and coincided with leakage from an irrigation pipeline. Its subsurface structure was investigated using UAV terrain analysis, four boreholes, laboratory testing, electrical resistivity tomography (ERT), multichannel analysis of surface waves (MASW), microtremor H/V (horizontal-to-vertical spectral ratio) measurements, ground-penetrating radar (GPR), and limit-equilibrium modelling. Boreholes identified mechanically weakened intervals at depths of 16.4–16.7 m and 18.4–20.0 m. The borehole observations were considered together with the ERT and MASW results to constrain the probable basal deformation zone and the adopted slip-surface geometry. H/V measurements provided supplementary spectral information; their depth estimates were treated as approximate equivalent thicknesses rather than independent confirmation of the MASW interpretation. The existing slope yielded factors of safety of 0.980 under static loading and 0.496 under pseudo-static loading at Kh = 0.16. A modelled groundwater lowering of 7.0 m increased these values to 1.214 and 0.616, respectively. Within the staged embankment-construction sequence, the calculated static factors of safety ranged from 1.372 to 1.499, whereas the corresponding pseudo-static values ranged from 0.657 to 0.689. None of the investigated stabilization scenarios reached Fs = 1.00 under pseudo-static loading at Kh = 0.16. No separate calculations were performed at Kh = 0.20. These factors of safety are conditional on the adopted model; the effects of alternative basal geometries and shear-strength parameters were not quantified. The results illustrate how the integration of geological, hydrogeological, electrical, and seismic observations can provide a field-constrained basis for evaluating groundwater sensitivity and stabilization scenarios.

papers.title: A Unified Multispectral Feature Framework for Independent Recognition of Floods, Burned Areas, and Landslides
papers.summary: Multispectral disaster recognition draws on common optical measurements, but differences in feature construction, target definitions and evaluation design complicate comparisons across tasks. We present a unified feature framework that applies the same six-band interface, 78-dimensional spectral–spatial descriptor and training-side learning procedure to independently fitted flood, burned area and landslide experts. Spectral summaries, local variability and gradients describe each window; paired date and source auxiliary inputs provide task-specific extensions. Evaluation covered 88 flood patches from 11 events, 656 burned area windows in 23 source/overlap groups, and a prespecified 100-patch subset of the official Landslide4Sense test partition. The shared representation achieved F1 values of 0.8504, 0.8485 and 0.8169, respectively, under training-side classifier selection. The burned area temporal extension increased F1 to 0.8997, with gains over matched support post-event descriptors under both inner-selected and fixed Random Forest evaluation. The landslide auxiliary extension produced a larger gain under classifier selection than under fixed Random Forest, identifying an interaction between representation and classifier. Training label controls and negative class metrics distinguished learned discrimination from positive class prevalence. The framework provides a reproducible basis for testing shared optical descriptors and task-specific information under the distinct evaluation requirements of each task.

papers.title: The Agency of Nonlife: Alliances with Planetary Forces
Rethinking cascading high-mountain hazards and early warning in the Himalayas
papers.summary: Abstract Glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) remain a major Himalayan hazard, but recent disasters show that destructive floods develop through several cascading pathways. Seven recent events across Nepal and the wider Himalaya show how lake outburst, avalanche, slope failure and supraglacial drainage can be amplified by sediment entrainment and debris-flow transformation, leading to similar downstream consequences. To reduce risk from such cascading hazards, we argue for a four-tier cascade-aware approach spanning from source-zone monitoring, failure detection, early warning to preparedness, planning and governance.

papers.title: Paradigms of Preparedness and Response: Crisis Management in the Gjerdrum Slide
Performance and Mechanistic Insights into an Early-Strength Eco-Friendly UHPC Grouting Material Modified with Nano-Calcium Carbonate
papers.summary: Ultra-high-performance concrete (UHPC) has potential as a grouting material for emergency landslide remediation due to its superior mechanical properties and dense matrix without coarse aggregates. However, its field application is restricted by the requirement for high-temperature curing, low early-age strength, and poor constructability under standard curing conditions. To enhance early-strength development under conventional standard curing conditions, nine eco-friendly UHPC mixtures incorporating steel slag micro-powder were prepared using an orthogonal experimental design. Four factors, including lithium carbonate as an early-strength admixture, nano-calcium carbonate as a reinforcing filler, steel fibers, and polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) fibers, were investigated. The effects of these factors were evaluated through compressive strength, flexural strength, and flowability tests at different curing ages. Field-emission scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and X-ray diffraction (XRD) were further employed to analyze microstructural characteristics and hydration-phase evolution. The results indicate that increasing the dosages of the four additives decreases fresh paste flowability. An appropriate dosage of lithium carbonate promotes ettringite formation and enhances early-age compressive strength, while nano-calcium carbonate improves the matrix compactness through pinning and pore-filling effects. The optimized eco-friendly steel-slag-based UHPC achieved compressive/flexural strengths of 23.4/6.4 MPa at 12 h and 45.5/13.8 MPa at 1 d under standard curing conditions. The developed UHPC exhibits potential for rapid emergency grouting applications in landslide remediation.

papers.title: Cloudburst susceptibility mapping of Pakistan using an innovative expert opinion and LLM-assisted weighted linear combination model
Method-dependent assessment of long-term soil erosion on the Loess Plateau
papers.summary: Differences between classification-based and quantitative approaches may affect interpretations of regional soil erosion patterns and long-term changes. Using Google Earth Engine, we compared the classification-based approach derived from the Standards for Classification and Gradation of Soil Erosion (SL 190-2007) with the Chinese Soil Loss Equation (CSLE) across the Loess Plateau, China, from 2000 to 2025. The comparison covered erosion intensity, spatial distribution, differences among land-use types, rainfall erosivity ranges, slope classes and fractional vegetation cover (FVC) classes, and erosion-grade transitions. Annual paired comparisons accounted for temporal autocorrelation and multiple comparisons. Soil erosion intensity showed marked spatial heterogeneity, with higher erosion grades concentrated in Qinghai, eastern Gansu, central Shaanxi, and along the Shaanxi–Shanxi border. Both approaches indicated an overall decline in erosion intensity but differed substantially in the areas assigned to individual erosion grades. Compared with SL 190-2007, CSLE mapped larger areas in the lowest and highest erosion grades, with differences of 8.57 × 10 4 and 2.33 × 10 4 km 2 , respectively. Grassland and cropland were the dominant land use types on the Loess Plateau, and intermethod differences in erosion-grade area proportions were greatest for grassland. Across all slope and FVC classes, CSLE estimated significantly lower proportions of area affected by mild or more severe erosion (Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). Despite broadly similar patterns of erosion mitigation during 2000-2010, CSLE identified increases in erosion grade across 11.56% of the assessed area, mainly in northern Ningxia, southern Inner Mongolia, and the Loess Hilly-Gully Region. During 2010-2025, erosion intensity declined overall, but CSLE identified increases in erosion grade across 9.01% of the assessed area, mainly in eastern Inner Mongolia, Ningxia, and northern Shaanxi. Assessment-method choice ca

papers.title: Analysis of Barrier Lake Breach Flood Mitigation Under Cascade Reservoirs Operation: A Case Study of the Mogangling Event, Dadu River
papers.summary: The southeastern margin of the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau is characterized by complex geological conditions and frequent disasters such as landslide-induced river blockage and subsequent barrier lake breaching. With the construction of cascade reservoirs in the basin, the potential impacts of historical barrier lakes under the current flood control system remain unclear. Reconstructing the breaching process of barrier lakes is of great guiding significance for regional flood control and disaster mitigation, risk management, and the safe operation of cascade reservoirs in the basin. In this study, the Mogangling landslide barrier lake in the Dadu River basin was selected as the research object. We constructed breach flood hydrographs for the 300 m and 600 m breach scenarios and established a one-dimensional and two-dimensional coupled hydrodynamic model of the barrier lake breach flood based on the integrated flood modeling system (IFMS). The model was used to simulate the propagation and inundation processes of the breach flood under natural propagation without reservoirs and under the joint operation of the cascade reservoirs. Spatially distributed socioeconomic data were then combined with the model to assess flood impacts and the potential disaster mitigation effect of the joint operation of the cascade reservoirs. The results show that the joint operation of the cascade reservoirs can reduce the peak discharge of the barrier lake breach flood by 30.7–97.9%, decrease the total inundated area of downstream riverside towns by 70%, and reduce the GDP losses and the affected population by 89% and 87%, respectively. In addition, artificial excavation of a spillway channel can reduce the peak discharge of the natural barrier lake breach by approximately 30%.

papers.title: Amplified transport variability in granular slope flows near the critical angle
papers.summary: Mechanical disturbances such as seismic shaking can set a granular slope in motion. Understanding the resulting transport before arrest is important for predicting topographic change, assessing landslide hazards and controlling powder flows in industrial processes. Experiments show that smaller disturbances can trigger avalanches and larger areas are mobilized as slopes approach their stability limit. Yet how much transport varies between events under the same macroscopic conditions and forcing remains unclear. Here we use numerical simulations to show that transport variability is amplified near the critical angle. We apply identical basal pulses to static granular layers with the same macroscopic conditions but different initial particle configurations. Although the mean transport increases approximately in inverse proportion to the angular distance from the critical angle, the standard deviation increases even faster and can exceed the mean. Thus, identical forcing can produce widely different transport amounts. Deterministic constitutive laws that assign a unique response to given macroscopic conditions cannot capture this variability. We introduce fluctuations into the energy balance to develop a stochastic model that captures the main features of the broadening transport distribution. These results show that assessing transport near the critical angle requires considering its distribution, not just its mean, and motivate constitutive descriptions that incorporate fluctuations.

papers.title: Vulnerability, resilience and lifelines in the Global South
papers.summary: This thesis examines the vulnerability and resilience of lifelines in informal and socially vulnerable settlements in the Global South. It focuses on how access to basic services and infrastructures, their disruption, and their restoration shape the impacts of natural disasters and the recovery of affected communities. The central research question consists of two parts: (1) How does limited access to and disruption of lifelines affect the vulnerability of informal or socially vulnerable settlements? (2) How do maintaining access to and restoring lifelines affect the resilience of informal or socially vulnerable settlements following natural disasters in the Global South?. The theoretical framework of this study is grounded in disaster risk, social vulnerability, resilience, critical infrastructure, and urban informality. The study adopts a comparative approach, analyzing three case studies from regions of the Global South: first, Cebu Island in the Philippines following the earthquake of September 30, 2025; second, the Dharavi slum in Mumbai after the August 2025 floods; and third, the Rocinha favela (favela Rocinha) in Rio de Janeiro in relation to recurrent landslides triggered by extreme rainfalls in 2010, 2018, and 2019. The analysis shows that the vulnerability of informal and socially vulnerable settlements stems not only from their exposure to natural hazards, but is shaped by the interaction of social inequality, fragile infrastructure, limited institutional capacity, and inadequate access to essential lifelines. In all three cases, the disruption of lifelines — such as water supply, sanitation, electricity, transportation, healthcare, communication, and housing - exacerbated vulnerability and delayed recovery. Despite differing geographical, social, and institutional conditions, a common mechanism emerges: unequal access to lifelines produces and reproduces vulnerability, while timely restoration, local knowledge, community networks, humanitarian support,

papers.title: Unravelling information on impactful geo-hydrological hazard events with HazMiner, a multilingual text mining method developed through a global scale coverage application
papers.source: Natural hazards and earth system sciences
papers.summary: Abstract. The incidence and impacts from geo-hydrological hazards (GH) such as floods, flash floods and landslides are changing globally due to anthropogenic environmental changes and increased exposure driven by population growth. Reliable datasets on GH are essential to deepen our understanding of these hazards and their impacts. However, existing GH datasets contain data gaps leading to biased interpretations, especially in the Global South where populations are commonly the most impacted. Text mining offers new opportunities in documenting GH by automatically extracting information from large text corpora. Despite its potential, current methodologies are not adapted to improve documentation in data-scared contexts. We present HazMiner, a paragraph-based text mining method designed to document the location, timing and impact of GH through large language models across multiple languages and at various scales. Applied here globally on 6,366,905 news articles published from 2017 through 2024 in 58 languages, HazMiner extracted 21,411 flood, 7,659 landslide and 3,606 flash flood events with known location and time information and, in some cases, impact data. Compared to existing hazard datasets, HazMiner significantly improved hazard documentation, reducing the data gaps in many regions, especially in the Global South. The new versatile multilingual method and its dataset advances both text mining and natural hazard research.

papers.title: Review article: rainfall-induced landslide early warning systems through the lens of the early warnings for all framework – advances, gaps, and perspectives
papers.source: Natural hazards and earth system sciences
papers.summary: Abstract. This review is necessary at this time to provide a comprehensive evaluation of the rainfall-induced landslide early warning system (LEWS) through the lens of the United Nations ‘Early Warnings for All’ (EW4All) framework. This study integrates EW4All pillars, incorporates overlooked literature, examines information sharing in academic publications, and evaluates the global feasibility of implementing EW4All for LEWS. Of 61 rainfall-induced LEWS identified in the literature covering 23 countries, 14 are considered operational, meaning they are currently implemented and actively used for warning purposes, across only 10 countries. Among local, regional, and national systems, local LEWS is often less scalable and more resource-intensive. Most operational systems target debris flows and shallow landslides and rely mainly on rainfall thresholds. While some include susceptibility maps, risk maps are largely absent. Real-time sensor data are used in some systems; however, high maintenance costs limit scalability. Reliability is further constrained by data scarcity, limited forecast verification, suboptimal use of AI, and the lack of standardised forecasting approaches. Community engagement and multi-hazard integration remain limited. Although EW4All is transformative, implementing effective LEWS in rainfall-induced landslide-prone areas worldwide by 2027 remains impractical without localised approaches, sufficient funds, and resources.

papers.title: Reducing false alarms in crackmeter-based early warning of small-scale slope deformation via deep learning-driven asynchronous displacement–rainfall data fusion
papers.source: Natural hazards and earth system sciences
papers.summary: Abstract. Real-time crackmeter-based warning systems for rainfall-induced small-scale slope failures suffer from prohibitively high false alarm rates. Across diverse geological settings, existing approaches relying on fixed thresholds or isolated rainfall–displacement relationships are highly sensitive to noise, lacking the robustness to reliably distinguish genuine deformation signals from spurious measurements. To address this operational bottleneck, this study reframes the early warning paradigm from a traditional fixed-threshold alerting process reliant on manual discrimination to an automated alert truth verification problem, proposing a real-time binary classification framework to isolate true early warnings from sensor-triggered false alarms. Utilizing a multi-source dataset of crackmeter displacement and rainfall measurements from diverse monitored slopes in Fujian Province, China, all true early warning instances were rigorously calibrated via field investigations. A patch-based dual-branch temporally-aware Transformer model was developed to explicitly address asynchronous multi-rate data fusion, strict temporal causality between rainfall and displacement, and stringent real-time decision constraints. By simultaneously capturing long-term rainfall-displacement interactions and high-resolution displacement dynamics, the model outperforms competitive baselines, achieving a precision of 90.91 %, a recall of 93.53 %, and an F2-score of 92.99 % in identifying true early warnings. Interpretability analysis reveals the model’s decisions are primarily driven by localized displacement trends and relative rainfall intensity, aligning with expert judgment. The proposed framework significantly curtails false alarms without compromising reliability, acting as a robust decision-support layer to enhance automated slope hazard monitoring. Future work will fuse additional sensor types to suppress false alarms via cross-validation of multi-physical responses.

papers.title: GIS-Based Statistical Modelling for Landslide Susceptibility Zonation in Parts of Northwest Indian Himalayas
papers.source: Journal of the Indian Society of Remote Sensing

papers.title: Causal Geospatial Intelligence Framework for Identifying Environmental Drivers of Landslide Risk in Mountainous Regions
papers.source: International Journal of Engineering Science and Information Technology
papers.summary: Landslide susceptibility models can effectively predict areas prone to landslides but generally provide limited evidence on whether specific environmental exposures causally influence landslide occurrence. This research proposes an integrated causal-geospatial framework combining predictive modeling with causal effect estimation and spatial heterogeneity analysis for landslide occurrence in Desa Wih Pase, Bener Meriah, Indonesia. An analytical dataset comprising 18,450 30 m × 30 m grid cells from observations in 2025 was analyzed using Random Forest and Logistic Regression for occurrence probability modeling, followed by Causal Forest to derive average treatment effect estimates together with grid-level Conditional Average Treatment Effects (CATE). The Random Forest model reached a discrimination performance of 0.91 in AUC-ROC, exceeding the 0.79 achieved by the Logistic Regression baseline, demonstrating stronger predictive discrimination under the imbalanced landslide dataset. Causal analysis estimated a positive effect of cumulative rainfall, with a 100 mm increase associated with a 0.142 increase in landslide occurrence probability (95% CI: 0.089–0.195). A 10° increase in slope produced an estimated effect of 0.218 (95% CI: 0.161–0.275). Spatial CATE analysis revealed substantial heterogeneity, with rainfall effects ranging from ?0.039 to 0.302 and slope effects from ?0.024 to 0.490 across valid 30 m grid cells. Sensitivity analyses showed that the positive causal effects remained stable across alternative confounder sets, rainfall accumulation windows, and spatial resolutions. The framework distinguishes predictive susceptibility from causal environmental effects and provides a basis for spatially targeted landslide risk reduction and environmental engineering interventions

papers.title: Limit-state geometry of trailing-edge tensile cracks in soil slopes with a tensile strength threshold
papers.summary: Abstract Trailing-edge tensile cracks can contribute to tensile–shear slope failure. Many analytical models prescribe a vertical crack and solve only for depth, and tensile strength, σₜ , is also often neglected or treated indirectly. This study develops a limit-state formulation for an initially intact, homogeneous cemented soil slope under drained conditions. Shear resistance follows the Mohr–Coulomb criterion, while tensile failure is governed independently by \(\:{\sigma\:}_{t}\). The formulation treats the limit-state crack depth L and inclination δ as coupled unknowns of the tensile–shear limit-state problem rather than prescribing the crack inclination in advance. The solution satisfies tensile and shear failure conditions, equilibrium, and geometric constraints. The formulation is examined using theoretical benchmarks, a bounded loess field comparison, and simulations using MatDEM. The benchmarks reproduce established depth trends. The field measurement falls within the calculated range for the adopted tensile-strength ratio. The simulations preserve the crack/no-crack distinction and show closer correspondence in inclination than in depth, with mean absolute differences of 4.22° and 1.66 m, respectively. Increasing σₜ reduces L and δ and may suppress a positive-depth solution. The cohesion intercept generally increases both, while unit weight mainly reduces L . Global Sobol analysis ranks cohesion > tensile strength > friction angle > unit weight for the zero-including depth response.

papers.title: Enhancing soil creep index prediction accuracy using optimized XGBoost and LightGBM models with bio-inspired optimization algorithms: SHAP- and LIME-based explanation methods
papers.summary: Soil creep, as a form of long-term deformation, significantly influences the performance of foundations and earth structures. As this deformation develops over time, it can lead to major geotechnical issues such as slope failures, differential ground movement, and excessive settlement. Consequently, accurate estimation of the soil creep index is essential for informed geotechnical decision-making. To address this, the primary aim of this study is to develop precise models for estimating the soil creep index using modern machine learning methods. This study develops fourteen predictive models, including seven based on XGBoost and seven based on LightGBM. These include the standard XGBoost and LightGBM models, as well as their optimized variants enhanced using grey wolf optimizer (GWO), whale optimization algorithm (WOA), bat algorithm (BAT), dragonfly algorithm (DOA), crayfish optimization algorithm (COA), and grasshopper optimization algorithm (GOA). To assess the reliability of creep index prediction, the models were evaluated under four separate sets of input variables. In addition, SHAP, LIME, and SelectKBest methods were applied to explore the influence of individual input factors on the prediction outcomes. Each model’s effectiveness was assessed through four principal statistical indicators: the mean absolute error (MAE), root mean square error (RMSE), correlation coefficient (R), and Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE). Based on the RMSE values, the top three hybrid XGBoost models were XGBoost-GOA (RMSE = 0.002259), XGBoost-GWO (RMSE = 0.002273), and XGBoost-COA (RMSE = 0.002316). Among the hybrid LightGBM models, the best performers were LightGBM-BAT (RMSE = 0.003813), LightGBM-GWO (RMSE = 0.003884), and LightGBM-COA (RMSE = 0.003885). For the standalone models, XGBoost (RMSE = 0.003084) outperformed CART (RMSE = 0.003398) and LightGBM (RMSE = 0.003972). The testing results indicate that XGBoost-based models provide a reliable and accurate approach for predictin

papers.title: Comment on egusphere-2026-4280
papers.summary: Abstract. The Marmara's Sea with its near-field tsunami complications in Europe and the eastern Mediterranean, is paradoxically surrounded by a densely urbanised, infrastructure-rich coastline and positioned above the North Anatolian Fault system with historical earthquake events, submarine slope processes and narrow-basin resonance that impact coastal water levels. This fact motivated the current study presenting a benchmark-consistent GeoClaw modelling roadmap on seven historical Marmara tsunami scenarios selected from 22-event source catalogue with numerical comparison through 20-lane. The lanes represent exclusively, different source-construction, turning strategy, comprising earthquake-only, earthquake-plus-landslide, adaptive sampling, hybrid site-blend, and close-loop correction variants. From the first lane to the final selected best lane of the simulations set, the benchmark error could be reduced from maximum 1.93 m to 0.019 m in MAE (Mean Absolute Error) and 2.26 m to 0.024 m in RMSE (Root Mean Square Error), with all seven events cases remaining below 10 % error and the largest absolute percent error is 2.4 %. After target-based scenario selection, the corresponding outputs such as gauge-history, travel-time, and bridge-ready hydrodynamic outputs, providing a reproducible chain from historical source interpretation to infrastructure demand inputs are extracted. The workflow is designed for regions where instrumental tsunami records are sparse, but historical runup constraints, bathymetry, mapped faults, and scenario logic can be combined transparently.

papers.title: Mitigasi dan Kesiapsiagaan Bencana di Indonesia: Telaah Literatur dan Implikasinya bagi Nusa Tenggara Timur
papers.source: Antigen Jurnal Kesehatan Masyarakat dan Ilmu Gizi
papers.summary: Indonesia and East Nusa Tenggara (NTT) face recurrent threats from earthquakes, tsunamis, volcanic eruptions, floods, and landslides, while the effectiveness of mitigation depends heavily on community preparedness and the reliability of early warning systems. This review aims to synthesize evidence on disaster risk reduction, community preparedness, and early warning systems, and to derive implications for NTT. A narrative-thematic literature review was conducted on 18 sources published between 2011 and 2026, selected using inclusion and exclusion criteria and supplemented with secondary disaster data for NTT from the regional disaster management agency and national media. The sources were analyzed using the LIPI-UNESCO/ISDR preparedness parameters. Three main patterns emerged. First, preparedness varies widely, from the not-ready category in a school near Mount Sinabung to the very-ready category in Pacitan Bay, with resource mobilization and drill frequency as the weakest components. Second, technology-based warning systems are often constrained by maintenance, budget, and communication chains, so they need to be combined with local wisdom such as smong. Third, discussions combined with drills, disaster literacy, and community institutions improve readiness. In NTT, 136 disaster events were recorded between January and April 2026, and the November 2024 eruption of Lewotobi Laki-laki killed 10 people. The implications are that mitigation in NTT should integrate contingency planning, regular drills, maintained early warning, and local knowledge, supported by preparedness surveys that remain scarce in this province.

papers.title: Machine learning-based landslide susceptibility assessment in the Uttarkashi District, Uttarakhand
papers.summary: Landslides are a major geological hazard that poses serious risks to infrastructure, transportation networks, and populations. This study develops a framework for evaluating landslide risk in the Uttarkashi District of Uttarakhand, India, using GIS and machine learning. With topographic, geological, hydrological, environmental, and anthropogenic characteristics, a landslide inventory comprising 1,994 landslide locations and the same number of non-landslide locations was prepared and evaluated using fourteen conditioning factors. Models like Random Forest (RF), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) were trained and evaluated using spatial five-fold cross-validation and an independent test dataset. Elevation, distance from roads, NDVI, aspect, lithology, and land-use/land-cover were found to be among the most significant predictors using feature-importance analysis, albeit their relative significance differed between models. The mean AUC values for RF, XGBoost and LightGBM were 0.8805, 0.8846, and 0.8840, respectively, based on the spatial cross-validation data. LightGBM obtained an AUC of 0.8950 on the independent test dataset, whereas RF and XGBoost obtained an AUC of 0.8988. High- and very-high-susceptibility zones were frequently identified on the resulting susceptibility maps along the Yamuna and Bhagirathi River systems as well as important transportation routes like the Yamunotri and Gangotri highways. Additionally, this study shows how machine learning combined with remote sensing and GIS can effectively assess the susceptibility of a region to landslides. In the Himalayan context, it offers spatial data to support infrastructure management, slope stabilization, land-use planning, and disaster risk reduction.

papers.title: Ein Erdrutsch in Mels, 1953
Three storms test a decade of multi-hazard warning in south-eastern Bangladesh
papers.summary: Abstract Landslides and flash floods in south-eastern Bangladesh share their storms but are warned for separately. This study compares the compound events of June 2017, August 2023 and July 2026 on the same slopes, using gauge-corrected rainfall, a date-checked landslide inventory, river records and situation reports. In 2017 the lower of two published rainfall thresholds for landslides was crossed 17 to 25 hours before the first failures and the higher one two to eight hours before, and gauges existed for both hazards but dedicated warnings for neither. By 2026 numbered landslide bulletins were issued for each sub-district under a draft national protocol and 38,422 people were sheltered. In Rangamati, where the district gauge recorded 343 mm in 24 hours in 2017 and 287 mm in 2026, deaths fell from 121 to one. A slope-stability model shows that the 2026 storm was no gentler on the slopes than that of 2017. The lower threshold is exceeded on 14 to 19 days of an average monsoon even at the region's two long-running gauges, while the higher one missed most dated landslides. The heaviest monsoon rain showed no detectable trend since 1950, but 3 °C of warming at about 7 % more rain per degree would make the higher threshold fire about 60 % more often. In 2026 the remaining landslide deaths concentrated in refugee camps on cut slopes despite warnings, suggesting that the missing part of the warning system lies between the warning and the people it reaches.

papers.title: Changes in root morphological and architectural traits are key factors influencing soil detachment capacity on shallow landslide scars during vegetation recovery on the Loess Plateau
papers.summary: The hypothesis of this study was that changes in root morphological and architectural traits are key factors influencing soil detachment capacity (Dc) on shallow landslide scars during vegetation recovery on the Loess Plateau. The dataset comprises the raw data used to generate Figs. 5–7. Figure 5 presents Dc at different slope positions and recovery times. Figure 6 shows root biomass and morphological traits, including root weight density, root length density, root surface area density, root volume density, root fractal dimension, and root fractal abundance. Figure 7 presents three-dimensional (3D) root architectural traits, including root topological index, root branching angle, and root link length, together with photographs of root systems at different recovery times. Data were collected from six shallow landslide scars representing 1, 3, and 5 years of vegetation recovery, and two newly formed scars used as controls (CK). Soil detachment capacity was measured using flume scour experiments at a slope gradient of 45° under five flow discharges (12–36 L min⁻¹). Root biomass and morphological traits were quantified through root scanning, while 3D architectural traits were characterized using root reconstruction. Measurements were obtained at different slope positions to capture spatial variations in Dc and root traits across recovery stages. The results identified root length density and topological index as key root traits influencing Dc during vegetation recovery. Changes in root morphological and architectural traits may also influence Dc partly through their effects on soil cohesion (c). The dataset provides a basis for examining how root morphological and 3D architectural traits vary with slope position and vegetation recovery time, and how these variations relate to changes in Dc. It can also support further investigation of the role of soil cohesion in mediating the effects of root traits on soil detachment.

papers.title: The Country and the City in the Himalayas
papers.summary: Kalimpong, a Himalayan foothill district in West Bengal, is facing an agrarian crisis as rice farming becomes increasingly unviable due to rising costs, water scarcity, and climate unpredictability. Sarah Besky analyzes how colonial “government estate” legacies, designed for rent extraction, now compound these challenges, pushing youth into service-sector migration. Meanwhile, homestay tourism—promoted as an alternative—commodifies local culture, relying on women’s unpaid care work and catering to Indian urban middle-class fantasies of a “Swiss-like” retreat. Yet, landslides, hydropower projects, and infrastructure strain worsen livability. This shift from farming to affective labor reveals how colonial and neoliberal logics converge, masking extraction behind nostalgia while deepening inequality and ecological precarity.

papers.title: MOVEMONT - Final Report
papers.summary: Landslides are common processes in mountain areas, forming an integral part of their long-term destruction. To society, such phenomena may mean risks and disasters on the one hand, having triggered a huge bulk of research. However, landslides may also represent significant natural and cultural heritage and offer services to society, aspects that are yet under-researched and may be included in the rather scarcely used concept of geosystem services. In this context, landslides also help us to learn how Earth surface systems are functioning. As landslides often represent spectacular phenomena creating remarkable landforms, they are suitable for generating enthusiasm for geo-scientific topics among people, and are therefore useful for demonstrating complex geomorphological processes. UNESCO Global Geoparks (UGGps) represent ideal environments of exploring and highlighting geosystem services related to landslides, particularly in Austria where the three existing UNESCO Global Geoparks (Karawanken/Karavanke, Erz der Alpen, Steirische Eisenwurzen) are characterized by the occurrence of a broad range of landslide types and magnitudes.

papers.title: Revisiting Crozier (2005)—Multiple-Occurrence Regional Landslide Events in New Zealand: Hazard Management Issues
papers.summary: Abstract This paper reviews the key contribution of Crozier (2005) on Multiple-Occurrence Regional Landslide Events (MORLE), a phenomenon with specific frequency, magnitude, and geomorphic impact, redefining regional-scale landslide hazard assessment. Using extensive landslide inventories and climatic datasets from New Zealand, the study correlates landslide distribution with rainfall intensity, antecedent moisture, terrain morphology, and lithology. The work highlights the limitations of site-specific hazard evaluation, advocates for regional, frequency/magnitude-based assessments integrating meteorological thresholds, and underscores the multi-hazard nature of MORLE. This new conceptual model has significantly influenced subsequent developments in susceptibility modelling, hazard evaluation, and early warning systems. The paper remains a milestone in landslide science, bridging geomorphology and risk governance while anticipating modern climate-driven hazard analysis and spatial modelling.

papers.title: Revisiting Guzzetti et al. (1999)—Landslide Hazard Evaluation: A Review of Current Techniques and Their Application in a Multiscale Study, Central Italy
papers.summary: Abstract This review analyses the article ‘Landslide hazard evaluation: a foundational insight to landslide hazard assessment’ by Guzzetti et al. (1999), who critically examined the concepts, assumptions and methods underpinning the field at the end of the twentieth century. The paper is rooted in the evolution of risk research and highlights its clear distinction between landslide hazard and landslide susceptibility. By exploring mapping units, modelling approaches and scale effects, and applying these to multiscale statistical analyses in Central Italy, the authors clarified both the potential and the limitations of Geographic Information System-based quantitative methods. The paper demonstrates how susceptibility modelling has consolidated as a legitimate planning tool. While it focuses on this specific aspect, the foundation it builds can pave the way for addressing broader questions of disaster risk, vulnerability and governance in subsequent research and applications. The analysis emphasises the paper’s conceptual rigour, methodological transparency and enduring relevance to modern research, situating its contributions within the hazard-centred paradigms that preceded later advances in integrated disaster risk studies.

papers.title: Compiled Data and Code for a Physics–Data Coupled Early-Warning Model for Rainfall-Induced Landslides
papers.summary: This repository contains compiled CSV data and code for “A Physics–Data Coupled Early-Warning Model for Rainfall-Induced Landslides.” The study focuses on landslides triggered by Typhoon Gaemi in Zixing City, China. The model combines a physics-informed neural network, rainfall infiltration, and infinite-slope stability analysis to estimate landslide occurrence probabilities. Data were compiled from published studies cited in the article. Please cite the associated article, this repository, and the original data sources when reusing these materials.

papers.title: A 3D Implementation of an Elastoviscoplastic Model and Application to Creep-Driven Slow-Moving Landslides
papers.summary: Abstract To analyze problems involving creep-driven slow-moving landslides interacting with structures and infrastructure and gain useful information for risk management, numerical modeling is the most comprehensive tool. When resorting to numerical simulations, appropriate constitutive modeling is key to capture the time-dependent behavior of geomaterials. However, a drawback of advanced constitutive models accounting for time dependency is the high number of parameters involved, which are commonly calibrated based on site-scale monitoring data, without accounting for the characteristic creep behavior of the material. This paper describes the implementation of an existing elastoviscoplastic model in a three-dimensional (3D) finite-difference software. The model, called SHELVIP (Stress Hardening Elastic Viscous Plastic), was derived from the classical theory of elastoplasticity by adding a viscoplastic component based on Perzyna’s overstress theory. After illustrating the model and the implementation procedure, the steps to tune the constitutive parameters, especially the viscoplastic ones, are described. First, the viscoplastic parameters are determined at the laboratory scale through an analytical calibration process based on laboratory creep tests. Then, tuning of some parameters at the site scale is performed, while other parameters are kept unchanged from their laboratory-scale value being representative of the intrinsic creep behavior. The final set of parameters can be used to run predictive analyses for problems of engineering relevance. The analytical calibration is exemplified with reference to triaxial creep tests on Palombini clays. Then, the implemented SHELVIP model is validated by comparing numerical, analytical, and experimental creep strains at different deviatoric stress levels. A three-dimensional numerical model of the interaction between a deep-seated landslide and an existing motorway tunnel is developed. The capability of the constitutive fram

papers.title: Spatiotemporal correlation of rainfall intensity and subsurface acoustic emission parameters for landslide initiation
papers.summary: Abstract Rainfall-induced landslides pose severe geohazards in monsoon-dominated mountain regions. This study presents a coupled rainfall–acoustic emission (AE) monitoring system deployed at a landslide-prone slope near Narendra Nagar, Uttarakhand, India (Lesser Himalaya). AE signals were recorded from active hollow aluminium waveguides installed through mapped shear zones, synchronized with sub-minute rainfall data from an Automatic Weather Station. Analysis of 4,884 one-minute windows over the 2025 monsoon season revealed: (i) a site-specific critical rainfall intensity threshold of 2 mm/min (r = 0.70, p 4 mm/min, 60 min at < 1 mm/min); and (v) a dual-criterion (rainfall + AE) warning system that reduces false alarms by a factor of three compared to rain-only thresholds. A site-specific intensity–duration threshold (I = 0.088D^0.36) was derived from 51 AE-confirmed rainfall events. These results demonstrate the feasibility of physics-based, multi-criterion AE-driven landslide early warning in complex Himalayan terrain.

papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: SAGE-GeoSuitability v1.0.0 — Scientific Spatial Risk Assessment SAGE-GeoSuitability is an open-source QGIS Processing plugin developed to support spatial machine learning, susceptibility mapping, and risk assessment using geospatial predictor data. The software provides a workflow for training, comparing, evaluating, and interpreting machine learning models for spatial applications, including wildfire susceptibility, flood susceptibility, landslide susceptibility, and other environmental risk assessment tasks. Key Features Multiple raster predictor inputs Machine learning model comparison Spatial cross-validation and optional independent test evaluation SHAP-based model interpretation and additivity validation Probability calibration and calibration assessment for supported classification workflows Five-level spatial risk classification and independent test assessment Raster quality assurance and out-of-distribution analysis Reproducible research outputs and scientific reporting Scientific Scope and Limitations The software is intended for research and decision-support applications. Predictive performance, probability calibration, and spatial generalizability depend on the quality, representativeness, and independence of the input data and validation design. Results must be evaluated for each study area and application. The software is not certified or universally validated for all environmental hazards or geographic conditions. papers.title: Comparative Evaluation of Statistical and Morphometric Models for Rainfall-Induced Shallow Landslide Susceptibility Mapping: A Case Study Along the Fujian–Guangdong Border
papers.summary: Extreme rainfall can trigger widespread shallow landslides, highlighting the need for reliable susceptibility assessment systems. This study compares an information value–logistic regression (IV-LR) model with a terrain-driven morphometric model in terms of their predictive performance for shallow landslides triggered by an extreme rainfall event along the Fujian–Guangdong border. The IV-LR model integrates 11 environmental predictors and was trained using 3633 landslide samples and an equal number of non-landslide samples, whereas the morphometric model relies on DEM-derived terrain attributes and required no landslide inventory for training. Both models were evaluated using a common spatially separated validation dataset comprising 2273 landslide and 2273 non-landslide samples. The IV-LR model achieved an ROC-AUC of 0.7537, an Earth Mover’s Distance (EMD) of 0.2524, and a Brier score of 0.2336, compared with 0.5225, 0.0084, and 0.4172 for the morphometric model, respectively. Within the highest-ranked 20% of the common assessment area, the IV-LR model captured 53.06% of validation landslides, compared with 23.89% for the morphometric model. These findings support the feasibility of using an IV-LR model for detailed susceptibility assessment, while the morphometric model, which relies only on DEM-derived inputs, shows limited discriminatory performance.

papers.title: Revisiting Corominas et al. (2014)—Recommendations for the Quantitative Analysis of Landslide Risk
papers.summary: Abstract Corominas et al. (2014) synthesised recommended methodologies for quantitative landslide hazard, vulnerability and risk analysis across spatial scales and for verification/validation of outputs. This chapter revisits the paper as a technical benchmark for quantitative landslide risk analysis, highlighting its structured decomposition of hazard (spatial, temporal and intensity components), exposure characterisation and physical vulnerability assessment. Strengths include the explicit linkage from susceptibility to hazard, the treatment of different landslide types and a comprehensive toolbox for model testing. Remaining challenges concern the scarcity of temporal information, the limited representation of landslide intensity and runout at broader scales and the consistent propagation and communication of uncertainty in risk estimates.

papers.title: Knickpoint Database for the Indian Subcontinent
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Knickpoints, abrupt steepenings in river longitudinal profiles, record base-level change, differential rock uplift, lithological contrasts and valley blockage by landslides and glaciers, but no consistent, openly available inventory exists for the knickpoints at a regional scale or continental scale. Here we present a spatially continuous database of 70,420 knickpoints along 2.5 million km of channel in the Himalaya–Karakoram arc and Peninsular India, derived from the 90 m MERIT DEM with the TopoToolbox knickpointfinder algorithm (vertical tolerance 50 m; streams draining more than 0.81 km2). Each knickpoint carries coordinates, elevation, height, drainage area, channel slope, basin, lithology and distance to the nearest active fault. We compare the database with OpenStreetMap waterfalls (46 % lie within 500 m of a knickpoint, 4.9 times the random expectation) and test its sensitivity to the elevation model in two basins using SRTM, Copernicus, FABDEM and ALOS PALSAR. The data are archived on Zenodo and are intended as a ready-to-use variable for tectonic geomorphology, landslide susceptibility, hydropower and hazard studies.

Effects of moss restoration on topsoil water dynamics in a temperate vineyard
papers.summary: Abstract. Climate change is intensifying pressure on vineyard soil and water management, particularly under-vine, where vegetation is commonly suppressed to minimize competition with grapevines. Bryophytes represent a promising but little-tested alternative to bare soil or cover crops. We evaluated moss restoration as an under-vine ground cover in a temperate, rainfed vineyard in southwestern Germany, comparing it with bare soil and cover crop (grass) over a 22-month field experiment. Continuous topsoil moisture measurements using time-domain transmission sensors were used to analyse the initial response time (the time between the onset of precipitation and the first increase in topsoil moisture) and the peak response time (the time between the onset of precipitation and the maximum topsoil moisture). We additionally quantified mean topsoil moisture and drying rates and monitored treatment development during and after maintenance. Moss restoration did not significantly delay topsoil moisture response times following precipitation compared to grass or bare soil. Initial response times followed the pattern grass > moss > bare soil; differences between treatments were most pronounced under light and moderate precipitation and declined with increasing intensity, with moss and bare soil converging under heavy events. Peak response times followed a similar pattern (grass > moss ≈ bare soil), with significant differences restricted to light and heavy precipitation events: grass exhibited longer peak response times than bare soil under light rainfall and longer times than both bare soil and moss under heavy rainfall. Mean topsoil moisture did not differ significantly among treatments, whereas drying rates were higher under moss and bare soil than under grass. Moss plots initially suppressed grass establishment and consistently exhibited the lowest variability in topsoil moisture response, although vegetation cover and functional differences between treatments gradually conv

papers.title: DRRT-PMD: Differentiable reflective ray tracing for surface form measurement and pose optimization in phase measuring deflectometry
Spatiotemporal variations of carbon-water-hydraulic risk for Pinus tabuliformis Carrière Plantations on the Loess Plateau under future climate change
papers.summary: Abstract. As a native perennial tree, Pinus tabuliformis L. (PT) has been widely planted on the Chinese Loess Plateau for ecological restoration. However, climate change impacts on water resources will poses a new challenge for sustainability of restored ecosystems. To clarify the plantations carbon sequestration and water consumption, as well as their underlying physiological mechanisms, this study coupled the integrated BBGC-Sperry model with CMIP6 meteorological data under SSP126, SSP245, and SSP585. Daily transpiration, soil water content, and leaf water potential, along with multi-site total growing-season transpiration and aboveground biomass data, were used to validate the BBGC-Sperry model. The validated model simulated the dynamics of NPP, actual evapotranspiration (ET) and annual average percentage loss of whole-plant hydraulic conductivity (APLK) for PT plantations at 130 meteorological stations on the Loess Plateau. We integrated a “carbon-water-hydraulic risk index” (CWHRI) based on NPP, ET, and drought-induced mortality risk probability (DMRP) to assess ecosystem sustainability. These simulations covered the baseline period (2000–2024) and three future periods (2025–2049, NFP; 2050–2074, MFP; and 2075–2099, FFP). The results indicate that the mean NPP will decrease by 4 %–27 % except in the FFP under the SSP585 while the mean ET and APLK will increase by 0.05 %–61 % and 13 %–84 %, respectively. The CWHRI will decline by 23 %–44 %, driven directly by NPP and indirectly by water-related environmental factors. The spatial dynamics of CWHRI will decline from southeast to northwest. These findings indicate the rising DMRP of PT plantations will threaten the sustainability of restored ecosystems on the Loess Plateau in the future.

papers.title: Radiation–convection coupling in turbine casing cavities under oxidation-related emissivity variation

Ecohydrological coupling and episodic hydrological connectivity in the Edwards Plateau
papers.summary: Abstract. In semiarid karst systems, the hydrologic budget is regulated by strong interactions among the water fluxes of precipitation, soil water dynamics, evapotranspiration, runoff, and groundwater recharge. In this study, we evaluated the temporal coupling among these fluxes in the Edwards Plateau Balcones Fault Zone (Texas, USA) using five years (2021–2025) of daily observations of precipitation (P), soil water content (SWC), evapotranspiration (ET), runoff (Rf), and groundwater (GW). Soil water content responses to precipitation exhibited threshold-dependent behavior under both dry and wet antecedent conditions, with breakpoints at 66.9 and 32.6 mm, respectively. Evapotranspiration dynamics were jointly controlled by SWC and temperature, with strong limitations under dry soil conditions and maximum ET values occurring only under warm and wet conditions. In contrast, Rf and GW responses were highly episodic and associated with the relatively rare large precipitation events. Although both fluxes increased rapidly following rainfall inputs, Rf responses were short-lived whereas GW responses persisted for several weeks to months. Groundwater recharge exhibited a clear threshold response, occurring only after precipitation events greater than 78 mm and never following events smaller than 62 mm. On the basis of these findings, we have developed a conceptual model for semiarid karst ecosystems whereby hydrological connectivity is activated during short-lived windows created only when precipitation pulses exceed both atmospheric demand and internal storage thresholds.

papers.title: Prediction of excess pore water pressure using B-spline interpolation and artificial neural networks for soil improvement monitoring
papers.summary: Monitoring excess pore water pressure (EPWP) during and after soil improvement is essential under certain ground conditions. In some cases, ground monitoring may be required throughout the service life of a structure, particularly in areas where the subsoil is susceptible to environmental changes. However, installing sensors at every location across a construction site and its surrounding area is often impractical due to various site-specific constraints. This study proposes a spatial prediction framework that integrates B-spline interpolation and artificial neural networks (ANNs) to estimate EPWP at uninstrumented locations using simultaneous measurements from existing sensors. Experimental data reported in the published literature are extracted and processed in MATLAB to develop the ANN model and integrates results by B-spline interpolation. The network architecture is appropriately configured, and the available data are divided into training, validation, and testing subsets to evaluate predictive performance and reduce the risk of overfitting. The results indicate good agreement between the ANN predicted EPWP (kPa) at uninstrumented location and the experimental results reported in the literature. The proposed framework aims to apply these findings to EPWP monitoring and liquefaction assessment during and after soil improvement.

papers.title: Slope stability and critical thresholds of red clay under rainfall and slope‐cutting effects: A case study of Hunan Province, Central China
papers.summary: Abstract Assessing the stability and critical thresholds of red clay slopes in Central China under rainfall and excavation is crucial for effective risk mitigation. Through field investigations and laboratory tests, a representative red clay slope was characterized at both macro‐ and micro‐scales. A finite element model was developed, and three scenarios were considered: rainfall (continuous and short‐duration), slope cutting (varying height and angle) and their combined effects. The factor of safety (FoS) for each scenario was calculated using the Morgenstern–Price method to determine critical thresholds. Results show that: (1) Although the slope currently exhibits favourable stability, the high illite content presents a significant risk for softening and shallow instability under prolonged rainfall. (2) Short‐duration rainfall had minimal impact, whereas continuous rainfall reduced the FoS below 1.0, highlighting a critical sensitivity to prolonged rainfall. The FoS decreased with increasing cut height and angle, directly reducing stability, though it did not change the slope's response to rainfall. (3) The failure thresholds for the three investigated scenarios were identified as 40 mm/day for rainfall, 10 m/60° for excavation and 20 mm/day of rainfall under critical excavation conditions, demonstrating their synergistic weakening effect. This research provides practical guidance for safe excavation and rainfall early warning in red clay regions.

papers.title: Hybrid AI-Physics Modeling in Geotechnical Engineering: A Next-Generation Review of Theory-Guided Machine Learning for Smart and Resilient Infrastructure
papers.summary: Machine learning (ML) has emerged as a transformative tool in geotechnical engineering, offering data-driven alternatives to traditional empirical and analytical approaches. This paper presents a critical narrative review of recent advances in theory-guided machine learning (TGML) applications in geotechnical engineering, including soil-property prediction, constitutive modelling, pile capacity prediction, seismic soil–structure interaction, foundation performance, and slope stability. The review organizes the literature according to the physical mechanisms through which theoretical knowledge is incorporated into machine-learning methods, including physics-guided features, hybrid constitutive models, physics-informed neural networks, physics-constrained surrogates, probabilistic hybrid frameworks, and multiscale models. Emerging trends such as hybrid physics-informed models, explainable artificial intelligence (AI) frameworks, and integration with numerical simulations, real-time monitoring and data assimilation, and digital-twin-enabled infrastructure assessment are also discussed. The paper identifies key research gaps and proposes future directions for improving model robustness, reliability, and practical implementation in engineering design and infrastructure management. This review provides a structured roadmap for advancing AI-driven methodologies in geotechnical engineering, and their integration into smart and resilient infrastructure systems, while highlighting the critical issues that must be addressed for broader adoption in practice.

papers.title: Geomechanical reserves for optimizing open-pit slope design during the final mine development stage
papers.summary: This study explores the potential for additional geomechanical optimization of the slope design for deep openpit mines during the final operational stage. Feasibility of applying a reduced safety factor of 1.2 for slope sections with the Koashva deposit as a case study. The research provides a detailed analysis of the risks associated with rock mass fracturing, presence of carbonate rock, oxidation processes, and groundwater inflow. An assessment is conducted regarding the inward shift of the top edge of the slope and the consequent reduction in the overburden volume through implementation of a dedicated final development phase. Slope stability calculations were performed using the limit equilibrium method with circular slip surfaces for critical profiles of the hanging wall, where the initial safety factor equals 1.31. Results indicate that shifting the top edge into the ore body by 28.4 to 31.5 meters aligns the slope coordinates at the minus 188 meter level with the design configuration while significantly increasing recoverable reserves at the lower levels. For the adjusted contour during the final development stage, the calculated safety factor ranges from 1.24 to 1.26, fully complying with the regulatory requirements. An integrated approach that combines refined geomechanical modeling, optimized blasting operations, and a hierarchical monitoring system, slope optimization in the analyzed sector is estimated at 4.5 billion Rubles, which is equivalent to eliminating 22.9 million cubic meters of conditional overburden.

papers.title: Integrated Geological Mineralogical and Geophysical Characterisation of the Efon Alaaye Basement Terrain in Southwestern Nigeria for Slope Stability and Infrastructure Development
papers.summary: Abstract Efon Alaaye, Ekiti State in southwestern Nigeria, is located within the Precambrian Basement Complex with features of rugged topography, heterogeneous crystalline rocks with variable weathering profiles. This study combines geological mapping, structural measurements, slope assessment, natural-electric-field/electromagnetic reconnaissance survey, X-ray fluorescence (XRF) and X-ray diffraction (XRD) to define the geology of the materials and its implications for slope stability, groundwater occurrence and infrastructure development. Based on field observations granite, quartzite, schist, laterite and minor pegmatite were picked out; and the discontinuities were mainly NW-SE and NE-SW. Five slope traverses were recorded on an inclination range of 25–42°, the maximum slope inclination is 42° and this slope inclination is the greatest recon level concern due to steepness, fracturing and erosion susceptibility. The results of XRF analyses are extremely silica-rich, from 97.12 to 98.44 wt. % SiO₂, with the other major oxides present at very low levels. The diffractograms shown here indicate that quartz reflections are significant in all three samples. Reconnaissance geophysical interpretation delineates surficial material, clayey/weathered horizons, partly fractured basement and deeper basement crystalline, it can be seen that engineering behaviour is controlled by combined effects of lithology, discontinuity geometry, weathering, groundwater and slope morphology. Steep, fractured, deeply weathered and seepage prone areas should be assessed geotechnically and properly drained, and development should be avoided on these areas.Gently sloping ground with a good drainage capacity underlain by verified competent material is preferable for development, while the steep, fractured, deeply weathered and seepage prone areas require detailed geotechnical assessment and drainage control.
