Influence of Microbially Induced Calcite Precipitation on the Hydraulic and Unsaturated Behavior of Coal Mine Overburden Waste: Experimental Insights and Numerical Correlations
papers.summary: Microbially Induced Calcite Precipitation (MICP) has emerged as a sustainable ground improvement technique, however its application for enhancing the performance by improving the mechanical behavior of Coal Mine Overburden Waste (CMOW) materials is very limited. Further, the impact of MICP technique on unsaturated properties governing dump slope stability such as hydraulic conductivity, pore size distribution and Soil Water Characteristic Curves (SWCC) has not been explored. Hence, the present research works have aimed to investigate potential of MICP technique in improving the unsaturated properties CMOW material using three Bacillus family (Sporosarcina pasteurii) bacterial strains ie, SP77 (Bacillus sp.), SP78 (Bacillus sphaericus), and SP79 (Bacillus subtilis) through detailed experiments, with microstructural modifications confirmed through Field Emission Scanning Electron Microscopy (FESEM) and Mercury Intrusion Porosimetry (MIP). The SWCC response of untreated and treated CMOW is further interpreted using models by Brooks and Corey, Van Genuchten, Fredlund and Xing, and Durner, providing new insights into the role of MICP in slope stability assessment. The untreated CMOW has exhibited a relatively saturated hydraulic conductivity of 1.48 × 10−5 m/s, which is reduced to the order of 10−7 m/s after MICP treatment with S. pasteurii strains, indicating a significant improvement in hydraulic conductivity. Further, SWCC results have pronounced the bacteria strain and depth-dependent changes in water retention after MICP treatment, associated with the redistribution of pore-size domains and heterogeneous carbonate precipitation. Pore structure analysis through MIP reveals a shift from a unimodal to a bimodal distribution, corroborated by FESEM images that confirm calcite precipitation in the form of vaterite and rhombohedral crystals. Curve fitting further indicated that the Fredlund and Xing model has provided the best representation of untreated CMOW, while the Du

papers.title: Pile as a remedial measure for slope stability against vehicle induced blast loading on hill-roads
papers.summary: The present study is aimed at mitigating the detrimental effects of vehicle induced surface blast on the upward slope. The role of pile foundations as a mitigation measure to reduce blast effects is not yet well understood and is therefore investigated in the present study. The lower portion of the pile can act as an anchor, providing stiffness to the upper half. The presence of a pile at a particular location increases the stiffness of that sub-domain. This may result in fewer surface deformations than in the no-pile condition. But at the same time, it can cause substantial movement and deformation of the piles. Pile should be appropriately designed to minimize the pile deformation at the top and flexural stresses. This study presents a quantitative analysis of a sloping domain incorporating piles as a mitigation measure. The pile length, out-of-plane spacing (s), relative soil density, and ground slope are identified as critical parameters governing the system response. A parametric study was conducted to demonstrate their influence. Lateral displacement and PPV of surface points and the pile head are considered response parameters. With an increase in the slope angle, overburden on the right side increases, offering greater passive resistance and resulting in a drop in surface displacements at the toe. At smaller pile spacing, the equivalent pile stiffness increases, leading to a decrease in surface displacement.

papers.title: Analysis of Slope Stability of Spoil Grounds Under the Coupling Effect of Reservoir Water Level Rise and Rainfall Infiltration
papers.summary: To investigate the seepage evolution and instability mechanism of gully-type spoil ground slopes under the coupled effect of reservoir water level rise and rainfall infiltration, a typical second-grade gully-type spoil ground of the Jinghe Dongzhuang Water Conservancy Hub was selected as the case study. The SEEP/W and SLOPE/W modules of GeoStudio were employed to perform coupled numerical simulations of unsaturated seepage and slope stability. The reservoir water level was set to rise from 90 m to 120 m at a rate of 1.2 m/d, combined with six continuous rainfall intensities (duration: 25 days) of 20, 40, 80, 120, 160, and 200 mm/d. Reference scenarios involving only reservoir water level rise and only rainfall infiltration were additionally considered. The zoning response characteristics of pore water pressure at the slope front and rear were analyzed, and the individual contributions and coupled effect of rainfall and reservoir water level were quantitatively distinguished using a contribution decomposition method. The results indicate that the pore water pressure at the slope front is mainly governed by reservoir water level rise, whereas the pore water pressure at the slope rear is highly sensitive to rainfall infiltration. As the rainfall intensity increases from 20 mm/d to 200 mm/d, the factor of safety under the coupled condition decreases from 1.611 to 0.969. Furthermore, the dominant factor of instability evolves with rainfall intensity: the contribution decomposition results show that under higher rainfall intensities (80–200 mm/d), the rainfall-only contribution rate ranges from 43.6% to 57.0%, while, under lower rainfall intensities (20–40 mm/d), reservoir water level rise becomes the dominant factor. Throughout all coupled scenarios, the additional coupling contribution rate ranges from 18.2% to 52.9%, indicating a significant non-additive coupled hazard effect between the two factors. papers.title: Highly selective cholesterol detection using a cholesterol oxidase-functionalized open-cavity fiber-optic Mach–Zehnder biosensor
Water Seepage Induced Deformation and Stability Control of Weakly Cemented Soft-Rock Roadway
papers.summary: Abstract Long-term groundwater seepage promotes continuous water–rock interaction, resulting in progressive deterioration of weakly cemented soft rock and posing significant challenges to the long-term stability of underground excavations. To investigate the deformation and failure mechanisms and stability control of argillaceous weakly cemented soft-rock roadways under long-term water-seepage conditions, the 110803 working face in Qingshuiying coal mine was selected as the engineering background. Field investigation, theoretical analysis, numerical simulation, and in-situ monitoring were conducted. The results indicate that the surrounding rock is dominated by argillaceous weakly cemented soft rock and has undergone significant deterioration under long-term water seepage. The original support system is characterized by a weak anchoring foundation, low prestress, and insufficient bearing capacity, which limits effective deformation control. Based on the changes in the slope and deformation rate of the convergence curve, the roadway deformation process is divided into three stages: initial rapid deformation, intermediate accelerated deformation, and late slow deformation. A coupled progressive failure mechanism involving water seepage and three weak links is identified, including water-induced softening and swelling of the roof rock, a weak anchoring foundation, a weak prestress transmission layer, and low surrounding-rock bearing capacity. These factors drive deformation from local damage toward global instability, with water–rock interaction acting as the dominant driving factor. Accordingly, a control strategy of water isolation and threefold strengthening is proposed to isolate water from the surrounding rock and enhance anchoring capacity, prestress transmission, and overall rock-mass strength. A fully enclosed support system comprising roof control, sidewall reinforcement, and floor strengthening is developed. Field application demonstrates that the proposed me

papers.title: Regional-scale assessment of climate change impacts on land use–specific hydrological processes in the Geum River Basin, South Korea
papers.summary: Study region Geum River Basin, South Korea, East Asia Study focus Climate change is expected to substantially modify hydrological processes: however, the mechanisms underlying these changes remain highly dependent on regional characteristics and land use patterns. In this study, we provide a regional-scale assessment of the effects of climate change on land use specifics hydrological processes in the Geum River Basin, South Korea, which is a key water-supply region characterized by rapid urbanization and a mixture of agricultural– and forested landscapes. New hydrological insights for the region Climate change is intensifying hydrological variability across the Geum River Basin, with fast-response components such as surface runoff generally increasing. However, slow-response components, particularly groundwater recharge and baseflow, are projected to decline. Runoff sensitivities to precipitation and temperature exhibit three distinct response patterns corresponding to urban land, agricultural land, and forestland–grassland, demonstrating that climate drivers propagate through hydrological processes in land use–specific ways. Although projected increases in precipitation enhance meteorological resilience, they do not necessarily translate into improved hydrological water availability, especially in highly urbanized sub-basins. These findings highlight the importance of regionally tailored adaptation strategies. For the Geum River Basin, expanding storage capacity, conserving permeable and vegetated surfaces, and improving seasonal water allocation are identified as priority measures for sustaining water and ecosystem resilience under future climate conditions.

papers.title: Extreme precipitation rapidly recharges desiccated deep soil and restores deep root water uptake in a rainfed apple orchard: Implications for water management in deep-rooted agroecosystems
papers.summary: Deep soil water is a critical resource for deep-rooted tree crops in water-limited regions, yet progressive desiccation of deep layers under rainfed plantations may erode the long-term drought resilience of these systems and threaten their productivity. However, the extent to which extreme rainfall events can recharge desiccated deep soil and restore deep root water uptake remains poorly quantified. To address this gap, we used the 2021 extreme wet year, when annual precipitation reached 920 mm—approximately 1.6 times the long-term mean—as a natural experiment in a mature rainfed apple orchard on the Loess Plateau of China. We compared soil water dynamics down to 20 m, tree transpiration, and stable-isotope-based water source partitioning in 2017 and 2023, representing conditions before and after the extreme wet year, to quantify how extreme precipitation altered deep soil water reserves and plant water use. Extreme precipitation rapidly replenished the 3–10 m soil layer, increasing water storage by about 350 mm. The infiltration rate reached 5 m yr⁻1—approximately 25 times faster than previously reported piston flow rates, indicating preferential-flow-dominated deep recharge. This replenishment reduced transpiration stress: despite a lower leaf area index in 2023 than in 2017, actual transpiration increased from 213 to 232 mm, and the Ta/Tp ratio rose from 0.57 ± 0.24 to 0.78 ± 0.31. In addition, the contribution of soil water from 3–10 m depth to transpiration increased from 50 ± 12% in 2017 to 62 ± 12% in 2023, indicating a shift in water uptake from shallow to deeper soil layers. These findings demonstrate that episodic extreme precipitation can reverse deep soil desiccation in deep-rooted rainfed orchards, and provide a quantitative basis for rainwater-harvesting and infiltration-enhancing strategies that convert such events into a hydraulic buffer against drought in water-limited agricultural regions under a changing climate.

papers.title: Impacts of post-fire straw mulching on plant diversity dynamics and mid-term persistence of introduced weed species in a Mediterranean chronosequence
papers.summary: Post-fire straw mulching is widely used to reduce soil erosion and facilitate vegetation recovery in fire-affected ecosystems. However, straw mulch may introduce agricultural weedy species, raising concerns about their persistence and potential effects on post-fire plant community assembly. This study evaluated the medium-term ecological implications of straw mulch application using a post-fire chronosequence in semi-arid Mediterranean ecosystems of southeastern Spain. Vegetation was surveyed in 54 plots (27 mulched and 27 untreated) distributed across sites representing 1, 2 and 6 years after fire (YAF). Species richness, diversity, composition and the abundance of agricultural weedy species were analysed to assess treatment effects across the chronosequence. Straw mulching increased species richness and diversity during the early post-fire stages, through the introduction of agricultural weedy species. Community composition differed significantly among post-fire stages and between treatments, although post-fire stage explained a substantially larger proportion of the variation than mulching treatment. The abundance of agricultural weedy species declined markedly along the chronosequence, and these species showed very low abundance at the site representing 6 YAF. Plant communities in mulched and untreated plots became more similar at the latest stage represented in the chronosequence. Overall, the results suggest that straw mulching can temporarily enhance plant diversity during early post-fire recovery without evidence of negative medium-term effects on vegetation recovery under the environmental conditions evaluated in this study. These findings support the use of straw mulching as a post-fire restoration measure in semi-arid Mediterranean ecosystems while highlighting the importance of considering straw provenance when assessing early community responses.

papers.title: Coupled Effects of Burial Depth and Surface Double Cracks on the Uplift Bearing Capacity of Strip Anchor Plates in Red Clay
papers.summary: Prolonged drought can induce shrinkage cracking in near-surface clay foundations, leaving persistent defects that may affect the uplift safety of underground structures before subsequent rainfall events. This study investigates how burial depth regulates the influence of two pre-existing surface cracks on the uplift bearing capacity and failure mechanism of a horizontal strip anchor plate in red clay. A two-dimensional plane-strain model was established in Optum G2 and validated against laboratory pull-out tests under crack-free conditions. Two burial-depth ratios, H/B = 3 and 8, were examined, and 360 cases were generated by varying normalized crack depth (h/B = 0.25–3), spacing (s/B = 0.25–3), and horizontal offset (d/B = 0–6). Under shallow burial, cracks readily intersect the potential sliding zone and the maximum capacity reduction reaches 81.6%, with pronounced transitions around s/B = 1 and d/B = 1. Under deep burial, the principal failure surface remains predominantly a deep elliptical arc and capacity reduction is generally below 15%. Burial depth therefore controls the spatial overlap between the environmentally damaged zone and the anchor-bearing zone. The results provide a mechanical basis for post-drought crack inspection, uplift-safety reassessment, and burial-depth selection. Hydraulic infiltration, suction, moisture evolution, and rainfall intensity are outside the present model.

papers.title: Modelling the spatial dynamics of flood inundation in Bayelsa State, Nigeria, using remote sensing and machine learning techniques
papers.summary: Abstract Flooding is a persistent environmental challenge in Bayelsa State, Nigeria, driven by low-lying terrain, high rainfall, and inadequate drainage systems. This study evaluates flood susceptibility in the Lower Niger Basin using a geospatial modelling approach. Ten flood-conditioning factors; rainfall, drainage density, slope, elevation, soil texture, land use/land cover (LULC), Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), and proximity to rivers were integrated within a Random Forest (RF) framework. Spatial datasets were processed using ArcGIS and Google Earth Engine, and the model was trained with historical flood and non-flood locations to produce a high-resolution susceptibility map. Results indicate that areas receiving 2500 to 3199 mm of annual rainfall, particularly Southern Ijaw, Ekeremor, and Brass, exhibit the highest flood susceptibility. Over 82% of the region is characterized by low slopes (0 to 3°) and elevations ranging from 16 to 41 m, increasing flood vulnerability. High drainage density zones (up to 0.677 km/km²) contribute to flash flooding, while clay and sandy clay loam soils (covering > 60% of the area) reduce infiltration and enhance runoff. Built-up areas and regions with NDVI < 0.1 are also associated with higher flood risk. The RF model achieved an accuracy of 91%, with high-risk zones predominantly located within 1 km of major rivers. This study demonstrates the effectiveness of integrating machine learning with geospatial analysis for flood susceptibility mapping in data-scarce, low-lying environments. The resulting map provides a reliable decision-support tool for flood risk management, land-use planning, and targeted mitigation strategies in Bayelsa State.

papers.title: Rainfall infiltration-induced vertical differentiation of pore structure and permeability in mine tailings: a throat-dominated mechanism
papers.source: International Journal of Mining Reclamation and Environment
papers.summary: Seepage-induced particle migration in tailings alters pore structures, risking dam stability. This study quantitatively assesses vertical pore structure differentiation during sustained rainfall infiltration using micro-CT and pore network modelling (PNM). Results show that total porosity varies by 5%, while connected porosity declines by nearly 20%. Surface layers develop high-connectivity networks via throat expansion, while deep-layer networks degrade due to pore isolation and particle depletion. PNM simulations validate that throat radius governs permeability evolution, showing significantly higher sensitivity than pore radius, consistent with Hagen-Poiseuille law. This reveals heterogeneous permeability distributions, indicating that characterising pore network topology is essential for understanding tailings seepage behaviour.

papers.title: Component-dependent sensitivity in tracking rainfall-related seismic velocity changes with a single-station at a tropical weathered soil site in central Brazil
papers.summary: Abstract Rainfall infiltration influences mechanical properties of the near surface and plays a fundamental role in controlling subsurface hydrological processes. Seismic ambient noise-based methods have emerged as valuable, non-invasive tools for monitoring hydrological dynamics. In this study, we investigate seismic velocity variations (δν/ν) derived from the coda portion of same-component autocorrelations and cross-component correlations of ambient seismic noise recorded by a single triaxial station installed at the Água Limpa Farm, in Brasília, Brazil. The objective of this work is to evaluate how δν/ν computed from different component combinations respond to precipitation and to assess whether rainfall-related hydrological processes can be tracked through single-station monitoring. A total of 420 days of continuous seismic data were acquired using a RaspberryShake RS3D sensor and processed through a workflow involving preprocessing, phase cross-correlation, temporal stacking, and velocity variation estimation via the Moving Window Cross-Spectral (MWCS) method. Seismic velocity series were then compared with rainfall records and Change Point Analysis was applied to identify significant velocity drops. Most component pairs showed increasing δν/ν during the climatological dry period and decreasing values during the rainy period, although component-dependent differences were observed. Strong correlations were observed between δν/ν drops and cumulative rainfall, particularly for horizontal component combinations. In contrast, vertical-component autocorrelations showed weaker and less consistent relationships with precipitation. We interpret the seismic velocity variations derived from single-station cross-component ambient-noise analysis as consistent with hydrological modulation. Moreover, the observed component-dependent sensitivity highlights the importance of incorporating multi-component data to enhance the detection and interpretation of subsurface hydromechan

papers.title: Numerical simulation and monitoring experiment of liquid injection diffusion range in ionic rare earth ores
papers.summary: Abstract Currently, in-situ leaching is the predominant method for extracting ionic rare earth ores. However, this technique still faces persistent challenges such as low resource utilization efficiency and environmental issues including water and soil contamination. Clarifying the diffusion characteristics of the leach liquid is crucial for addressing these problems. Geophysical methods, particularly conductive electrical techniques, have been widely employed to monitor the diffusion range of the leach liquid. Nevertheless, these methods suffer from limitations such as operational complexity, high costs, and poor timeliness. To overcome these drawbacks, this study first utilizes numerical simulation to determine the influence range of liquid injection, and subsequently evaluates the effectiveness of the high-density resistivity method in delineating its diffusion extent. Based on the deep structural characteristics of a rare earth mine in Fujian, China, identified through high-density resistivity method, a suitable site was selected for a comparative experiment. The experiment compared time-lapse resistivity tomography monitoring with seepage numerical simulations of liquid injection faced actual geological model, and the results demonstrated good consistency in the diffusion ranges identified by both methods. Through theoretical analysis and comparative monitoring results, this study proposes that the integrated approach of “detailed deep structure investigation & seepage numerical simulation of liquid injection” can effectively characterize the diffusion behavior of the leach liquor. This provides theoretical support for the precise placement of injection wells and the design of anti-seepage systems in ionic rare earth mining. contributing to improved mineral recovery rates and reduced environmental pollution from liquid injection.

papers.title: Modelling-Based Assessment of Managed Aquifer Recharge: Impacts on Groundwater Quantity and Quality in the Upper Friuli Plain (Italy)
papers.summary: In the Friuli Venezia Giulia (FVG) region of northeastern Italy, declining groundwater levels and changing precipitation patterns have raised concerns about the long-term sustainability of groundwater resources. This study evaluates the potential of Managed Aquifer Recharge (MAR) in the upper Friuli Plain, with a focus on the Sammardenchia site. Surface water and groundwater quality in the study area were characterized through the analysis of inorganic and organic compounds, as well as microbiological indicators. A three-dimensional groundwater flow model was developed to simulate the regional and local site-specific hydrogeological conditions. MAR performance was assessed under different recharge scenarios, including an infiltration pond, a recharge well, and a combined pond-well recharge, based on the existing recharge structures at the site. In addition, solute transport simulations were conducted to analyze the behaviour of faecal indicator bacteria (E. coli), detected in the surface water to be used for MAR. The simulation results show that recharge through both the infiltration pond and the well increased the groundwater levels near the MAR site, with the combined recharge scenario producing the highest simulated rise in groundwater levels (~ 2.68 m) and storage. Microbial transport simulations showed substantial attenuation of E. coli during subsurface transport, particularly under the pond-recharge scenario (> 4 log) due to longer residence times. Overall, the modelling results indicate that MAR can effectively contribute to groundwater storage enhancement and attenuation of microbial contamination in the study area. Combined pond−well recharge shows the greatest potential to increase groundwater storage. Longer travel times help reduce simulated E. coli concentrations in groundwater. Different recharge configurations offer distinct benefits, depending on groundwater management objectives.

papers.title: Forest structural mediation of hydrological processes and ecosystem multifunctionality: mechanisms, trade-offs, and adaptive management
papers.source: Frontiers in Forests and Global Change
papers.summary: Forests provide multiple ecosystem services, including water regulation, water supply, soil retention, carbon sequestration, habitat provision, biodiversity conservation, and timber production. These services arise from coupled processes operating across vegetation, litter, soil, and watershed compartments. Changes in climate, land use, forest structure, or management can therefore alter several services simultaneously, but the direction of change depends on the process pathway, environmental context, and scale of assessment. Here, we synthesize advances in the quantitative assessment of interactions between forest hydrological functions and other ecosystem services, emphasizing how environmental drivers and management reorganize forest structure, how structural states alter hydrological partitioning and water-carbon coupling, and how these process changes propagate to ecosystem-service outcomes. We first establish a process-based framework covering canopy interception, throughfall, stemflow, litter interception, infiltration, evapotranspiration, soil-water storage, deep drainage, groundwater recharge, lateral flow, baseflow, and surface runoff. We then evaluate field experiments, watershed observations, process-based and ecosystem-service models, spatial statistics, machine learning, and causal inference, with explicit attention to their assumptions and scale limitations. Quantitative evidence from global thinning syntheses and classical catchment experiments is used to distinguish relatively consistent responses from context-dependent ones. A long-term Korean pine forest-management experiment on Changbai Mountain is included as an illustrative case study: the treatments persisted for 27 years, whereas the hydrological measurements summarized here represent observations made in 2023 rather than a continuous 27-year hydrological time series. The case illustrates how post-treatment structural states are associated with differences in precipitation partitioning and so

papers.title: Combined aeromagnetic, GIS, and remote sensing evaluation of flash-flood susceptibility and groundwater potential in an arid environment: Wadi Marwani, Western Saudi Arabia
papers.summary: Introduction Groundwater is the primary dependable freshwater source in the arid coastal catchments of western Saudi Arabia, where natural recharge is limited and occurs mainly through episodic rainfall and flash‐flood infiltration along wadi systems. This study assesses groundwater potential in the Wadi Marwani basin (≈2,347 km 2 ), a major tributary of the Khulais system southeast of Rabigh, by integrating multi‐source remote sensing, GIS, and aeromagnetic data. Methods Lithology was mapped from Sentinel‐2 imagery using support vector machine (SVM) classification, while structural fabrics were constrained using Sentinel‐1C SAR lineaments and aeromagnetic structural analysis. Terrain attributes (e.g., elevation, slope, drainage and flow indices, topographic wetness, and ruggedness) derived from a 30 m digital elevation model (DEM), together with NDVI, soil moisture, rainfall, and 10 m land‐cover data, characterized the surface conditions that control infiltration and storage. Aeromagnetic data were reduced to the pole, upward continued, and enhanced using the modified Elliott function (MEF) filter and Center for Exploration Targeting (CET) grid analysis. Source Parameter Imaging (SPI) was then applied to estimate relative depth to magnetic basement. Results Surface and magnetic lineaments consistently define a dominant N–S to NNW–SSE trend with subsidiary NW–SE and NE–SW sets that remain coherent at depth, reflecting reactivated Pan–African structures. A magnetically subdued, elongate basement depression along the central wadi axis, widening westwards, coincides with high lineament density and thick Quaternary alluvium, indicating favorable conditions for groundwater accumulation. The integrated groundwater potential map divides the basin into five classes; comparison with existing wells yields an AUC of 0.789, indicating acceptable to good predictive skill. papers.title: SlopeTH
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: SlopeTH is a stand-alone Windows program for two-dimensional slope stability analysis by the limitequilibrium method. It finds the critical circular slip surface and reports the factor of safety (FS) by fivemethods, for dry, saturated and unsaturated soils, reinforced and improved ground, earth dams andslopes under rainfall. Main features Methods: Ordinary (Fellenius), Simplified Bishop, Janbu simplified (with correction factor f0),Spencer and Morgenstern-Price (half-sine), the last two by the general limit equilibrium (GLE)formulation. Geometry: any number of soil layers, polygon material regions (e.g. the clay core of a dam),bedrock (impenetrable) materials, slopes facing left or right, choice of slip direction. Water: phreatic surface or pore-pressure ratio ru; reservoir (ponded) water on the slope face; rapiddrawdown. Unsaturated soils: matric suction by the φb, Khalili or Vanapalli models; soil-water characteristiccurve (SWCC) by van Genuchten, Fredlund-Xing, Brooks-Corey or Gardner; hydraulic conductivityfrom the SWCC. Suction profiles: hydrostatic, constant, steady rainfall/evaporation flux, and transient rainfallinfiltration by the Richards equation, giving FS against time. Ground improvement: geotextiles, geogrids, soil nails and anchors; pile and cement-column rows(piled embankments); improved-ground zones (DCM blocks) with a composite-strength calculator. Loads: surcharges and a pseudo-static seismic coefficient kh. Search: grid of centres × tangent lines with FS contours and automatic refinement. Output: text report, slice-by-slice table, FS-time chart, pore-pressure contours, CSV export andfigures in PNG, PDF or SVG. Units. SlopeTH uses kN, m, kPa, kN/m³, degrees, seconds (hydraulic conductivity in m/s) and hours(rainfall time). Rainfall intensity is in mm/h.Copyright and disclaimer. SlopeTH version 1.0. papers.title: Drought to Flood Abrupt Alternation Events Across Monsoon Region in China: Characteristics, Mechanisms, and Crop Exposure
papers.summary: Abstract Climate change is altering the frequency and intensity of hydroclimatic extremes, increasing the likelihood of drought to flood abrupt alternation (DTFAA) events which creates compound risks. Here, we identify DTFAA events across the monsoon region of China (MRC) during May–September from 1961 to 2023 using the daily Standardized Weighted Average Precipitation index. We identify 3,575 DTFAA events, with most transitions occurring within 1–2 days and a modest maximum in June. Generally, DTFAA frequency and intensity in MRC increase significantly at rates of 0.29 times decade⁻¹ and 0.26 decade⁻¹, respectively, with high frequencies concentrated in the middle and lower Yangtze River Basin, southern coastal China, and parts of North and Southwest China. Dynamically, governed by jet-waveguide interaction, the transition initiates with high-latitude easterly anomalies anchoring upstream blocking and the westward-extending subtropic high priming baroclinicity. Subsequently, the intensified and westward-extending subtropical jet establishes a mid-latitude meridional potential vorticity gradient conduit, routing trapped energy in blocking downstream to drive deep dynamic suction and moisture convergence, unleashing the abrupt flooding. Furthermore, crop exposure is crop-specific heterogeneous: maize and wheat show extensive high-exposure belts, whereas rice exposure is more fragmented; maize exhibits significant increases in both frequency and intensity exposure during 2000–2019. These results demonstrate that DTFAA events in the MRC arise from coordinated large-scale circulation and moisture-transport processes and that their agricultural consequences are strongly crop and region dependent, providing a dynamical and impact-oriented framework for improving monitoring, prediction, and adaptation to rapid hydroclimatic transitions.

papers.title: Management of Stormwater through Green Infrastructure Systems in Coastal Urban Areas: Hydrological Modelling, Compound-Flood Response, and Water-Quality Performance
papers.source: AlQalam Journal of Medical and Applied Sciences
papers.summary: In seven different GI scenarios, a representative 120 ha coastal urban drainage catchment, typical of Alexandria, Egypt, on the Mediterranean coast of the Nile Delta, was analyzed using SWMM 5.2 with its low impact development (LID) extension. The scenarios included four single-practice scenarios: green roof, permeable pavement, bioretention cell, and infiltration trench, each aimed at mitigating 20% of the impervious area, and three mixed portfolios with targets of 10%, 20%, and 30% impervious areas (MIX10, MIX20, MIX30). The catchment has an area-weighted imperviousness of 81.9%, and drainage is discharged from the tide gate to receive storm surge, astronomical tide, and sea-level rise (SLR) scenarios of +0.0, +0.5, and +1.0 m, together with an incrementally diminishing infiltration capacity due to rising shallow coastal groundwater levels. For a 10-year 2-hour return period design storm of 39.7 mm, baseline simulation provided 0.79 runoff coefficient, 14.09 m³/s of peak runoff, and 11,693 m³ of system flooding. Scenarios MIX30 reduced 27.9%, 35.1%, and 59.5% of runoff volume, peak runoff, and flood volume, respectively. Permeable pavement resulted in the largest flood volume reduction (56.9%) among single practices. Efficacy of GI systems decreased with an increase in storm size, as flood-volume reduction for MIX30 varied from 88.6% for a 2-year storm to 42.9% for a 50-year storm. A SLR scenario of +1.0 m increased baseline flooding by 17.1% and MIX30 flooding by 30.5%, hence decreasing the flood-volume reduction efficacy of MIX30 from 59.5% to 54.8%, including 204 m³ of water caused by limitations in infiltration associated with rising shallow groundwater level. Event loadings of total suspended solids (TSS), total nitrogen (TN), and total phosphorus (TP) were reduced with MIX30 by 44.4%, 40.5%, and 39.6%, respectively. A Monte Carlo Analysis (60 runs for each scenario) revealed that differences between BL, MIX20, and MIX30 scenarios were statistically significa

papers.title: Soil erosion response to future climate variability and best management practices in the Kesinga catchment, India
papers.summary: Abstract Soil erosion poses a growing threat to watershed sustainability under changing climatic conditions, particularly in monsoon-dominated regions. This study integrates the Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT) with bias-corrected CORDEX–South Asia climate projections to quantify present and future sediment yield and to evaluate the effectiveness of structural best management practices (BMPs) in the Kesinga catchment, eastern India. The watershed was delineated into 33 sub-catchments, and model calibration and validation (2003–2020) demonstrated very good performance for streamflow during calibration (NSE = 0.86) and good performance during validation (NSE = 0.72). Sediment-yield performance was satisfactory during calibration (NSE = 0.52) but unsatisfactory during validation (NSE = 0.49), according to the performance criteria adopted in this study. Future projections under RCP4.5 and RCP8.5 scenarios indicate increases in streamflow (26–73%) and sediment yield (5–36%), with the greatest amplification under end-century RCP8.5 conditions; these sediment projections should be interpreted in light of the unsatisfactory validation performance. Spatial analysis revealed persistent sediment hotspots in central and eastern sub-catchments, where high slope gradients and projected precipitation intensification interact to enhance erosion risk. Across the future periods and scenarios, 40.2–51.2% of the catchment area was projected to fall within the severe-to-extreme erosion categories, with the highest proportion occurring under end-century RCP8.5. Structural BMPs, including grassed waterways (GWW) and vegetative filter strips (VFS), were implemented in priority sub-catchments. Under historical conditions, VFS and GWW reduced soil loss by 13% and 25%, respectively, while their combined application achieved up to 38% reduction. Although absolute sediment loads increased under future climates, combined BMP implementation consistently mitigated erosion by 27–36%, demonstra

papers.title: Context-specific targeting of conservation agriculture reduces short-term yield penalty risk for maize and beans in Rwanda
papers.summary: Context and Objective Soil erosion is a major threat to smallholder farming systems in Rwanda. Terraces, while effective, are costly and reduce cultivable land area. Conservation agriculture (CA) offers a promising complementary practice if short-term yield penalties relative to current tillage (CT) remain acceptable to farmers. We assessed the seasonal and cumulative yield performance of a CA system relative to CT, farmers’ perceptions of soil erosion control under CA, and the site-level conditions under which CA yields remain within farmer-acceptable bounds. Methods A CA system combining reduced tillage, intercropped cover crops, and residue retention in a maize–bean rotation was evaluated over six cropping seasons (three years) across 473 farms in ten agroecological zones of Rwanda. A farmer-informed threshold for acceptable CA yield performance (CA:CT yield ratio ≥ 0.90) was derived from the empirical relationship between observed yield ratios and farmers' stated adoption intentions. Random forest models were used to identify site-level drivers of CA performance, and to inform a targeting approach based on observable field characteristics. Results and conclusions On average, CA yields were 19% lower than CT for maize and 24% lower for beans, yet farmers consistently perceived erosion reduction under CA, highlighting a trade-off between short-term yield penalties and longer-term soil protection. The amount of mulch cover at planting, accumulated rainfall, and weed pressure were the key drivers of CA performance. Site-level targeting increased the probability of achieving acceptable yield performance from 30% to 50%, though only ~20% of sites were initially identified as suitable for CA. Site-level targeting offers a realistic pathway to managing the trade-off between short-term yield penalties and longer-term soil protection benefits of CA. papers.title: Comment on egusphere-2026-5806 - No compliance with the code and data policy
papers.summary: Abstract. Groundwater is the largest store of liquid fresh water, yet because it is hidden beneath the surface, it is primarily understood through models of porous-media flow. Richards' equation, a physically faithful description of variably saturated groundwater flow, remains costly for basin-scale groundwater modelling. Consequently, operational models use reduced physics, either by assuming linearity or by using approximate solutions. Here, we introduce a scalable, open-source, three-dimensional solver for variably saturated groundwater flow implemented in G-ADOPT, an automated finite-element platform built on Firedrake. The implementation combines a locally conservative discontinuous Galerkin discretisation, Newton iteration with an exact Jacobian, implicit time integration through the Irksome library, used here with Backward Euler, and vertically lumped multigrid preconditioners designed for the extreme aspect ratios of production scenarios. We verify accuracy, convergence, and strict local mass conservation on two- and three-dimensional benchmarks, and apply the solver to the Lower Murrumbidgee floodplain in New South Wales, Australia. The model covers approximately 30 000 km², contains several hundred million degrees of freedom, and uses public stratigraphic, rainfall, and water-table data. Our scaling experiments show that the effectiveness of the preconditioner is controlled primarily by the physical regime in which the model is integrated. A single-level method (e.g., block-Jacobi ILU(0)) suffices at the short time steps of an infiltration study, but at seasonal time steps, the admissible time step decreases significantly under horizontal refinement. In a near-saturated profile without specific storage, such single-level methods do not converge at any tested step size. By contrast, a vertically lumped coarse-space preconditioner takes the full three-month step on every mesh, requiring four to ten linear iterations per Newton step and reducing wall-clock ti

papers.title: Hydro-chemical Evolution and Groundwater Quality Dynamics under the Influence of Narmada Canal Irrigation in the Sanchore Region of Jalore District, Rajasthan, India
papers.source: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology
papers.summary: Groundwater is the main and last source of water for residential and agricultural use. The present paper deals with the influence of Narmada Canal irrigation system in the dry zone of low rainfall regions of the western Rajasthan namely the Sanchore area of Jalore district on ground water recharge, agricultural development and chemical features of the water. The present study deals with the assessment of hydro-chemical composition and groundwater quality in the command area of canal irrigation. Groundwater samples were collected from selected villages and analyzed for key physicochemical parameters like pH, Electrical Conductivity (EC), Total Dissolved Solids (TDS), Total Hardness (TH), Calcium, Magnesium, Bicarbonate, Chloride, Sulfate, Nitrate and Fluoride using standard analytical methods. The results showed that the Groundwater is generally neutral to slightly alkaline and the dissolved ion concentrations showed significant regional variation due to water-rock interactions, mineral dissolution, evaporation, canal seepage, irrigation return flow and agricultural activities. The results of the study show that the hydro-chemical character of groundwater in the area is controlled by natural geochemical processes and anthropogenic activities. The present study will be helpful in analyzing the groundwater quality, sustainable irrigation, water resource planning and long-term groundwater management in the Narmada Canal command region of western Rajasthan.

papers.title: Progressive shallow deformation of a railway-adjacent loess slope under sequential rainfall and train-induced vibration: field evidence from dynamic and hydraulic monitoring
Research on risk assessment and control of water level rising during operation of Jinan Metro based on similar physical model experiments
papers.summary: Introduction Underground metro structures can obstruct groundwater flow, causing upstream water-level rise and pore-pressure redistribution. This study investigates the groundwater-blocking effect associated with Jinan Metro and evaluates measures for reducing the resulting engineering risk. Methods A physical model system was developed to reproduce groundwater seepage during metro station construction and operation under different hydraulic gradients and diversion conditions. Pore-water pressure responses were monitored, and repeated tests were conducted to assess measurement repeatability. Six indicators were selected for risk assessment, with subjective and objective weights determined using the analytic hierarchy process and principal component analysis, respectively. TOPSIS and a normal cloud model were applied to 12 validation cases. Results Without diversion, the maximum upstream water-level rise reached 2.10 m at a hydraulic gradient of 0.07. Diversion reduced water-level backwater by 74.07%–98.09% across the tested conditions. The 3,000 mm 2 gravel channel provided the greatest reduction, while the 700 mm 2 gravel channel and the seven connecting pipes of 5 mm diameter also performed effectively. The normal cloud model agreed with the reference results in 75.00% of cases, compared with 58.33% for TOPSIS. Discussion The experiments clarify the mechanisms of local groundwater blocking and support the selection of diversion measures and risk-based engineering controls. The normal cloud model showed better agreement within the tested cases; however, the limited validation sample and simplified aquifer representation require further verification using site-specific monitoring and hydrogeological data.

papers.title: Assessment of hydrological response and water balance components using the Variable Infiltration Capacity model in the Cauvery River Basin, India
papers.summary: Accurate estimation of water balance components at the river basin scale is essential for sustainable water resources management, particularly in regions experiencing increasing climatic variability and growing anthropogenic pressures. The Cauvery River Basin, one among the major river basins of peninsular India is taken up in this study. This study presents a comprehensive water balance analysis of the Cauvery River Basin using the Variable Infiltration Capacity (VIC) model integrated with satellite based remote sensing datasets. Meteorological forcing from the India Meteorological Department (IMD), MODIS-derived vegetation parameters, and Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM) topographic data were used to capture the spatial heterogeneity of the basin. Long term simulations were performed for the period 1951–2019 to assess the spatial and temporal variability of surface and subsurface components. The results indicate pronounced interannual variability in rainfall, which strongly influences runoff generation, while evapotranspiration remains a relatively stable and dominant loss component across the basin. Reduced rainfall during the late 1990s and early 2000s resulted in diminished runoff and increased hydrological stress, whereas post 2005 conditions show partial recovery in basin water availability. The runoff-to-rainfall coefficient and evapotranspiration ratio for the basin are estimated as 0.26 and 0.68, respectively. Reservoir representations were incorporated to analyze inflow dynamics for major reservoirs. Model performance evaluation demonstrated overall good agreement between simulated and observed discharge, with stronger performance at Hemavathy (r = 0.93, NSE = 0.87, KGE = 0.93; RMSE = 72.68 m3/s, MAE = 37.43 m3/s, PBIAS = -4.47%) compared to Krishna Raja Sagara (r = 0.85, NSE = 0.68, KGE = 0.13; RMSE = 116.26 m3/s, MAE = 68.99 m3/s, PBIAS = 23.33%). Overall, the integration of remote sensing datasets with the VIC framework provides a robust approac

papers.title: Physically Based Rainfall Intensity–Duration Thresholds for Multilayered Slope Stability and Early Warning Strategies
papers.summary: Natural slopes commonly exhibit stratified soil profiles due to depositional and pedogenic processes, and differences in hydraulic properties between soil layers can affect rainfall infiltration and slope stability. However, conventional rainfall intensity–duration (I–D) threshold curves are generally developed under the assumption of homogeneous slopes and therefore cannot adequately represent the hydraulic responses and failure mechanisms of multilayered slopes. This study evaluates the stability of multilayered unsaturated slopes using critical suction stress–depth profiles and establishes physically based rainfall I–D threshold curves to investigate the effects of permeability contrasts and interlayer failure mechanisms. The results indicate that interlayer failure mechanisms are a key factor controlling the stability of multilayered slopes. During rainfall infiltration, pore-water pressure development is strongly dependent on soil-layer configuration and hydraulic conditions, causing the distribution and relative position of rainfall threshold curves to vary with failure depth and rainfall pattern. These variations may alter the threshold criteria and lead to prediction errors in practical early warning applications. Accordingly, an adjustment framework for early warning strategies is proposed for multilayered slopes to improve the applicability and reliability of rainfall threshold curves under stratified geological conditions.

papers.title: Raised bed with modified furrow system and supplemental irrigation for sustainable dryland agriculture in Alfisols of semi-arid India
papers.summary: Aim: To develop an improved rainwater harvesting technique for field crops in drylands, and to study its efficacy to promote moisture conservation, mitigate soil erosion, in order to enhance crop productivity and water use efficiency. Methodology: This experiment was laid out in a strip-plot design with soil and water conservation (SWC) treatments and supplemental irrigation during 2021 to 2023 with maize -pigeonpea crop rotation. The SWC treatments were: M1- Raised bed with modified furrow system (RBMF); M2- RBMF with coir pith compost; M3- RBMF with farmyard manure; M4- RBMF with tank silt and M5- Control (without raised bed/ Farmers practice). The irrigation treatments were: I0-No irrigation (NI); I1-With supplemental irrigation using sub-surface (10 cm) drip (SSDI) and I2-With supplemental irrigation using surface drip (SDI) in three replications. Maize and pigeonpea was taken up in alternate years. The observations included soil physical and chemical properties, runoff, soil loss and grain yield. Results: During normal year, RBMF with coir pith compost or farmyard manure in the furrows increased the grain yield in maize by 17.0-18.4% and pigeonpea yield by 38.2 -54.2%, respectively.These treatments improved the soil moisture by 2-3% (dry basis) and controlled soil loss by 55 to 60%. Along with these treatments, two irrigations increased the pigeonpea yield by 80-88% whereas one irrigation in maize increased the yield by 33-35%. Among irrigations, the sub-surface drip system resulted in more crop yield and higher water use efficiency (WUE) of 3.25 to 3.40 kg ha-1 mm-1 during the period of drought year. Interpretation: RBMF along with coir pith compost or farmyard manure in the furrows had improved the soil moisture, reduced soil erosion, enhanced nutrient status of soil, crop productivity and water use efficiency considerably in the Alfisols. Key words: Alfisols, Drylands, Moisture conservation, Raised bed, Sub-surface drip, Supplemental irrigation

papers.title: Physicochemical and Microbiological Quality of Household Borehole Water in Garoua Cameroon
papers.summary: Abstract Access to safe drinking water remains a major public-health challenge in developing countries, where the consumption of poor-quality water contributes to the prevalence of waterborne diseases. This study assesses the physicochemical and bacteriological quality of borehole water in the city of Garoua (northern Cameroon) and examines user perceptions and practices. The methodology combined a cross-sectional survey of 340 households with laboratory analyses of 34 boreholes. The results reveal a marked reliance on groundwater, with 32.36% of households relying exclusively on boreholes. In physicochemical terms, the water is generally acidic (mean pH of 5.67), with electrical conductivity peaking at 2120 µS/cm, reflecting heterogeneous mineralization. Alarming nitrite concentrations (up to 410 mg/L) were detected, far exceeding drinking-water standards. Microbiologically, although contamination was sporadic, the presence of Escherichia coli at certain water points (F19 and F29) and of fecal streptococci (up to 10 CFU/100 mL) confirms fecal pollution of anthropogenic origin. The study highlights an apparent association between educational attainment and awareness of health risks. However, despite a high level of awareness (91.43%), the vulnerability of boreholes to surface infiltration (from latrines and inadequate waste management) remains a concern. These findings underscore the urgent need for regular water-quality monitoring and improved sanitation infrastructure to protect the health of Garoua’s population.

papers.title: Spatial Analysis of Flood Risk Zones in The Usuma Watershed Federal Capital Territory, Nigeria
papers.summary: This study examined flood risk zones within the Usuma Watershed in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nigeria, with the aim of identifying spatial patterns of flood vulnerability and informing sustainable flood risk management. The objectives were to map flood-prone areas, analyze flood frequency, and evaluate the biophysical and anthropogenic factors contributing to flood risks. Data were collected through satellite imagery, Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM) digital elevation data, hydrological datasets, and field observations. The Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP) and Geographic Information Systems (GIS) were used for data analysis, allowing for the integration of thematic layers including slope, elevation, land use/land cover, rainfall, drainage density, Soil Permeability Index (SPI), and Topographic Wetness Index (TWI). The study reveals that areas of very high to high flood risk accounted for approximately 24.51% and 24.25% of the watershed respectively, predominantly in the central, southern, and eastern portions of the floodplain, including communities such as Gwagwalada, Kuje, and parts of Abuja Municipal Area Council. Flood frequency analysis between 2018 and 2023 showed that the worst flood event occurred in 2022, during which about 70,058 hectares were inundated. Key factors influencing flood risk included low elevation, moderate slopes, high rainfall, sparse vegetation, and dense drainage networks. Based on the findings, the study recommended the enforcement of land use regulations in high-risk areas, the development of sustainable urban drainage systems, regular updates to flood risk maps, and community-based early warning systems. The study concluded that spatial analysis techniques offer critical insights for flood risk reduction, and its approach can serve as a model for other flood-prone regions in Nigeria and across sub-Saharan Africa.

papers.title: High-pyrolysis-temperature acidified straw biochar improves soil hydrological functioning and increases maize yield in saline soils
papers.summary: Biochar contributes to the restoration of soil fertility and crop productivity in saline-affected farmlands. Soil hydrological functioning is a key indicator for assessing the degradation and rehabilitation of saline soils. However, the mechanisms by which acid-modified maize straw biochar produced at different pyrolysis temperatures regulates the hydrological properties of saline soils remain unclear. In this study, a four-year soil amendment experiment was conducted in moderately saline soils of the Hetao Irrigation District in China to evaluate the effects and underlying mechanisms of acidified biochar produced at three pyrolysis temperatures (C1: 300 °C, C2: 500 °C, and C3: 700 °C) and applied at two rates (T1: 10 Mg ha - ¹ and T2: 20 Mg ha - ¹) on soil hydrological properties. The results showed that: (1) application of acidified biochar significantly decreased soil salinity, pH, and bulk density, while increasing soil water content and organic matter. Moreover, it markedly enhanced crop yield and biomass; (2) acidified biochar markedly improved soil hydrological properties (0–40 cm), with the C3T1 treatment performing best, increasing soil saturated water-holding capacity, field capacity, soil water storage, and saturated hydraulic conductivity by 17.35%, 27.91%, 14.31%, and 26.92%, respectively; (3) Principal component analysis (PCA) and Mantel test results indicated that soil hydrological properties were positively correlated with crop yield, biomass, clay content, soil organic matter, and total porosity (p < 0.05), but negatively correlated with bulk density, electrical conductivity, and sand content (p < 0.05). Random forest analysis further highlighted that improvements in soil hydrological properties were primarily driven by changes in biomass, SOM, bulk density, clay content, and total porosity. Overall, this study demonstrates that acidified biochar produced at a high pyrolysis temperature (700 °C) and applied at 10 Mg ha - ¹ effectively enhances the p

papers.title: Improving flood-modeling accuracy with refined NRCS Curve Number and Lag Time estimation via remote sensing-based land cover classification correction
papers.summary: Land use/cover change (LULC) is a major driver of hydrological alteration and flood risk, yet reliable estimation of Curve Number (CN) and Lag Time (T lag ) remains challenging in data-scarce regions where conventional empirical formulas often fail to capture local watershed conditions. This study develops an integrated framework for enhancing the empirical Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS) equations through the combined use of remote sensing, hydrological modeling, and parametric error correction. The framework applies multitemporal satellite imagery, Principal Component Analysis (PCA)-driven classification, Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI)-based land degradation assessments, and geospatial manual delineation of high-runoff zones to characterize LULC shifts and associated hydrogeomorphic consequences. The Hydrologic Engineering Center–Hydrologic Modeling System (HEC-HMS) model was implemented to simulate rainfall-runoff processes and calibrated using a major flood-event hydrograph. The parameters were subsequently refined using observations from an extreme flood event. Results indicate that urbanization and deforestation were associated with changes in hydrological responses and measurable changes in watershed runoff characteristics and the estimated CN and T lag parameters over the study period. The proposed α-correction framework reduced CN estimates by 3.8–19% relative to conventional NRCS values and increased T lag estimates by 26.3–210.2%, reflecting an improved representation of local watershed conditions. For the 2019 calibration event, residual errors of 14.8% for peak discharge and 22.22% for runoff volume remained. The findings of this study underscore the necessity of dynamic parameterization in hydrological models because static frameworks fail to capture anthropogenic forcings on catchment resilience. This work highlights the integration of geospatial analytics and adaptive modeling for sustainable flood risk mitigation and lan

papers.title: Regional covariation between climate-normalized storm rarity and landslide magnitude in Taiwan is sensitive to rainfall timing
papers.summary: Abstract Climate-normalized rainfall rarity may facilitate comparisons across climates, but pooled rainfall–landslide associations can obscure regional structure and rainfall timing. We examined 994 reported rainfall-induced landslides in Taiwan (1987–2018) using 2-km hourly precipitation and generalized extreme-value climatologies for 1980–2019. Rainfall rarity ( T max ) was defined as the maximum of 1–72-h duration-specific return periods, not the recurrence interval of an entire storm. Retrospective whole-storm T max was available for 912 records, including 708 with estimated volume. Within 18 selected spatial cells, 16 contained 393 volume-bearing records. Contextual decomposition yielded a positive between-cell rarity–volume coefficient ( β between = 0.945, 95% confidence interval (CI) = 0.642–1.248), but no detectable positive within-cell association ( β within = − 0.105, 95% CI = − 0.288–0.078). Cell-clustered inference was less decisive. The between-cell coefficient decreased to 0.279 after adjusting for absolute 24-h rainfall and to 0.317 after excluding Typhoon Morakot. When rarity was calculated using only rainfall preceding recorded failure, the positive between-cell association was not recovered ( β between = − 0.276, 95% CI = − 1.115–0.563; 361 volume-bearing records), although analytical populations differed. These findings identify a Morakot-anchored, inventory-specific association that is sensitive to absolute rainfall and exposure timing.

papers.title: Refugee Settlement-Environmental Degradation Nexus in Kassala, El Gedaref, and White Nile States, Sudan
papers.source: CGSPace A Repository of Agricultural Research Outputs (Consultative Group for International Agricultural Research)
papers.summary: Sudan hosts some of Africa's largest and longest-standing refugee populations in fragile drylands already strained by unreliable rainfall, land degradation, and conflict. This study examines whether refugee settlements are linked to environmental decline across 19 camps in Kassala, El Gedaref, and White Nile states, to help guide camp siting and sustainable hosting. Using satellite imagery, we tracked changes in land use, vegetation, soil, and land conditions between 1978 and 2025. Camps were grouped by age — long-established (pre-1990, Kassala), established (2011–2019, White Nile State), and recently established (2020 onward, El Gedaref) — and changes were measured across four distance bands around each camp (0–10, 10–20, 20–30, and 30–50 km). The results show a strong, consistent link between settlements and environmental change over space and time. Because the study included no comparison landscape without camps, this is an association, not proof that camps alone caused the damage. Farmland and built-up areas expanded steadily, replacing shrublands, grasslands, forests, and wetlands. Older camps showed the greatest total change; newer camps changed the fastest each year. Degradation spread outward from inner zones to the edges, with less healthy land remaining throughout. Refugee settlements are best seen as part of wider landscapes whose pressures reach far beyond camp boundaries, weakening nature's benefits and raising the risk of drought, flood, and resource conflict. Older camps need restoration; newer ones need prevention. Humanitarian agencies, governments, donors, communities, and researchers should build environmental checks from the start, promote clean energy and nature-based restoration, manage land use by zone, and sustain shared monitoring with early warning.

papers.title: Groundwater quality dynamics and hydrochemical indicators of water insecurity in the semi-arid Sokoto Basin, Northwestern Nigeria
papers.summary: Abstract Groundwater is the surest water source in semi-arid regions, where surface water is seasonal and subject to climatic fluctuations. Growing climatic stress, along with anthropogenic pressures, in the Sokoto Basin of northwestern Nigeria poses a threat to groundwater quality and the region's water security. This paper has explored groundwater hydrochemistry and identified significant hydrochemical predictors of water insecurity across different geological environments in the Western Sokoto Basin. Fifty-four groundwater samples were collected from hand-dug wells and boreholes in the basement complex and sedimentary formations. The analysis of physicochemical and heavy-metal parameters was performed according to the standard APHA (2017) methods, and multivariate (PCA, HCA, correlation) and geostatistical (Ordinary Kriging, variogram modelling) analyses were used to demonstrate spatial patterns, controlling factors, and predictive accuracy. Findings indicate that groundwater quality differs considerably with lithology: basement complex aquifers are more mineralised and enriched in metals (Mn, Cr, Al, Zn, As) than sedimentary rocks, mainly due to extended water-rock interactions, weathering, and climatic concentration processes. Spatial interpolation revealed unique hot spots of contamination, especially in low-lying and high-evaporation areas, suggesting a magnifying effect of climate stress on solute buildup. High predictability (R 2 > 0.9 in most metals) of kriging models and uncertainty zones (as revealed by nRMSE mapping) was observed in areas of hydrochemical instability. Theoretically, the research will enhance geostatistical understanding of groundwater dynamics in data-limited, climate-sensitive basins by integrating climatic, geological, and geochemical factors into a single explanatory model. In practice, the results deliver early-warning hydrochemical indicators to track groundwater insecurity and can be used to enable evidence-based interventions to

papers.title: Multi-Temporal Assessment of Groundwater Dynamics and Recharge Variability in Semi-Arid Ecosystems: Integration of Satellite-based Gravimetric Analysis and Distributed Hydrological Modelling in the Kalahari-Karoo Basin
