papers.title: Impact of the spatial layout of effective impervious area increments on urban stormwater peak flow and runoff volume
papers.source: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
papers.summary: To reveal the influence mechanism of the layout of effective impervious area (EIA) on urban stormwater processes，a refined stormwater model was constructed，and upstream and downstream sub-catchments were delineated. Taking the Shuangqiaobang runoff plot in Changzhou，Southern Jiangsu，China，as a typical study area，the impact on peak flow and runoff volume were systematically analyzed by setting different scenarios of EIA increments with different locations and scales. Results showed that the location of the EIA，infiltration capacity of the original pervious surface，and rainfall magnitude are key factors affecting the hydrological response. The spatial location effect of newly added EIA is significant，with the growth rates of peak flow and runoff volume in downstream areas being significantly higher than those in upstream areas，showing maximum difference of 18.48% and 7.70% under the moderate-infiltration scenario，respectively. Pervious areas with stronger original infiltration capacity exhibit a greater proportional increase in runoff after conversion to EIA. The growth rates of peak flow and runoff volume tend to decrease with increasing rainfall return period，exhibiting an amplification effect under low-return-period rainfall events. This study provides a scientific basis for optimizing the spatial patterns of underlying surfaces in urban settings and guiding the rational layout of stormwater facilities.

papers.title: Assessment of Fully Polarimetric Biomass Data for Soil Moisture Retrieval
papers.summary: Water management for irrigation is an essential activity especially in agricultural areas or where water is scarce. Water storage in the soil affects the vapour transpiration but also its heat storage capacity, its thermal conductivity and the energy separation between latent and sensible heat fluxes. From a hydrological perspective, soil moisture links the partitioning of rainfall into runoff and infiltration and therefore it has an important role in several ecological applications as flood forecasting, crop yield expectation, meteorological prediction, erosion and slope failure forecasting, water reservoir management, etc. Most of the soil moisture models describe only the bare soil response. In a real scenario, the presence of bare soil is not common as most of the time some kind of vegetation may be found on top. In order to reduce the amount of vegetation responses in addition to the soil moisture estimation longer wavelength can be used. In this study we like to explore the polarimetric and interferometric response of the BIOMASS mission, which operates in P band wavelength. Polarimetry can be used to define the scattering mechanisms and is able, when using decomposition methods to separate the ground and vegetation contribution. To perform this separation a physical model is employed and fully polarimetric data is needed in order to invert for the different involved parameters. It is worth mentioning that for extracting the ground response and the corresponding soil moisture, a significant degree of penetration into vegetation is required. For this reason, SAR soil moisture inversion has traditionally been investigated with L-band. In this study we use quad polarimetry in P band to investigate the sensitivity to bare soil and vegetated soil for soil moisture estimation [R1]. Differential SAR interferometry, a popular technique for measuring displacements of the Earth's surface, is potentially influenced by changes in soil moisture. Different mechanisms for th

papers.title: Urbanization-Induced Shifts in Hydrological Response of a Metropolitan Watershed
papers.source: Khazar Journal of Water and Environment
papers.summary: Rapid urban expansion in semi‑arid metropolitan areas alters hydrological response, yet the shift in the minimum rainfall depth required to initiate surface runoff—the runoff initiation threshold—has received limited quantitative attention. This study assesses this temporal shift in a part of Tehran metropolitan using Landsat‑based land‑use mapping, Random Forest classification in Google Earth Engine, and the SCS‑CN hydrological model. The novelty lies in three aspects: explicitly targeting the runoff initiation threshold as a primary response variable, isolating land‑cover change effects from interannual precipitation variability, and providing a replicable framework for data‑scarce semi‑arid catchments. Impervious surfaces expanded from 38.2% to 64.7% of the study area, while pervious cover declined from 56.8% to 31.2%. Consequently, the runoff initiation threshold decreased from approximately 10 mm to 8 mm, meaning that smaller and more frequent rainfall events now generate surface runoff. Direct runoff depth increased from 282 mm to 314 mm, although annual precipitation varied between 227 mm and 289 mm without a consistent upward trend. The Mann–Kendall test confirmed the statistical significance of these changes at the 95% confidence level. These findings demonstrate that urban expansion has measurably lowered the rainfall threshold for runoff generation, increasing flash flood risk under previously innocuous events. For District 22, low‑impact development interventions—permeable pavements, rain gardens, and infiltration trenches—are recommended, particularly in the intensively developed western and central sectors. The proposed framework can support evidence‑based stormwater management in rapidly growing cities with limited hydrological data.

papers.title: Deciphering morphometric and terrain-driven controls on groundwater recharge and agricultural suitability using geospatial and multivariate modeling
papers.summary: This study presents an integrated assessment of basin morphometry, groundwater recharge potential, and agricultural suitability in the Lower Thamirabarani River Basin, Tamil Nadu, using geospatial datasets and statistical analyses. The morphometric results indicate an elongated basin (Rf = 0.268; Re = 0.584) with a moderate drainage density (1.4 km/km 2 ), reflecting a balanced runoff response and a reduced tendency toward flash flooding. High relief (820 m), steep terrain (17.23%), and a high Melton Ruggedness Number (0.0333) signify strong erosional forces in the western highlands. Flow accumulation analysis shows that 18.7% of the basin experiences concentrated runoff, while curvature mapping identifies concave surfaces that enhance infiltration. Land-use and land-cover mapping indicates agricultural predominance (59.9%) and highlights the influence of expanding settlements on hydrological processes. The Recharge Potential Index (RPI) mapping reveals that moderate recharge zones cover 67.6% of the basin, with high recharge areas primarily located in the eastern floodplains. The Agricultural Suitability Index (ASI) indicates that over half of the basin is of low to moderate suitability, and unsuitable areas coincide with rocky, saline, or steep landscapes. A strong positive correlation exists between ASI and RPI ( R = 0.78, p < 0.001), indicating a close relationship between agricultural potential and groundwater recharge conditions. Principal Component Analysis and Hierarchical Cluster Analysis identify relief-related parameters as the major contributors to spatial variability. The novelty of this study lies in the development of an integrated framework that links basin morphometry, recharge potential, and agricultural suitability, supported by multivariate validation. The results support the prioritization of watersheds, erosion control, and sustainable land and water management practices.

papers.title: An outlook on varied ecological engineering solutions for landslide prevention
papers.source: Journal of Environmental Science Health & Sustainability
papers.summary: This review assesses ecological engineering solutions for landslide prevention and slope stabilization by synthesizing evidence identified through scientific databases. The review encompasses the idea of applying vegetation-based techniques, including live stakes, brush layering, revegetation, grasses, herbaceous plants, bamboo plantations, and lithophytic life forms, together with conventional and structural measures such as natural geotextiles, live wooden crib walls, wattle fences, live silt fences, and live gully breaks. The reviewed evidence highlights the importance of species with strong root systems, which can influence the effectiveness of bioengineering interventions. Species such as Vetiver, Bermuda Grass, Ryegrass, Alder, selected Ficus species, and bamboo show deep-rooted control over soil reinforcement, erosion, and slope stabilization, while lithophytic life forms and pioneer colonizers may support the restoration of exposed rocky and landslide-affected surfaces. The review also examines the contribution of artificial intelligence, remote sensing, unmanned aerial vehicles, LiDAR, interferometric synthetic aperture radar, and machine learning models in landslide susceptibility assessment, monitoring, and advance warning. Overall, the findings revealed that integrated ecological engineering and data-driven monitoring may complement conventional stabilization measures, reduce landslide risk, restore degraded slopes, and inform sustainable land-management planning.

papers.title: Numerical simulation of wicking nonwoven geotextiles embedded in unsaturated soil subgrade
papers.summary: Excess moisture in unsaturated subgrade layers is a primary cause of long-term deterioration in transportation embankments, leading to reduced soil stiffness and degraded performance under environmental and traffic loading. Conventional drainage systems, including traditional geotextiles, are ineffective in partially saturated soils governed by negative pore-water pressures. Recently developed wicking nonwoven geotextiles provide a promising alternative because they transmit water under both saturated and unsaturated conditions through capillary action. This study presents a numerical investigation of transportation embankments incorporating a wicking nonwoven geotextile. A finite element model based on Richards’ equation is developed to simulate unsaturated flow and is validated using laboratory column tests that reproduce soil capillary-rise behavior. The validated model is extended to full-scale embankment simulations to evaluate geotextile performance. The analyses consider two rainfall intensities, moderate and heavy, two soil types (sand with 23.4% silt and sand with 8.8% silt), and installation configurations including single- and multilayer applications. Water content and matric suction distributions are analyzed to quantify geotextile control of moisture migration. Changes in average resilient modulus are estimated using an empirical MEPDG relationship to assess the potential stiffness implications of moisture reduction. Results show that the wicking nonwoven geotextile reduces moisture under unsaturated conditions. The direct wicking depth of a single layer ranges from approximately 10 to 25 cm below its installation level, depending on soil type and embankment location, while the broader VWC influence zone can extend through the full 0.5 m embankment depth. Based on the MEPDG relationship, the estimated average resilient modulus increases by approximately 15% to 70%, indicating the potential benefit of wicking geotextiles for mitigating moisture-related d

papers.title: Landslide detection using deep learning models and remote sensing data
papers.summary: Landslide detection using remote sensing has advanced significantly with the rise of deep learning, yet the field remains fragmented in terms of methodological approaches, data sources, and geographic coverage. This paper presents a systematic review of 152 peer-reviewed studies published across 23 journals, with the aim of synthesizing methodological trends, identifying research gaps, and assessing the global representativeness of current work. We classify existing approaches into five categories—data type-based, model type-based, task-based, data fusion-based, and transfer learning/pre-trained models—and critically evaluate their applications. Our review highlights a strong reliance on optical and SAR datasets (for instance, Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, PlanetScope, and UAV imagery). In terms of models, encoder–decoder segmentation architectures (particularly U-Net variants) dominate, alongside object detection frameworks (YOLO and RCNN), temporal models (LSTM), and unsupervised CNN-based change detection, yet comparative evaluations across these remain sparse. We also identify an uneven geographic distribution of study areas: research is heavily concentrated in Asia and South America, especially in regions affected by earthquake- and rainfall-induced landslides, while Europe, Africa, and North America are comparatively underrepresented. This imbalance reflects both data availability and hazard prevalence but also limits the generalizability of findings. By synthesizing these patterns, our review underscores the need for standardized evaluation practices, greater methodological diversity, and broader geographic representation to enhance the global applicability and robustness of deep learning in landslide hazard detection.

papers.title: Data and Code for Delineating grey-green substitution thresholds for climate-resilient highway drainage
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: This study defines a substitution index, the share of required grey drainage upsizing that a feasible green footprint can displace, and derives grey-mandatory, hybrid and green-only regimes from hydraulic reliability and life-cycle cost. A weighted 15-model CMIP6 ensemble with non-stationary extreme value fits, station-corrected satellite design rainfall, curve-number runoff and Green-Ampt infiltration were applied to 433 one-kilometer segments of two Chinese expressways. Existing drainage exceeded its reliability target on every segment under all three emissions scenarios.

papers.title: Progress in the Application of Distributed Fiber Optic Sensing Technology for Geohazard Monitoring and Early Warning: Principles, Applications and Development Trends
papers.summary: Driven by intensifying global climate change and anthropogenic engineering activities, geological hazards-such as landslides, rockfalls, debris flows, and land subsidence-exhibit characteristics of high incidence, wide distribution and complex evolutionary processes, thereby imposing more stringent requirements on monitoring and early warning technologies. Distributed Fiber Optic Sensing (DFOS) technology has emerged as a pivotal development direction in geohazard monitoring, owing to its distinct advantages, including long-distance continuous measurement, high spatial resolution, immunity to electromagnetic interference, and multi-physical-field collaborative sensing capabilities. This paper provides a systematic review of the fundamental principles and primary technical categories of DFOS, followed by an analysis of their respective characteristics and engineering applicability. Concurrently, research progress in DFOS is comprehensively summarized across three key dimensions: laboratory physical model testing, field engineering monitoring, and intelligent early warning systems. Furthermore, integrating current engineering practices, the inherent limitations and critical challenges confronting DFOS are discussed. An outlook is also presented on its deep integration with multi-source monitoring technologies (such as GNSS, InSAR, and LiDAR) alongside emerging technologies including artificial intelligence (AI), digital twins, and smart disaster prevention. Looking forward, DFOS is poised to gradually establish an integrated full-process monitoring and early warning framework encompassing “continuous sensing, intelligent analysis, risk prediction, and decision support,” ultimately providing more precise, efficient, and intelligent technical support for the hazard risk mitigation of major geological hazards.

papers.title: Climate-Informed Integrated Assessment of Flood and Landslide Susceptibility Using Spatially Validated Machine Learning in a Humid Mountainous Watershed
papers.summary: Future flood–landslide maps support engineering decisions by distinguishing persistent spatial priorities from changes sensitive to modelling assumptions. An integrated framework combines statistically downscaled precipitation with random forest (RF), boosted regression trees (BRT) and support vector machines (SVM) in the Tajan watershed, northern Iran. Nested spatial cross-validation is complemented by geomorphic assessment and historical evaluation of climatic inputs. Four Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) cover 2024–2054 and 2055–2085, alongside four prescribed land-use experiments. Using mean annual maximum five-day precipitation ( Rx5day ), RF achieved mean outer-fold areas under the receiver operating characteristic ( ROC ) curve ( AUC ) of 0.928 for floods and 0.832 for landslides; an independently constructed geomorphic flood index (GFI) achieved AUC = 0.904. Across eight nominal futures, relative to 1985–2014, high/very-high flood susceptibility area increased by 4.38–4.96% and threshold-defined spatial overlap (Both) by 2.68–3.33%. High/very-high landslide area decreased by 6.31–15.39%, but this direction reversed when mean annual precipitation ( MAP ) replaced Rx5day , identifying descriptor dependence rather than established hazard reduction. Both area increased under all nine local threshold pairs and all eight tests transferring the full 2015–2023 simulated–observed discrepancy (full stress); combined land-use changes offset the nominal increase in two of four near-future cases. Road length in high/very-high flood classes increased by 23.84–24.67% nominally, but full-stress changes ranged from −3.85% to +15.30%. Settlement counts within Both increased in all eight full-stress cases. The Both category represents spatial co-susceptibility, not cascades or calibrated joint probability. The framework separates persistent screening priorities from input-dependent exposure changes, supporting targeted drainage, road-crossing and slope assessments.

papers.title: Displacement Increment Isosurface-Based Local Factor of Safety Method Considering Shear-Tensile Coupling for Slope Stability Analysis
papers.summary: Slope stability evaluation is essential for geotechnical hazard prevention and engineering safety design. Conventional factor of safety (FS) methods provide effective overall stability assessments but cannot adequately describe local progressive failure processes. This study developed a shear-tensile coupled local factor of safety (LFS) method based on displacement increment isosurfaces to address two limitations of existing LFS approaches: interference from cumulative displacement in sliding-zone identification and neglect of tensile failure. Potential sliding zones were identified by iteratively adjusting the maximum principal strain increment threshold until the extracted localization regions showed substantial spatial agreement with concentrated displacement increment isosurfaces. The shear local factor of safety (SLFS) and tensile local factor of safety (TLFS) were formulated using the Mohr-Coulomb criterion and the maximum principal stress criterion, respectively, and the smaller value was taken as the governing LFS. The global FS was then obtained through stress-weighted aggregation of elements within the identified potential sliding zone. The method was evaluated using the Extra11 benchmark slope, the Fengtongshan landslide, and the three-dimensional ZFDC engineering slope. The dual sliding-surface mechanism of the Baiyi landslide and the reinforcement performance of the ZFDC slope were further examined. The results showed that displacement increment isosurfaces reduced the influence of preceding deformation and boundary constraints on potential sliding-zone identification. The proposed LFS formulation captured both shear yielding and tensile cracking and described the progressive development of local instability. The calculated global FS agreed well with conventional limit equilibrium methods, with relative differences generally below 7%. The proposed method provides a unified framework for local and global stability evaluation of complex slopes.

papers.title: Geotechnical Parameters in the Preliminary Geoenvironmental Assessment of the Tortosendo Cemetery, Portugal
papers.summary: Cemeteries should be understood not only as collective - use infrastructures and symbolic spaces, but also as active geoenvironmental systems in which burial - related sources, subsurface migration pathways, and potentially exposed receptors interact over time . Within this framework, soil geotechnical properties play a critical role, as they influence infiltration, vertical percolation, cont aminant attenuation, and subsurface water circulation. This study analyses the main geotechnical parameters of soils at th e Tortosendo Cemetery, in the municipality of Covilhã, central Portugal, and its immediate surroundings, to evaluate their contribution to the preliminary interpretation of subsurface geoenvironmental behaviour. The methodological approach combined geomorphological and geological characterisation of the study area with in situ geotechnical investigation, piezometer installation, and labor atory soil testing. Ten piezometers were installed using two complementary me thods: Dynamic Probing Super Heavy (DPSH) and shallow boreholes drilled using a mechanical auger. The DPSH tests provided information on the vertical variability of soil resistanc e, whereas the auger boreholes enabled the collection of representative distu rbed samples for particle - size distribution analysis and determination of Atterberg limits. Additional soil samples were collected from open graves at a depth of approximately 2 m. T he interpretation was further supported by derived parameters, including e mpirical estimates of permeability. The results indicate that the cemetery is situated on a low - gradient hillslope within a small headwater zone divided between two local sub - basins, a geomorphological setting that may influence both surface runoff patterns and subsurface flow organisation. DPSH profiles revealed low resistance values in the shallowest layers, consistent with loose granitic residual soils, followed by a gradual increase in resistance with depth, suggesting denser or l

papers.title: Green Roofs as a Tool for Urban Climate Adaptation: Hydrological Performance, Evapotranspiration Potential and Methodological Challenges in the Central European Context
papers.summary: Green roofs are often presented as a simple adaptation measure for two urban problems at once: rapid stormwater runoff and the overheating of dense built - up areas. In reality, their performance is not a fixed property of the roof assembly, but the result of a changing water balance. Substrate depth, antecedent moisture, rainfall intensity, vegetation condition, evaporative demand and season all determine how much water is retained, how quickly runoff begins and how much cooling can be produced through evapotranspiration. This is especially important in Central Europe, where a roof may retain a large part of annual rainfall through many small and medium events, but may provide much weaker protection during intense storms or in periods when the substrate is already saturated. The direct transfer of retention values from wetter or milder climates into regional design practice can therefore lead to misleading expectations. This paper evaluates green roofs as a coupled hydrological and microclimatic measure using a case study of an administrative building in Prague with a flat roof area of 514.38 m². Three vegetated assemblies, extensive, semi - intensive and intensive, are compared with an impervious reference roof. Annual runoff is calculated from runoff coefficients used in Czech design practice, while maximum retained volume is derived from the manufacturer - declared water capacity of the individual roof layers. The short - term hydraulic response is assessed by a fifteen - minute design - storm calculation according to ČSN EN 12056 - 3 and ČSN 75 9010. Evapotranspiration potential for the 2019 – 2023 period is estimated by the Penman – Monteith method for a reference grass surface using meteorological data for Prague. The results show that replacing the impervious roof with a vegetated assembly can substantially reduce calculated annual runoff and peak discharge. The impervious reference roof discharged about 270 m³ per year, while the calculated annual runoff de

papers.title: Resilient River Defenses in the Vicinity of the Titicaca Deltas: Slope Stability Analysis of Dikes
papers.summary: Flooding in the Lake Titicaca basin poses a critical risk to communities and infrastructure, and endangers human lives. Dikes are commonly used to protect against flooding, but their stability is essential to their effectiveness. This study examines the stability of embankment slopes on the Ilave River dams through hydraulic and geotechnical modelling, using the limit equilibrium method with specialized software. This analysis was applied to sections between 2 and 5 m in height, with variable slopes, and considering scenarios of constant seepage and seismic loading (0.12 g). The hydraulic analysis of the design flow rate Q100 of 1360 m³/s determined a maximum water level of 3819.56 m a.s.l. and was used to establish the crest elevation of the embankments. The slope of 1.5:1 upstream and 1.75:1 downstream on a dam of ≤ 2 m yielded safety factors of between 1.45 and 1.54 under critical conditions. Embankments ranging from over 3 m to 5 m in height, reinforced with a drainage system and a cut-off trench rather than 2.0-metre piping, showed an increase in the safety factor from 2.5 to 11.6. They therefore possess high stability and resilience, making them safe in the face of extreme events. Adaptive design, redundancy and seepage control are essential to reduce the risk of extreme flooding and protect riverside communities that were vulnerable along certain stretches of the river. It is hoped that the recommendations from this research will contribute to improving the safety of riverside communities based on hydraulic and geotechnical modelling, thereby ensuring the long-term viability of these river defenses.

papers.title: How Does Forest Litter Extraction Commonly Used in the Past Affect the Runoff Reaction to Heavy Rainfalls?
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Until the middle of the 20th century, organic material was removed from the forest floor in Central Europe and used as bedding in the stables. The mixture of excrements and organic material was finally spread as fertilizer on the fields. The presented study aims at quantifying the hydrological effect of this historical extraction practise, also called litter raking, at extreme rainfall events. We measured surface runoff before and after such an intervention at four experimental plots simulating a rainfall intensity of 100 mm/h. Additionally, soil moisture has been recorded continuously on the plots with litter extraction and nearby control plots. The results of the rainfall simulation campaigns were as follows: One of the four experimental plots, which already produced a high amount of surface runoff without litter extraction, reacted with an increase of the surface runoff coefficient from 0.49 to 0.63 following this intervention. Another plot showed a slight reaction after litter extraction, with an increase of the surface runoff coefficient from 0.01 to 0.16, and on two plots there was hardly any reaction. After almost a year, the surface runoff that occurred after the intervention had already decreased again. The removal of ground vegetation and reduction of organic layers' thickness by litter raking causes faster changes in soil moisture and a more pronounced short‐term response. Combining the different results of this study reveals a complex interplay of precipitation type, organic layers properties, its system status and the characteristics of the underlying mineral soil, which all together also controls the occurrence and intensity of surface runoff.

papers.title: SUBDIVISION PLAN AND STORMWATER DRAINAGE NETWORK FOR AN INFORMAL SETTLEMENT: THE CASE OF SOUSSONOUBOUGOU, BOUAKE (CÔTE D’IVOIRE)
papers.summary: Informal settlements in sub-Saharan Africa often lack infrastructure, and upgrading programmes rarely integrate household sanitation assessment, spatial planning and drainage-flow estimation. This study combines these components in Soussonoubougou, a 49-ha neighbourhood of Bouaké, Côte d’Ivoire. A survey of 350 households conducted in August 2021 found that 67% relied exclusively on wells and 29% used wells alongside rainwater. Stormwater was mainly managed by natural infiltration (65%); where an outlet existed, it was usually the street (92%). Informal dumping was reported by 48% of households, pit emptying was manual in 65% of cases, and 71% of households that had emptied a pit did not know where the sludge was discharged. Using GPS observations, a digital terrain model and CAD/GIS tools, the urban plan was adapted to existing buildings and topography. The proposal includes 600-m² plots, roads of 25, 15 and 10 m, and reserved public-facility plots, and no subdivision of the flood-prone low-lying outlet area in the south. Eighty-four sub-catchments covering 44 ha were delineated from the proposed road and block layout and combined in series and parallel using the Caquot surface method for a 5-year return period. Calculations at 75 nodes and seven outlets produced elementary peak flows of 0.05–1.38 m³/s and a peak flow of about 8.2 m³/s for the 25.7-ha northern collector. The approach provides a practical basis for drainage design, but primary collectors require a 10-year check, and runoff coefficients, relocation needs, solid-waste management and sludge disposal require further assessment.

papers.title: Quantifying macroporosity and preferential flow variations in soil under rice and wheat cultivation
papers.source: Soil Science Society of America Journal
papers.summary: Abstract Soil macropores play a vital role in movement of water in agricultural fields, yet their spatial and structural dynamics under intensive crop rotation systems remain poorly quantified. This study investigates the contrasting effects of rice‐wheat cultivation on soil hydraulic properties, macropore function, and preferential flow dynamics. Field experiments were conducted post‐harvest of rice and wheat crops at an agricultural plot in IIT Kanpur. Dye‐tracer experiments were performed for visual confirmation of preferential flow. Tension disc and double ring infiltrometer measurements were taken at six different locations at 3 depths (10, 25, and 50 cm). The parameters for matrix ( and ) and macropore ( ) domains were estimated. Wheat soil exhibited significant difference depth‐wise in infiltration rate (). Critically, the steady‐state flux at 25 cm was 77.53% greater, indicating the sporadic activation of deep, high‐capacity macropores within a restrictive layer. No significant depth‐wise variation was observed in parameters under rice cropping (). Matrix parameters were significantly higher under wheat when compared to rice (mean: cm h −1 , cm −1 for rice; 24.26 cm h −1 , for wheat) and showed significant depth‐wise variation at 25 and 50 cm. This trend confirms the restorative and deep‐reaching effect of the wheat root system on pore continuity and subsoil structural stability. The findings emphasize that preferential flow under rice and wheat cultivation is dynamic and crop‐dependent, governed by alternating phases of structural degradation and recovery.

papers.title: Spatial and vertical variability of soil physico‐hydraulic properties and subsurface lithology in the Upper Indus Plain of Pakistan
papers.summary: Abstract Accurate characterization of soil physico‐hydraulic properties is critical for irrigation and drainage design, solute transport, soil–water–plant, and rainfall–runoff relationships. However, spatially representative datasets for these properties remain limited for the Indus Basin of Pakistan, where hydrological studies often rely on generalized parameters derived from other regions, introducing uncertainties in model‐based assessments. This study presents a basin‐scale integrated assessment of soil texture, bulk density, infiltration behavior, and soil moisture retention characteristics covering the Upper Indus Plain of Pakistan. Field‐based in situ measurements were conducted at 66 spatially distributed sites across four doabs (area between the two rivers) at surface, 0.5‐m, and 1.0‐m depths. An integrated methodological framework was employed, combining hydrometer analysis for soil texture, improved double‐ring infiltrometer tests for infiltration, pressure‐plate extractor for soil water retention, oven‐dried weight for bulk density, and resistivity survey for subsurface lithological assessment. Infiltration datasets were analyzed using the Horton and Philip cumulative infiltration models, while soil water retention behavior was quantified using hanging water column and pressure plate methods and parameterized using the van Genuchten model. Results indicate that the Horton infiltration model outperformed the Philip model for estimation of cumulative infiltration. Silty clay loam, sandy loam, and silt loam are the dominant texture classes. The soil with infiltration rates up to 30 mm/h remain predominant across the study area. This study provides robust and accurate baseline datasets along with an integrated methodological framework to support basin‐scale improved hydrological modeling, flood simulations, recharge estimation, and effective water resource management.

papers.title: GIS-Based Morphometric Analysis and Hydrological Assessment of the Hor Al-Shuwaicha Drainage Basins, Eastern Iraq
papers.summary: This study presents a comprehensive quantitative morphometric analysis of the five drainage basins of Hor Al-Shuwaicha in eastern Iraq, which cover a total area of 22,245.54 km². Previous morphometric studies have primarily focused on three basins (Torsaq, Shosharin, and Galal Badra), the morphometric characteristics of the entire drainage system insufficiently characterized. A 30 m Digital Elevation Model was processed using Geographic Information System techniques to delineate watershed boundaries and extract the drainage network, followed by the calculation of twenty-one linear, areal, and relief morphometric parameters using standard equations. The seventh-order stream represents the highest stream order. The Sayed Ghazal Basin exhibits the highest basin relief and a drainage intensity of 0.41, suggesting that rugged topography may enhance drainage. In contrast, the lowest drainage intensity (0.38) in the Galal Badra Basin suggests lower drainage response and potential temporary surface-water accumulation, which may contribute to localized flooding in some areas. Drainage density analysis reveals that the Shosharin Basin exhibits the highest drainage density (1.15 km/km²), indicating a potentially greater tendency for rapid surface runoff. Whereas the Mandaly Basin, with the lowest drainage density (1.09 km/km²), indicates relatively higher groundwater recharge potential. Furthermore, drainage texture ranges from very coarse to fine, while the form factor, circularity ratio, and elongation ratio consistently indicate predominantly elongated basin geometry, suggesting a potentially lower tendency for rapid concentration of runoff. These findings provide quantitative morphometric evidence that can support preliminary flood-hazard assessment and groundwater-recharge evaluation.

papers.title: Landslides: Challenges and Mitigation Strategies
papers.source: Journal of Mechanical Civil and Industrial Engineering
papers.summary: Landslides are among the most significant natural hazards worldwide, causing extensive financial and human losses and destroying natural resources annually. Therefore, comprehensive investigation of these hazards is an unavoidable requirement for future human life. A landslide is a natural disaster that claims human and animal victims every year. In addition to loss of life, landslides cause millions of dollars in financial damage globally. According to NASA records, the highest numbers of landslides occurred in Brazil, India, China, Peru, Afghanistan, Nepal, Indonesia, and the Philippines between 1900 and 2011, resulting in heavy human and financial losses (USGS, 2014). A landslide is the movement of a portion of earth materials and is a general term for the downward movement of rock fragments and detached masses under the influence of gravity. This process operates on sloping lands and may cause the destruction of houses and facilities, blockage of roads and rivers, and in some cases, when its volume is enormous, it can create a disaster. Afghanistan, due to its high mountains, rugged relief, severe physical erosion, and its location in the Mediterranean–Indonesian seismic belt—especially in the central and northeastern regions—has a high potential for fall and landslide processes. The present study aims to identify the types of landslides, their triggering factors, control methods, and mitigation strategies. This research employs a library-based methodology, including descriptive and analytical approaches. The findings indicate that recognizing the type of landslide and its triggering factors is the first and most important step in reducing associated risks. Furthermore, the implementation of geotechnical, physical, and biotechnical measures can significantly mitigate landslide hazards. The study concludes with recommendations for relevant authorities to allocate specific budgets for landslide hazard assessment and mitigation across Afghanistan.

papers.title: Integrated Drought Vulnerability Assessment and Mapping of Bangalore City, India
papers.summary: Drought vulnerability mapping is essential for understanding the spatial distribution of water scarcity and its associated socio-environmental impacts. The present study assesses the overall drought vulnerability of Bangalore urban district, Karnataka, India, through an integrated approach combining the Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP) and Geographic Information System. Four thematic components: meteorological, agricultural, hydrological and socio-economic were selected, standardized and weighted using AHP to develop individual and composite vulnerability maps. The key meteorological parameters included land surface temperature (25.9-29.4°C), specific humidity (9.51-11.5 g/kg) and evaporation (1,490 -1,690 mm/year). Agricultural factors comprised of soil type, soil texture, NDVI (-0.18 to 0.50), curvature, land use/land cover and crop area (123-170 sq.km). Hydrological parameters included elevation (793- 1,003 m), slope, aspect and groundwater level (3.24- 16.0 m bgl). Socio-economic factors involved agricultural dependency (19.4-27.9%), groundwater use (33-50.5%), population density and poverty level (14.5-19.1%). The final Drought Vulnerability Index (DVI) ranged from 0.227 to 0.722, classified into five categories from very low to very high. ROC-AUC validation confirmed strong model reliability, with individual AUC values of 0.873 (meteorological), 0.856 (agricultural), 0.882 (hydrological), 0.842 (socio-economic) and an overall DVI AUC of 0.894, indicating an accuracy of about 89.4%. The results highlight that northern and northeastern zones exhibit high vulnerability due to elevated temperature, reduced vegetation and groundwater depletion, while southern and central regions show moderate to low risk. This integrated approach provides a comprehensive spatial framework for drought management and adaptive planning in rapidly urbanizing regions.

papers.title: An Integrated GIS and Machine Learning-based Landslide Susceptibility Mapping in Wayanad District, Kerala, India
papers.summary: Landslides are among the most destructive natural hazards in the Western Ghats, frequently causing substantial loss of life, infrastructure damage and environmental degradation. Wayanad District, Kerala, is particularly vulnerable because of its rugged topography, intense monsoon rainfall and complex geological conditions. This study presents an integrated Geographic Information System (GIS) and machine learning framework for landslide susceptibility mapping using Random Forest (RF), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) and Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) models. A total of 800 historical landslide inventory points and eleven landslide conditioning factors including elevation, slope, aspect, rainfall, Topographic Wetness Index (TWI), geology, geomorphology, land use/land cover (LULC), lineament density, distance to roads and NDVI, were employed to develop the predictive models. The dataset was divided into a 70:30 training-testing ratio and model performance was evaluated using fivefold cross-validation, confusion matrices, Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves, Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-score, Cohen's Kappa and Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC). Among the evaluated models, LightGBM achieved the highest predictive performance, with an Accuracy of 96.11%, Precision of 94.62%, Recall of 97.78%, F1-score of 96.17%, ROC-AUC of 0.961, Cohen's Kappa of 92.22% and MCC of 92.30%, outperforming XGBoost and Random Forest. Feature importance and SHAP analyses identified rainfall (23.5%), slope (20.8%) and TWI (15.4%) as the most influential conditioning factors governing landslide occurrence. The susceptibility outputs of the three models were integrated to generate a final landslide susceptibility map, classified into Very Low, Low, Moderate, High and Very High susceptibility zones. The integrated model effectively reduced prediction uncertainty and showed strong agreement with historical landslide locations. The proposed GIS-integrated ensemble

papers.title: Distribution network configuration and its link to transport CO2e emissions
Plastic Pollution in Aquatic Environments: Connecting Water and Wastewater, Hydrology, Groundwater and Its Impacts on Sustainable Aquaculture and Fisheries
papers.source: Asian Journal of Fisheries and Aquatic Research
papers.summary: Plastic pollution is commonly investigated within separate compartments, although particles and plastic-associated materials move through wastewater infrastructure, stormwater networks, rivers, sediments, aquifers, aquaculture facilities and fishing grounds. This disciplinary separation impedes source attribution, comparison of exposure estimates and evaluation of controls. This critical narrative review integrates evidence published from 2008 to 31 August 2026, drawing on verified experimental, observational, modelling and synthesis studies. It examines how material properties, hydrological connectivity and treatment processes jointly shape plastic transport, retention and biological exposure, with particular attention to sustainable aquaculture and fisheries. Conventional wastewater treatment captures substantial fractions of the particles measured in plant influent, but retained material is frequently transferred to sludge, and residual discharge remains relevant where effluent volumes are large. River emissions are strongly influenced by episodic runoff, floodplain retention and remobilisation; consequently, instantaneous concentrations poorly approximate catchment-scale delivery. Groundwater contamination is documented in karst, shallow and other vulnerable aquifers, yet filtration, preferential flow, sampling artefacts and limited temporal coverage restrict the estimation of subsurface fluxes. Aquaculture systems receive plastics through source water, equipment, feed and atmospheric inputs, while fishing activity generates additional macroplastic hazards through lost gear. Laboratory studies demonstrate organism-level responses under some exposure conditions, including oxidative stress and reproductive effects, but these findings cannot automatically be translated into population-level losses or human health risks. A source-to-receptor framework is proposed that separates particle abundance from mass flux, identifies changes in particle characteristics across

papers.title: Gender differences in international research collaboration in European Union
Defect engineering in metal-organic frameworks for enhanced hydrogen storage: Unlocking hidden active sites – A review
papers.summary: While hydrogen is a promising clean energy carrier to achieve carbon neutrality, its widespread adoption has been hindered by the absence of efficient, safe, and scalable hydrogen storage solutions. Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) have emerged as a new class of materials with tunable pore structures, high surface areas, and versatility in structure that recently have been explored for hydrogen storage. The performance of pristine MOFs is, however, limited by weak hydrogen–framework interactions and lack of active adsorption sites. To solve such problems, defect engineering has emerged as a promising approach by building engineered defects such as open metal sites, hierarchical porosity, hidden active centers, and enhanced transport pathways. This review discusses defect engineering strategies to improve hydrogen storage in MOFs, including hydrogen adsorption mechanisms, synthesis methods, defect chemistry, active-site generation, and defect-induced transport occurrences. The importance of integrating experimental characterization and computational modelling for understanding defect behaviour is emphasized. Recent advances in materials informatics, machine learning, and AI-assisted discovery of defect-engineered MOFs are also discussed. Lastly, the main difficulties in defect control, stability, scaling up, and predictive design are presented, along with future prospects for the development of next-generation MOFs for sustainable hydrogen-energy applications.

papers.title: Prioritizing Fuel Treatments to Reduce Post-Fire Debris Flow Risk in Utah
papers.summary: Wildfire is a natural part of many forest ecosystems, but in the western United States, wildfires have become larger, more frequent, and more severe in recent decades. There are serious problems after severe wildfire, including erosion, flooding, and debris flows that threaten water quality, roads, and communities. Because of this, land managers need better ways to decide where fuel treatments, such as prescribed burning or thinning, can most effectively reduce wildfire damage and post-fire risks. In this dissertation, I studied how fuel treatments might reduce wildfire severity and lower the risk of post-fire debris flows in Utah. First, I built a model to predict how severely forests are likely to burn across the state. Next, I used simulated treatment scenarios to test how different fuel treatments changed wildfire severity in different forest types and under different weather conditions. Finally, I applied those results to real watersheds in Utah to estimate how treatments could reduce post-fire debris-flow risk. The results showed that treatment effectiveness depends strongly on forest type. In some forests, especially ponderosa pine, spruce-fir, and lodgepole pine, reducing fuels had a strong effect on lowering fire severity. In other forest types, weather played a larger role, which made treatments less effective. Across most forests, treatments that reduced both canopy fuels and surface fuels produced the greatest reductions in wildfire severity. At the watershed scale, treatment costs and benefits also varied. Prescribed burning was generally the most cost-effective treatment. In several watersheds, including Electric Lake, Big Cottonwood Canyon, Panguitch Lake, and Rockport, cost-effective treatments provided the greatest reduction in post-fire risk for the money invested, making them especially important areas for management. Other watersheds showed less cost-benefit tradeoffs in decision making, where intensive treatments can be prioritized for maximal b

papers.title: Strange New Worlds: Philosophical Issues in (Exo)Planetary Science
The Role of Bank Failure in Postfire Debris-Flow Sediment Recruitment: A Field-Based Case Study from the Grizzly Creek Fire, Colorado
papers.summary: Postfire debris flows often exhibit abrupt downstream increases in volume growth rate. Although these sudden volume increases have been identified in the past, their cause remains incompletely understood. In the Grizzly Creek burn area of Glenwood Canyon, Colorado, we combined field observations, repeat LiDAR differencing, and post-event imagery to quantify the contribution of localized mass-wasting processes in debris-flow sediment recruitment. Our observations indicate that lateral erosion and episodic bank collapse along channel margins supply the majority of sediment for debris-flow growth. Bank failures contribute to local channel widening and rapid debris-flow volume growth, particularly where debris flows erode into weak lithologies near contacts or colluvial deposits at the base of cliffs. Field documentation and LiDAR-derived volume changes demonstrate that bank erosion is the primary control on debris-flow growth in this landscape. This case study underscores the importance of explicitly incorporating lateral instability, material strength contrasts, and threshold reach behavior into postfire debris-flow hazard assessments and predictive modeling frameworks.

papers.title: TellusPM: a GPU-accelerated material point method for large-deformation geomechanics driven by an AI agent, calibrated against analytical, numerical and experimental benchmarks
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: TellusPM is a material point method (MPM) program for geotechnical large deformation, written in Rust, whichruns one explicit algorithm in 2D and 3D on a CPU or, through a run-time compiled CUDA engine, on an NVIDIAGPU, and which an engineer, an embedded AI agent or any Model Context Protocol client can drive through thesame 28 tools. We verified it against closed-form solutions and calibrated it against other programs and experimentsin a campaign of about 120 runs on one RTX 4090. The code converges at second order on the vibrating bar, matchesthe logarithmic-strain oedometer within 0.6 % and Terzaghi consolidation within 3.9 % of the initial pore pressure,and gives a factor of safety of 1.34 to 1.40 for the Griffiths and Lane slope, against 1.35 to 1.40 from finite elements.The calibration showed that a per-step FLIP/PIC blend, local damping under displacement control and the absenceof volumetric averaging each changed answers by up to a third, and that the remaining errors in granular runout, a 25% short runout of aluminium rods and a 1.3 to 1.7 times long runout of tall columns, belong to the rate-independentMohr-Coulomb model. On the 2026 Patong debris flow, a single-source back-analysis matches a coupled DEM–SPH model on the deposition along Nanai Road, and releasing every cell whose saturated infinite-slope factor ofsafety is below 1, with the strength reduced by γ𝑠𝑎𝑡/γ’ = 1.96, reproduces the 99th-percentile travel of a finiteelement and DEM–SPH chain on the same release within 6 %, although the median travel is 38 % longer. The GPUengine reproduces the CPU engine at about 40 times its speed, and a whole-hillside scenario of 546,738 points on9.4 × 107 cells ran in 12 min.

papers.title: Comment on egusphere-2026-5589
papers.summary: Abstract. Debris flows are a severe natural hazard in mountain regions. As a spatially and temporally highly irregular phenomenon, meaningful quantitative description and generalization of the underlying processes in contrasting environments as well as associated robust local prediction of debris flows is hindered by a lack of sufficiently detailed observations. As a consequence, debris flows are frequently predicted based on simple regional precipitation (or rainfall) intensity-duration thresholds that lump many channels over larger spatial domains, irrespective of potentially different underlying debris flow trigger processes due to hydro-climatic or geomorphic differences between the channels. Based on long-term debris flow records of up to 18 years, hydro-climatic observations and modelled hydrological variables across three contrasting active debris flow channels (ID1-ID3) in the Austrian Alps, this study (1) analyses differences between the local debris flow regimes in these channels, based on their strength of temporal coupling with hydro-climatic and hydrological extremes, (2) quantifies differences between regional and local debris flow initiation thresholds that emerge from these differences in their temporal coupling, and (3) identifies the pairs of threshold model variables that allow the most reliable debris flow predictions in each of the three study channels. We have found that the three study channels are characterized by considerable difference in seasonal debris flow timing. In channel ID1, debris flows events are largely confined to early summer, occurring, on average, several weeks before the wettest conditions in each year, thus being only weakly coupled to hydro-meteorological extremes. In the close-by channel ID2, debris flows occur throughout summer, on average a few days after the wettest conditions of any specific year. The high debris flow frequency in this channel in addition suggests multiple cycles of sediment exhaustion and re-supply t

papers.title: Sustainability and environmental impact of artisanal mining in DR Congo with pathways for ecofriendly practices
papers.summary: Artisanal and small-scale mining (ASM) serves as a primary source of livelihoods and mineral supply in sub-Saharan Africa, particularly in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where it contributes substantially to rural economic activity and the production of strategic minerals such as cobalt, tin, tantalum, tungsten, and gold. Despite its socio-economic significance, ASM is associated with substantial environmental degradation, governance challenges, and sustainability concerns. This study systematically reviews the environmental and sustainability dimensions of ASM in the DRC and identifies pathways for advancing eco-friendly mining practices. A comprehensive literature search was conducted using Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar for studies published between 2014 and 2024. A total of 1,837 records were identified, of which 183 studies met the predefined inclusion criteria and were included in the qualitative synthesis. The review examined ASM practices, spatial distribution, and associated environmental impacts, including deforestation, soil erosion, water pollution, habitat destruction, and health hazards. It further evaluated sustainability interventions, policy frameworks, and emerging eco-friendly approaches, including improved mineral-processing methods and bioleaching, while considering their feasibility and constraints within the predominantly informal mining sector of the DRC. The findings reveal a persistent gap between policy intentions and implementation on the ground, driven by weak governance, limited technical capacity, and poverty-related operational pressures. The review provides an evidence base for understanding the environmental and sustainability challenges associated with ASM in the DRC, identifies critical research and policy gaps, and proposes pathways for environmentally responsible and socially inclusive ASM practices aligned with responsible-sourcing principles and global sustainability frameworks.

papers.title: Erosion and sediment transfer by debris flows on Miocene intrashelf clinoforms, offshore New Jersey, USA
papers.summary: We integrate legacy 2-D and high-resolution 3-D seismic data with Integrated Ocean Drilling Program Expedition 313 cores and logs to investigate downslope sediment transport on the Miocene New Jersey shelf (offshore eastern United States). Medium- to coarse-grained glauconite and glauconitic quartz sands were recovered at the bases of Lower to Middle Miocene intrashelf clinoforms despite the apparent absence of canyons, channels, or other organized sediment conduits before ca. 13.5−12.7 Ma. 3-D seismic imaging, however, reveals closely spaced U- and V-shaped erosional features at the base of sequence m5.47 (ca. 18 Ma) and within sequence m5.3 (ca. 16.6−16.1 Ma). These morphologies, interpreted as grooves and irregular depressions, record erosion by debris flows transporting sand-rich sediment downslope. Their lengths (≤700 m) and low length-to-width ratios (∼3) suggest incision by substrate blocks locally entrained and rapidly abraded during transport. We propose that basal erosion reflects patchy coupling between the debris flow and the substrate, involving bulk entrainment of loose sands, localized stick-pluck detachment of semi-cohesive blocks that form irregular depressions, and short-lived dragging that produces grooves. Grooved and scarred basal surfaces overlain by debrites are restricted to sequences m5.47 and m5.3. Sequence m5.47 shows deeper incision that disrupts clinoform geometry and partially truncates underlying sequences, whereas m5.3 preserves normal progradation. Both sequences record similar erosional processes with an oblique transport direction (∼50°) relative to clinoform progradation direction, which we attribute to a regional trough to the south. These results demonstrate that debris flows can occur on low-angle intrashelf clinoforms and that both frequent smaller-volume and rare, large-volume mass-wasting events are important in shaping intrashelf stratigraphy.

Thermo-hydraulic behaviour of energy pile in chalk: First experimental characterisation and field-scale performance assessment under unsaturated conditions
papers.summary: Energy piles—foundation elements that simultaneously provide structural support and exchange heat with the ground—offer a direct response to the growing heating and cooling demands of north-western Europe, where chalk is the primary bearing stratum for pile foundations. Despite the widespread occurrence of chalk and its frequently unsaturated state, its coupled thermo-hydraulic behaviour has not yet been characterised as a host medium for energy piles: existing estimates of chalk thermal conductivity correspond to discrete saturation states rather than to a continuous conductivity–saturation relationship established experimentally, representing a gap in geothermal foundation design. This study addresses that gap by delivering the first chalk-specific experimental dataset, constitutive framework, and validated numerical model for energy pile performance in unsaturated chalk. Thermal conductivity was measured on intact chalk specimens using a transient needle-probe across controlled degrees of saturation, and the data were used to calibrate a thermal conductivity function. A fully coupled thermo-hydraulic formulation was implemented in the finite-element framework COMSOL Multiphysics and verified against two independent benchmarks: a field thermal response test on an energy pile in saturated clayey sand and a laboratory model energy-pile test in unsaturated sand. The validated model was then applied to a three-dimensional field-scale energy pile in three chalk formations, and compared with representative sand, silt and clay, to examine the effect of saturation on thermal performance under a seasonal heating–cooling cycle. For the investigated configuration, increasing GWT depth from 0 to 29 m reduces the end-of-extraction heat rate by 6.1%, 8.8% and 11.9% for Estreux, Château-Landon and Seaford chalk, respectively, compared with 3.6% for clay, 8.6% for silt and 26.0% for sand. At 29 m, the chalk cases retain 159.4–169.9 W m − 1 , compared with 135.5 W m − 1 for sand.

papers.title: A Modified Quirk-Millington Equation for Partially Saturated Reactive Porous Media
papers.summary: Diffusion-induced mineral precipitation in partially saturated porous media is observed in various subsurface applications for future energy needs, such as CO 2 sequestration, deep geothermal reservoirs, and deep geological disposal of nuclear waste. The presence of gas might promote mineralization, which can significantly alter the pore space (e.g., geometry, connectivity, diffusivity), possibly causing porosity clogging, and leading to pressure build up and fracturing. Assessing the safety and stability of such systems requires understanding of the effects of mineral precipitation on porosity and effective diffusivity and quantifying the resulting reductions in these properties. Here, we developed a 3D column-diffusion experiment monitored with time resolved micro computed tomography (micro-CT) to evaluate celestine precipitation patterns within partially saturated porous media. In the scans, we can observe enhanced precipitation at the gas-liquid interface and a decrease in porosity with time. The 3D pore structures are used for tracer injection simulation with lattice Boltzmann to determine effective diffusivity. Results from three different experiments with increasing gas content show a decrease in effective diffusivity with time and are used to determine a modified porosity-diffusivity relationship in an evolving pore space as function of water saturation. A comparison with the established power law function of Quirk-Millington (QM) for sandy porous media shows that it overestimates effective diffusivity by several orders of magnitude for some cases. We propose a revised relationship of QM for describing mineralization in partially saturated porous media.

papers.title: Using soil moisture and seed germination timing to understand annual grass invasion post-fire and restoration implications
papers.summary: Abstract In semiarid ecosystems, precipitation and soil-water storage in shallow soils contribute to differences in seed germination of native perennial species and invasive annuals grasses. Invasive annual grasses contribute to wildfire, which displaces native vegetation and changes surface soils through post-fire erosion and loss of organic matter, decreasing surface soil moisture storage, impacting seed-based restoration, and the prevalence of invasive grasses. To understand how soils, precipitation, and fire contribute to surface soil moisture and seed germination, we used the Soil Heat and Water model (SHAW) and seed germination models to estimate shallow soil moisture and seed responses of three native species relative to Bromus tectorum. Across the semiarid regions of the Great Basin, USA, we found variation in sand content produced differences in surface soil moisture duration comparable to those generated by the wettest and driest years on record. The shallow soil environment and precipitation regimes impacted seeds differently, with greater reductions of germination probabilities in sandier soils and during years with lower-than-average spring precipitation. On average, germination probability decreased by 4% for every 10% increase in sand content. The negative effects of sand content on germination were reduced when soils had higher water content following a wetter-than-average winter. Using a literature review, we also estimated an average fire-effect on soil texture and bulk density. Based on the average fire-effects on soils, the modeled number of days of plant-available soil moisture decreased by four days, and germination probability decreased by 6% across species, soils, and precipitation regimes. Because resource availability, contributes to differences in post-wildfire recovery and annual grass invasion, soil plays a critical role during restoration. papers.title: Theoretical and Applied Framework of River Geophysics
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Abstract: Rivers and their adjoining catchments form interconnected physical systems comprising river water, groundwater, soils, rock formations, and riverbanks. Stage fluctuations, bank erosion, unsaturated infiltration, and flood propagation occur across different spatial scales, making it difficult to distinguish underlying mechanisms using a single observation type or parameter set. This review examines representative processes, measurable quantities, and observational approaches at three terrestrial scales: the channel-riverbank, hillslope-vadose zone, and catchment-river network. It compares the contributions and limitations of studies on river-groundwater exchange, near-surface geophysical monitoring, conceptual hydrological modelling, and uncertainty analysis, and distinguishes measured properties from effective model parameters. Ancient Martian channels and water-/ice-related landforms are also considered as potential comparative targets, not as evidence that terrestrial hydrological mechanisms can be transferred directly to other planets. A framework linking phenomenon identification, joint observation, mechanism-based modelling, uncertainty assessment, and independent validation is then summarized. This perspective supports testable cross-scale interpretation and may inform bank protection, flood-risk assessment, and monitoring design; practical benefits require independent field and cross-event evaluation. Keywords: River geophysics, river-groundwater exchange, unsaturated flow, planetary river geophysics © International Journal of Ground Sediment & Water, © Sun Jichao, The website is Web1: https://ijgsw.eu.org/ Web2: https://ijgsw.net/

papers.title: A Simplified CPT-Based Method for Estimating the Friction Angle of Partially Saturated Compacted Soils
papers.summary: Embankments and other compacted earth structures are widely used in civil engineering, and their mechanical behaviour depends on the properties of compacted soils, which are often affected by unsaturated conditions and matric suction. This study presents an empirical methodology aimed at the preliminary estimation of the peak friction angle of compacted unsaturated soils from cone penetration test (CPT) data, intended to support engineering assessments when laboratory testing and site investigation are limited. The approach was developed using CPT measurements collected at three levee test sites in northeastern Italy (Grizzaga, Panaro, and Tagliamento Rivers), combined with laboratory shear test results on undisturbed samples and supplemented by selected data from the literature. Three empirical equations were proposed and compared using different normalization schemes of cone tip resistance with respect to in situ stress conditions, while considering the influence of matric suction. For the soils examined in this study, the estimated peak friction angles were generally consistent with laboratory results, suggesting that the proposed relationships may provide a reasonable first approximation under similar soil conditions. The proposed procedure is intended as a preliminary engineering tool to complement, rather than replace, detailed laboratory testing in the geotechnical characterization of levees, embankments, and other compacted earth structures.

papers.title: Pollutant Concentration Reconstruction in Porous Media from Localized Measurements
papers.summary: Reliable environmental monitoring and groundwater protection heavily rely on the ability to reconstruct full pollutant concentration fields from sparse, partial field measurements. In porous media, dissolved contaminants are transported by groundwater flow while undergoing hydrodynamic dispersion and complex chemical or biological reactions. To address practical contamination challenges, this work investigates the reconstruction of pollutant distributions using water samples collected at discrete locations in unsaturated or saturated soils via sampling tubes equipped with ceramic tips. While these suction samplers provide critical local data, they inherently capture only a fraction of the subsurface environment, leaving wide areas unmonitored. Motivated by this real-world monitoring procedure, we propose steady and time-dependent advection-diffusion-reaction models to simulate contaminant transport. Our main contribution is a generalized unique continuation result demonstrating that, under appropriate physical and mathematical assumptions, two concentration fields coinciding on a non-empty observation region must match throughout the entire space-time domain, even when originating from different source configurations. We investigate this problem from both theoretical and numerical perspectives, backing our mathematical uniqueness results with numerical simulations that validate the efficiency and practical utility of our approach. The theoretical proofs combine regularity properties away from source singularities with unique-continuation principles for parabolic and elliptic partial differential equations, providing a robust framework for environmental risk assessment and site remediation.

Characterization of physical and chemical properties controlling the transport of 129I and 99Tc in ultra-high-performance grout
papers.summary: Ultra-high-performance grout (UHPG) was evaluated as an engineered barrier for encapsulating solid waste generated during nuclear waste processing. The objective of this study was to measure geochemical, hydrological, and physical properties related to 129 I and 99 Tc transport through UHPG. 99 Tc and 129 I are key health-risk drivers associated with near-subsurface nuclear disposal facilities. To provide context, a second flowable Baseline grout currently used in nuclear waste disposal facilities was also characterized. Compressive strength and bulk density were appreciably greater in the UHPG (120.5 MPa and 2.2 g/cm 3 , respectively) than the Baseline grout (8.4 MPa and 1.5 g/cm 3 ). UHPG had appreciably lower porosity (0.15 cm 3 /cm 3 ) and hydraulic conductivity ( K = 5.8 ×10 −14 cm/sec) than the Baseline grout (porosity = 0.32 cm 3 /cm 3 ; K = 9.4 ×10 −7 cm/sec). Desorption partitioning experiments indicated that both grouts had similar 129 I partitioning coefficients (C Solid /C Liquid ; K d ), of ∼100 (moles/g)/(moles/mL) and had similar aqueous iodine speciation: I - > > IO 3 - > organo-I. 99 Tc aqueous concentrations appeared to be controlled by solubility (7 ×10 −8 mol/L) in the UHPG, likely because slag in the UHPG formulation produced a reducing environment that converted the highly mobile aqueous TcO 4 - to a much less mobile Tc(IV) solid species, TcO 4 · n H 2 O. 129 I and 99 Tc observed diffusivity ( D obs ) were 6 and 7 orders of magnitude less, respectively, in the UHPG than in the Baseline grout. These tests provide multiple lines of evidence indicating that UHPG possesses excellent characteristics for encapsulating 99 Tc and 129 I waste.

papers.title: Incorporating physical guidance into deep learning through hard constraints for water transport modeling in unsaturated zone
Drivers of basal respiration rate in intact samples from carbon-rich lowland soils across Denmark
papers.summary: Soil basal respiration rate (BRR) measured under controlled laboratory conditions is an important indicator of a soil's microbial CO 2 production potential. Although temperature and drainage status are known to control BRR, the relative importance of physical, chemical, and microbial controls remains poorly understood, particularly in organic soils. BRR was measured on intact topsoil samples from 112 carbon-rich lowland soils in Denmark at 15°C at a soil-water matric potential corresponding to field capacity (pF = 2), alongside a range of soil physical, chemical and biological properties. Among the reported individual soil properties, mesopore volume showed the strongest association with BRR (R 2 adj = 0.359), followed by the inverse Campbell pore-size distribution index (1/b; R 2 adj = 0.297). The best-performing two-predictors model, combining total nitrogen and 1/b, explained even more variability in BRR (R 2 adj = 0.506; RMSE = 0.490 mg C-CO 2 h -1 kg -1 soil). Alternative models incorporating other indicators of organic matter characteristics or pore structure also showed relatively good fit to the observed data. Samples from semi-natural sites showed higher BRR compared to those in agricultural areas, indicating an association between land-use and laboratory-measured respiration. Overall, the results identify soil properties associated with variation in BRR under standardised incubation conditions. Further validation is required to establish the robustness and transferability of statistical relationships and to determine whether laboratory BRR can inform predictions of field soil CO 2 emissions.

papers.title: Effects of h-BN modification on the diffusion and mechanical properties of cement-based anchorage grouting materials
Sustainable silty sand reinforcement using stipa tenacissima Fibers: insights from triaxial testing
papers.source: European Journal of Environmental and Civil engineering
papers.summary: As a sustainable alternative, natural plant fibre reinforcements offer an economical and environmentally friendly solution for enhancing the mechanical performance of earthen construction materials. This study investigates the use of Stipa Tenacissima (Alfa) plant as inclusions to improve silty sand’s mechanical properties. Initially, unsaturated triaxial tests at a constant water content were conducted on, compacted silty sand soil reinforced with 2% Alfa fibres, enabling the evaluation of the complete stress-strain behaviour while controlling confinement and suction. Alfa fibres, which were either cut into 10 mm stems or milled, were blended with natural silty sand, and specimens were compacted under optimum proctor conditions prior to triaxial shear testing. The results indicate an increase in shear strength of 8-15% and an improvement in stiffness modulus exceeding 50%, together with a notable increase in friction angle. Microstructural interactions analysed using scanning electron microscopy reveal smooth fibre surface morphologies that facilitate physical adhesion and interlocking at the fibre-soil interface. While cut fibres primarily enhance the apparent cohesion, milled fibres are shown to modify the mechanical interlocking with the soil particles and to increase the frictional interaction. These findings present novel perspectives and analysis using Alfa fibres-reinforced soil as a sustainable natural reinforcement material.

papers.title: Interpreting changes in soil pore-size distribution following vegetation establishment in a salt marsh: an exploratory case study in the Yellow River Delta, China
A coupled Terzaghi – Biot model for blast-induced liquefaction
papers.summary: We investigate the impact of short-wave impulses on soil liquefaction and fluid pressure dynamics. Using a Biot poroelastic model with an elasto - plastic representation of the sand matrix, numerical simulations are conducted to evaluate soil displacement, pore pressure, and wave velocities. Comparisons between coupled (Biot) and decoupled (Terzaghi) models reveal critical differences in displacement and pore pressure predictions. The originally developed analytical solutions which are presented here for the first time, show quantitatively that soil saturation significantly amplifies liquefaction zones and the magnitude of displacements, with fully saturated soils showing the greatest effects. These observations are supported by results of a field test conducted in silty sands (the Ashkelon site) where high excess pore pressures were obtained, in agreement with the coupled Biot model. The effect of saturation levels on tunnel wall displacements in response to nearby blasting is shown to demonstrate the vulnerability of buried structures to blasting under various groundwater schemes. The findings offer insights into geotechnical applications involving dynamic loading, particularly in excavation and blast engineering in soils. We therefore suggest that a coupled Biot model must be utilized to correctly model ground and buried structures response to blasting.

papers.title: Integrated Geotechnical and Seismic Stability Assessment of Tropical Residual Slopes in Sitinjau Lauik, West Sumatra, Indonesia
papers.summary: Sitinjau Lauik, a national road corridor in West Sumatra, Indonesia, is one of the most landslide-prone segments of the Bukit Barisan volcanic belt. This study assesses the geotechnical and seismic stability of three tropical residual soil slopes at this location by combining cone penetration testing (CPT), laboratory index testing, consolidated-drained direct shear testing (DST), and Morgenstern–Price limit-equilibrium analysis under static and pseudo-static seismic loading. CPT profiles revealed a weak layer (qc = 0.4–0.6 MPa) at 1.2–2.8 m depth in Slope 1. This slope also has a high plasticity index (PI = 39.7%), a high void ratio (e = 1.50), and a low dry density (γd = 10.06 kN/m³), resulting in lower shear-strength parameters (c' = 17.8 kPa, φ' = 19.2°) than Slopes 2 and 3 (PI < 10%). Static factors of safety (FS) were 1.08, 1.54, and 1.49 for Slopes 1, 2, and 3, respectively. A pseudo-static coefficient of kh = 0.15, consistent with regional peak ground acceleration zoning, reduced the FS values to 0.77, 1.23, and 1.17, making Slope 1 unstable during earthquakes. At kh = 0.20, none of the slopes met the minimum FS of 1.1 required by the Indonesian National Standard (SNI) 8460:2017. High plasticity, a high void ratio, and low CPT resistance distinguished the critical Slope 1 from the other slopes. Because only three slopes were examined, these findings are site-specific; nevertheless, they provide a basis for prioritizing slope remediation and early warning along this corridor.
