papers.title: Pemetaan Kerawanan Tanah Longsor di Desa Bonto Lojong Kecamatan Uluere Kabupaten Bantaeng dengan Metode Frequency Ratio
papers.summary: Background: Landslides are a natural disaster that often occurs in Indonesia, particularly in areas with steep slopes and high rainfall. Bonto Lojong Village in Uluere District, Bantaeng Regency, exhibits these characteristics, yet there is no landslide susceptibility map for the area. Aim: To map the level of landslide susceptibility in Bonto Lojong Village, Uluere District, Bantaeng Regency, as a basis for disaster mitigation. Methods: Landslide susceptibility mapping was performed using the frequency ratio method, landslide inventory with Google Earth Pro, soil texture analysis using the hydrometer method, c-organic analysis using the Walkley and Black method, soil permeability using the constant head method, and bulk density using the gravimetric method. Results: Landslide susceptibility maps were divided into three classes of susceptibility, namely low, medium, and high, which were influenced by slopes > 45%, sandy clay texture, medium permeability (5,2-6,3) cm/jam, medium bulk density (1,20-1,34 g/cm³), and low c-organic (1,73-1,84%). The low-vulnerability class had an area of 684 ha in the western part of the study, the medium-vulnerability class had an area of 1,047 ha in the central-eastern part, and the high-vulnerability class had an area of 224 ha in the northern-southern part. There were 44 landslide occurrence points in Bonto Lojong Village, with 20 landslide occurrence points in the high vulnerability class, with variations in fr ranging from 1.0-12.28, the medium vulnerability class had 18 occurrence points, whereas in the low vulnerability class, there were six landslide points. Conclusions: Landslide vulnerability mapping using the frequency ratio method can produce maps with a good level of accuracy (AUC = 0.80). The resulting map can be used as a basis for disaster mitigation through the application of soil conservation technique

papers.title: Assessment of sediment production, connectivity, and delivery in mountainous catchments under environmental changes. The role of shallow landslides in the Upper Llobregat Basin (Pre-Pyrenees, Catalonia)
papers.summary: (English) Soil erosion in mountainous landscapes is strongly influenced by shallow landslides, particularly during extreme precipitation events. Despite their geomorphic significance, quantitative soil erosion studies often prioritize fine sediment dynamics and agricultural land-use calibrations, thereby underrepresenting the complexity of landslide processes driven by intrinsic slope parameters and external triggering forces. This study examines sediment production and connectivity from shallow landslides under climate change and land-cover transitions. The primary objective aims to quantify sediment mobilization from slope instabilities to fluvial networks, focusing on the Saldes River Basin (102 km²) for model calibration and applying the results to the Upper Llobregat River Basin (504 km²). The quantification approach used a distributed, event-based method with the FSLAM landslide stability model. Projected climate scenarios predict increased extreme precipitation events, resulting in heightened slope mass wasting. Future simulations indicate landslide mobilization rates increase by 10%, peaking at 16% during 20-year rainfall events. These findings underscore the significance of hillslope processes in sediment budget assessments and the role of extreme rainfall in sediment production. To address sediment connectivity, this study introduces the Random Connect (RC) model. The model uses a random-walk framework and applies the Index of Connectivity (IC) to estimate sediment volume fluxes from source areas to channel networks. The input data includes a digital elevation model, IC maps, and sediment source maps derived from shallow landslides. The model outputs consist of raster maps that describe sediment flux. The receive maps show accumulated sediment volumes along transfer paths, and the release maps indicate the source cells contributing sediment to the target river. papers.title: Landslide susceptibility assessment for the Nihotupu reservoir system applying machine learning algorithms under different sampling strategies and mapping units
papers.summary: This study developed a landslide susceptibility modelling framework for the Nihotupu reservoir system, located in the Waitākere Ranges, Auckland, New Zealand, to evaluate how different spatial representations of terrain influence model performance and susceptibility mapping. A landslide inventory derived from Auckland Council was used as the primary input for the analysis. For this dataset, a sampling strategy was designed based on landslide scarp centroids and source-area boundary points, complemented by random sampling of non-landslide locations across the study area. Following this procedure, a balanced database of landslide and non-landslide samples was constructed and combined with a set of conditioning factors representing topographic, hydrological, geological, anthropogenic, and rainfall-related variables. Three mapping unit scenarios were implemented: pixel-based, slope-unit-based, and 20 m buffer-based representations of the terrain. Based on these scenarios, a feature reduction was performed using Pearson correlation analysis, variance inflation factor (VIF) filtering, and Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) importance prior to model training. The resulting predictor sets were subsequently used to train three machine-learning algorithms: Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest (RF), and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost). Then, model performance was assessed under spatial cross-validation using standard classification metrics, including area under the ROC curve (AUC), F1-score, accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, and precision–recall AUC (Pr-AUC). The results indicate that SVM consistently delivered the strongest predictive performance across the three scenarios, achieving the highest AUC values in the pixel-based (0.853), slope-unit-based (0.794), and buffer-based (0.846) workflows, while RF remained highly competitive, particularly in the buffer scenario. papers.title: A framework for spatio-temporal assessment of slope stability along mountainous transport corridors
papers.summary: Globally, research on the interaction between roads and landslides has largely focused on roads as triggering factors. Existing susceptibility assessments typically represent roads through static conditioning factors such as distance to road or road density, while limited attention has been given to how road infrastructure itself responds to dynamic slope processes. Consequently, their outputs often lack practical relevance for infrastructure resilience, particularly under evolving climate and environmental conditions. The aim of this research is to develop a dynamic, spatio-temporal framework that integrates hydrological conditions with slope stability analysis to assess landslide susceptibility along transport corridors. The approach couples daily soil water balance with a modified version of the physically based Transient Rainfall Infiltration and Grid-Based Regional Slope-Stability (TRIGRS) model. The framework was applied to the 24.7 km long Mukamira'Kabaya road and its 16.8 km² surrounding corridor in northwestern Rwanda, a steep environment frequently affected by shallow rainfall-induced landslides. A tartan-style visualisation was developed to depict dynamic landslide susceptibility along the road, illustrating how instabilities originating from either roadcut or upslope zones influence specific 10 m-long road sections through time. The coupled hydrological'mechanical model captured the temporal response of slope stability to variable rainfall. As part of model validation, the framework was applied using 2016 rainfall data and corresponding landslide records. It identified pronounced peaks in the proportions of roadcut and upslope areas with FoS ' 1.0 on 8 May (day 129 of the year), reaching 64% and 16 %, respectively ' coinciding with well-documented landsliding events in the corridor. papers.source: Repository at Universitas Pendidikan Indonesia (Universitas Pendidikan Indonesia)
papers.summary: Bencana tanah longsor merupakan salah satu bencana alam yang sering terjadi pada wilayah dengan topografi curam, curah hujan tinggi, serta perubahan tutupan lahan yang tidak terkendali. Kota Cimahi sebagai wilayah dengan morfologi perbukitan dan perkembangan pembangunan yang pesat memiliki potensi kerawanan tanah longsor yang tinggi. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk menganalisis perubahan tutupan lahan di Kota Cimahi pada tahun 2024 dan 2026, mengkaji tingkat kerawanan tanah longsor di Kota Cimahi berdasarkan analisis parameter curah hujan, kemiringan lereng, jenis batuan, tutupan lahan, dan jenis tanah dengan menggunakan analisis Sistem Informasi Geografis (SIG) melalui teknik scoring dan overlay, serta menganalisis pengaruh perubahan tutupan lahan terhadap tingkat kerawanan tanah longsor di Kota Cimahi. Metode yang digunakan adalah deskriptif kuantitatif dengan pendekatan Sistem Informasi Geografis (SIG) melalui teknik change detection serta teknik scoring dan overlay. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa terjadi perubahan tutupan lahan sebesar ±37,73 ha dengan peningkatan kawasan terbangun sebesar ±1.446,24 ha yang tersebar terutama pada wilayah dengan aktivitas perkotaan yang tinggi, sedangkan penurunan tutupan lahan terjadi pada vegetasi berupa sawah dan tegalan/ladang dengan total ±1.291,38 ha. Tingkat kerawanan tanah longsor terbagi menjadi beberapa kelas dari tidak rawan, agak rawan, rawan, dan sangat rawan, dengan dominasi pada wilayah berlereng curam dan curah hujan tinggi. Perubahan tingkat kerawanan terjadi pada beberapa wilayah, dengan peningkatan kerawanan terbesar ditemukan pada Kelurahan Cibeber sebesar 24,30 ha, Leuwigajah sebesar 4,88 ha, dan Cibeureum sebesar 3,93 ha. papers.title: Analisis Tingkat Kerawanan Longsor Lahan Di Kecamatan Ile Ape Timur Kabupaten Lembata Provinsi Nusa Tenggara Timur (NTT)
papers.source: UMS Library Center of Academic Activities (Universitas Surakarta)
papers.summary: Landslides are a common natural disaster in areas with steep topography, including Ile Ape Timur Subdistrict, Lembata Regency, East Nusa Tenggara. This disaster is caused by a combination of natural factors, such as high rainfall, slope gradients, soil types, and human activities that alter land use. This study aims to analyze the landslide susceptibility levels and identify mitigation efforts in Ile Ape Timur Subdistrict. This research employed a descriptive method with a Geographic Information System (GIS) approach. The data used included slope gradient maps, soil type maps, rainfall data, and land use maps, analyzed using a weighted overlay technique to produce a landslide susceptibility map. Primary data were collected through field observations, while secondary data were obtained from relevant agencies such as BPBD and PUPR of Lembata Regency. The results show that the landslide susceptibility levels in Ile Ape Timur are categorized into four classes: not susceptible (3,174 hectares), less susceptible (25 hectares), susceptible (718 hectares), and highly susceptible (6 hectares). The main factors influencing susceptibility are steep slopes, Andosols soil prone to erosion, and relatively high annual rainfall. Recommended mitigation efforts include structural approaches, such as terracing and the installation of early warning systems (EWS), as well as non-structural approaches, including community education and disaster simulations. This study is expected to serve as a basis for the government and local communities to implement effective landslide disaster mitigation measures, minimizing material losses and casualties.

Mechanical Root Reinforcement for Slope Stability: A State-of-the-Art Review and a Proposed Trait-Based Functional Root Classification System
papers.summary: Vegetation has been used for slope stabilization for centuries, with conventional measures like soil nails and piles serving to complement the root reinforcement. Vegetation contributes to reinforcement through mechanical reinforcement provided by the root, and hydro-mechanical effects associated with evapotranspiration. Despite decades of research, translating root reinforcement into engineering practice remains unclear because most studies focus on specific plant species rather than on mechanically meaningful root traits, limiting comparability and predictive capability. This paper provides a comprehensive review of root characteristics and root types relevant to mechanical root reinforcement, specifically root morphology (e.g., diameter) and architecture (e.g., orientation and root area ratio (RAR) distribution). It also reviews the state-of-the-art of existing methods for quantifying mechanical root reinforcement: theoretical models, experimental methods from laboratory to field-scale, and numerical approaches based on FEM and DEM. Building on identified gaps and the need for functional trait-based root classification, a three dimensional finite element model with an explicit representation of simplified roots is developed and validated against field scale direct shear tests on vegetated soil. A systematic parametric analysis quantifies the effects of RAR, geometric arrangement (radial vs. square), structural versus non structural root systems, and root orientation relative to the shear plane. The results show that RAR alone is insufficient to uniquely characterize mechanical root reinforcement, because root systems with the same RAR can mobilize substantially different strength increases depending on the presence of dominant structural roots, their orientation relative to the shear plane, and their spatial arrangement. papers.title: Understanding the rainfall triggering post-fire debris flows in California
papers.summary: Post-fire debris flows (PFDFs) are a cascading hazard resulting from the interaction between intense rainfall and susceptible terrain altered by wildfire. These events have proven devastating in the past, damaging infrastructure and communities, particularly in California, where fire season in the warm months is closely followed by rainfall during the cool season. The expansion of wildfire occurrence, along with pronounced variability in terrain and climate across California, highlights the need to better understand the rainfall conditions associated with this hazard under both current and future climates. Consequently, this dissertation integrates multiple datasets and methods to characterize rainfall and atmospheric conditions associated with storms triggering post-fire debris flows, providing new insight into the rainfall environments, precipitation-system structure, predictive controls, and future changes in PFDF hazard across California. First, an inventory of PFDF is compiled and used to characterize rainfall conditions associated with event occurrence using nearby rain gauges, including storm duration, rainfall accumulation, antecedent rainfall, and short-duration peak intensity. Results show that rainfall triggering PFDFs in California occurs within diverse storm environments, from long, persistent, and wet cool-season storms to shorter and intense warm-season storms. However, short-duration peak rainfall intensities capable of triggering PFDFs occur across seasons, suggesting that similar triggering bursts may arise within very different broader storm environments. The following research chapter uses a radar-based tracking approach to characterize the structural properties of precipitation systems and reflectivity affecting burned areas during storms known to have triggered PFDFs. papers.title: Surface Soil Moisture in Challenging Environments: Methodological Advances and Drought Monitoring Applications
papers.summary: Surface soil moisture (SSM) is a key environmental variable controlling water and energy fluxes at the land-atmosphere interface. As part of the water cycle, SSM influences infiltration, runoff, evapotranspiration and determines plant water availability. Its accurate monitoring is essential for early agricultural drought detection, hydrological modelling and climate change adaptation. Over the last decades, satellite-based approaches have become prominent to monitoring SSM, providing temporally and spatially continuous observations in near-real-time. In particular, the Sentinel-1 satellites, carrying C-band synthetic aperture radar, provide SSM retrievals at an unprecedented sub-kilometer resolution, distributed through the Copernicus Land Monitoring Service. Despite the potential of the operational Sentinel-1 SSM, the product shows limitations over dense vegetation and complex topography, limiting its applicability for environmental monitoring in these landscapes. This thesis first describes methodological advances to address the dense vegetation and complex topography limitations, then demonstrates the potential of Sentinel-1 for agricultural drought monitoring in subtropical context.The first study investigates the impact of vegetation on the Sentinel-1 SSM retrievals across Europe. Three new products are developed by applying vegetation masks derived from optical and microwave datasets to selectively discard densely vegetated backscatter pixels during the resampling from 20 m to the kilometer scale. The validation with both ERA5-Land and in-situ observations highlights that selective masking for non-sensitive pixels significantly improves retrieval accuracy, particularly over mixed pixels combining agricultural and forested land cover.The second study extends SSM retrievals over the Austrian Alps, where approximately 80% of the CLMS product is masked due to topography masking. papers.title: Development of an advanced computational approach for early warning and predictions of rainfall-induced slope failures
papers.summary: Rainfall-induced landslides are among the most common natural hazards, threatening lives, homes, and infrastructure worldwide. This research develops a novel approach to predict landslides and provide early warning, even when field data are limited. The study creates advanced computer models that represent real soil conditions and simulate how slopes respond to heavy rainfall. These physics-based models are then combined with machine learning that learn continuously from monitoring data, allowing predictions to be updated and refined over time. By improving prediction accuracy, this research supports more effective landslide early warning systems and helps reduce damage and loss of life.

papers.title: Analisis Spasial Kerawanan Longsor untuk Penentuan Titik Shelter di Kecamatan Petungkriyono Kabupaten Pekalongan
papers.source: UMS Library Center of Academic Activities (Universitas Surakarta)
papers.summary: Landslide susceptibility is a condition that indicates the level of potential for an area to experience landslides which is influenced by factors such as slope gradient, rainfall, soil type, geology, and land use. This study aims to analyze landslide susceptibility for determining shelter points in Petungkriyono District, Pekalongan Regency using a GIS (Geographic Information System)-based overlay method with ArcGIS 10.8 software. The data used include landslide occurrence data, DEMNAS Indonesia, RBI Indonesia, rainfall in 2014–2025, land use in 2025, distribution of disaster mitigation shelters, soil type, and geology of Petungkriyono District. The results of the study indicate that the level of landslide susceptibility in Petungkriyono District is dominated by high class with an area of 6930.5 Ha or 84.58%, medium class with an area of 1228.3 Ha or 14.99%, and low class with an area of 34.9 Ha or 0.43%. In general, every village in Petungkriyono District is characterized by high landslide vulnerability. Curugmuncar Village is the most vulnerable area, with a high vulnerability percentage reaching 96.68%. Disaster mitigation shelters are divided into four types: government, education, health, and worship shelters. There are three government shelters, 14 education shelters, one health shelter, and 27 worship shelters spread across all villages in Petungkriyono District.

papers.title: Innovative soil management and technological integration to enhance sustainability and soil health in hilly vineyards of North-West Italy. Adopting good practices and advanced technologies for investigation of water-soil dynamics and mitigation of soil degradation in viticulture.
papers.summary: In recent decades, the intensification of agricultural management has introduced significant environmental challenges, particularly in soil and water conservation, biodiversity, sustainability, and ecosystem services.The increasing awareness of soil as a non-renewable resource and its crucial role in climate change mitigation has driven global efforts to adopt sustainable soil management practices in various agri-ecosystems, including viticulture.This thesis aims to evaluate the effects of introducing and promoting optimal soil management techniques in hilly wine-growing environments in North-West Italy to mitigate soil degradation phenomena such as erosion and compaction.The conservation and improvement of soil health, while maintaining vine quality and papers.title: RAINFALL-INDUCED LANDSLIDE SUSCEPTIBILITY MODELLING FOR PREDICTION AND EARLY WARNING
papers.source: CINECA IRIS Institutional Research information system (University of Urbino)
papers.summary: Landslide detection and prediction rely on Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) as well as historical documentation of past events. Utilizing multiple elevation datasets and a landslide inventory, logical optimization methods to partition terrain into Slope Units (SUs) used as modelling units for landslide prediction is introduced. Landslide area, counts as well as terrain characteristics like homogeneous slope aspect are used and later unified into segmentation metrics to assess their performance in landslide susceptibility models. These terrain units are continued to be used in dynamic landslide susceptibility modelling through Generalized Additive Models (GAMs) to approach real-time landslide warnings for disaster and risk management. Particularly for rainfall-induced landslides, the integration of rainfall as a dynamic covariate in statistical modelling is approached. Keeping the selection of the mapping unit to SUs, first we utilize cumulative antecedent rainfall information by testing multiple time-windows to select the most-representative temporal bracket for the region. Secondly, while the first technique still remains using rainfall in a scalar form, we implement a functional GAM to utilize the time-series information and present rainfall as a temporally dynamic variable. The model performances undergo a number of validation techniques and the drawbacks of lacking information is explained with varying prediction power. These enhances in methodologies are presented to support Landslide Early Warning Systems (LEWS) for disaster risk and mitigation measures.

papers.title: Strengthening process-based modelling of cropland flux dynamics under various abiotic conditions: Integrated assessment and development of Daisy soil–plant–atmosphere model for a Walloon cropland
Characterizing Hydrophysical and Biogeochemical Alteration and DNA Recovery in Highly Compressed Peat under Access Road Disturbance in a Boreal Fen
papers.source: Libraries and Cultural Resources (University of Calgary)
papers.summary: Boreal peatlands store carbon and regulate hydrology because saturation slows decomposition and allows peat to accumulate. Roads interrupt these controls by compressing peat and blocking lateral groundwater flow, producing persistent changes in water-table position, oxygen exposure, solute movement, and decomposition. As road removal and peatland reclamation become more common, restoration must be guided by how disturbance continues to affect ecosystem function below ground, rather than only whether vegetation or surface hydrology appear to recover. The first aspect of this thesis examined how a mineral access road altered hydrophysical structure, peat compression, and chemistry across depth in a moderate-rich treed fen near Slave Lake, Alberta. Road loading compressed and displaced peat horizons, while reduced hydraulic conductivity beneath the road divided the site into wetter upgradient and drier downgradient zones. These hydrological contrasts were consistent with differences in nutrient transport, ionic conditions, and decomposition patterns. Because subsurface compression can persist after mineral fill is removed, restoration planning must address both lateral hydrological reconnection and the altered vertical arrangement of peat that controls water storage, redox conditions, and substrate availability. The second aspect of this thesis followed up on these findings by asking whether the same changes in peat structure and organic matter chemistry also affect molecular monitoring. DNA-based methods can identify microbial responses before visible ecosystem recovery, but only when extraction differences reflect biological conditions rather than peat chemistry. The study therefore evaluated how disturbance, depth, and humification influenced DNA yield and purity, and whether modified extraction protocols reduced the effects of nucleic acid binding and humic inhibitor carry-over. papers.title: Effects of root architecture of different wheat cultivars on soil structure
papers.source: AMS Dottorato Institutional Doctoral Theses Repository (University of Bologna)
papers.summary: Plant roots play a crucial role in maintaining soil health by influencing physical structure and hydraulic properties. This study investigates relationships between root morphology of wheat genotypes and their impacts on soil structure and hydraulic characteristics. Using shovelomics, we characterized root systems of wheat cultivars (Paragon, Bologna) and landraces (Senatore-Cappelli, Watkins238) selected for contrasting root morphologies. X-ray computed tomography (CT) was applied to examine soil pore networks at cylinder and aggregate scales, while soil hydraulic properties were measured using Wind evaporation and dew point techniques. Results demonstrated significant genotype-driven differences in soil morphology and hydraulic functions. Structural analyses (Minkowski functionals, percolation theory) showed significant variability in bioporosity and pore connectivity among genotypes compared to bare soil. Senatore-Cappelli exhibited notably larger biopores (>1 mm diameter). Hydraulic characterization using a van Genuchten bimodal model revealed statistically significant differences in soil water retention curves and hydraulic conductivity among genotypes. Root traits, including total root length, branching frequency, lateral root length, and root diameter, significantly correlated with soil pore size distribution and hydraulic parameters. This analysis underscores the importance of root architecture in modulating soil structure and water dynamics, highlighting the potential of specific wheat genotypes to affect soil health, water retention, and agricultural sustainability.

papers.title: EFFECTS OF DOLOMITE AMENDMENTS ON PER- AND POLYFLUOROALKYL SUBSTANCES (PFAS) LEACHING IN AGRICULTURAL SOILS
papers.summary: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are often found in agricultural soils due to land application of biosolids, wastewater-derived materials, and atmospheric deposition. However, PFAS transport behavior in variably saturated agricultural soils remains poorly studied. This study evaluates PFAS mobility within unsaturated soil using both intact soil cores (diameter: 3 inches, referred to as large columns (LC)) and packed, homogeneous soil columns (diameter: 1 inch, referred to as small columns (SC)) under the presence and absence of dolomite, which was recently reported to be able to reduce PFAS mobility through adsorption. All columns were amended with a biosolid (Milorganite) and half of the large and small columns received a powdered dolomite amendment at the surface. Columns were subjected to episodic infiltration based on precipitation data from 2019, and the leachate was collected at the base of each column for PFAS analysis. Our results showed that (1) the leaching of PFAS was strongly dependent on the structure and properties of the PFAS, and (2) dolomite amendments could lower the leaching of PFAS. The findings from this research will improve our quantitative understanding of how PFAS move through agricultural soils and the potential risks associated with land application, as well as the design and implementation of science-based management practices and regulation frameworks.

papers.title: Effect of dispersed clay and soil pore size on the hydraulic conductivity of soils irrigated with saline-sodic water
papers.source: University of Southern Queensland ePrints (University of Southern Queensland)
papers.summary: A shortage of good quality water has led to the use of low quality, high saline-sodic water that was considered unsuitable for irrigation purposes in the past. Using such water can increase the potential of soil degradation, soil pore blockage and consequently reductions in soil saturated hydraulic conductivity (Ks). This can limit crop growth in the long term through the impacts on water and nutrient availability. Most studies use reductions in soil Ks as an indicator of soil pore blockage when saline-sodic irrigation water is used. However, the use of saline-sodic irrigation water requires improved understanding of the of cation exchange processes, soil structural degradation and the potential for soil pore blockage. In order to address this three laboratory trials were conducted to investigate the effect of soil pore size on soil cation exchange processes, dispersed clay movement and the mechanisms of soil pore blockage in relation to changes in soil Ks. An initial study was conducted on two soils packed into soil cores at two different bulk densities (ρb) and leached with solutions containing varying concentrations of clay sediments. Measurements of soil Ks showed that increasing soil ρb and the concentration of clay sediment in the applied solution significantly increased the percentage of clay sediment retained within the soil columns. This in turn significantly decreased soil Ks particularly for compacted soils. Soil pore blockage occurred near the soil surface in compacted soils while soil pore blockage occurred at depth in soil packed at low ρb. This confirmed that soil pore size has a significant effect on dispersed clay movement and potential soil pore blockage. The soil pore size distribution does not provide information about the mechanism of soil pore blockage. It was hypothesised that clay sediment migration and soil pore blockage occurs in saline-sodic soils and that the soil response will vary depending on clay mineralogy and the quality of irrigati

papers.title: Understanding preferential water flow and its contribution to inrush hazard susceptibility in block cave mining : an integrated modelling approach
papers.summary: Water infiltration dynamics in block cave mining are critical to understanding and managing inrush hazards that threaten mine safety and operational continuity. Primary water sources, groundwater aquifers, water-bearing faults, and surface water entering through the subsidence crater interact within the cave muck pile through preferential flow pathways that develop and evolve during mining. How that water then partitions within the broken ore column has received less attention. This research investigates the development and flow behaviour of these pathways using an integrated physical and numerical modelling approach. A conceptual model of a draw column is proposed and tested, characterized by central compressive plug flow zones (PFZ) bounded by finer-grained shear bands (SB1, SB2) that respond differently under unsaturated and saturated conditions. A 76-day quasi-two-dimensional physical experiment, instrumented with seven dielectric moisture sensors and a continuous load-cell mass balance, was complemented by a continuum-flow simulation in MIN3P-HPC, providing an independent benchmark of the within-medium hydraulic behaviour. Grain-size distribution contrasts between the shear bands and plug-flow zones govern infiltration patterns more strongly than geometric position does. The fines-rich shear bands retain three to three-and-a-half times the moisture content of the surrounding plug flow zones across all applied flux conditions. Moisture accumulates by capillary imbibition, drawing water laterally from the PFZ into the fines and holding it against gravity drainage on operationally relevant timescales. Sensor integration and continuum simulation give consistent end-of-experiment within-medium storage of 10.5-11.7 L and 11.75 L, respectively. The simulation also identifies the highest moisture contents along the drawbell walls, flanking the drawpoints, a zone too thin to be resolved by the sensors but implicated as the mechanically weakest plane in the draw column d

papers.title: Study on hydraulic conductivity behaviour with regard to soil characteristics in landfill performance
papers.summary: Municipal solid waste generation continues to increase in Malaysia, placing greater demands on landfill containment systems to effectively prevent leachate migration and protect groundwater resources. The engineering performance of compacted landfill liners depends largely on the hydraulic conductivity achieved after compaction, which is governed by the combined influence of soil physical properties and compaction behaviour. However, the hydraulic performance of landfill-sourced residual soils in Malaysia remains insufficiently understood, particularly regarding the interaction between soil characteristics and hydraulic conductivity under realistic moisture and loading conditions. Therefore, this study investigates the relationship between hydraulic conductivity and residual soil characteristics obtained from the Tanjung Dua Belas (T12) and Air Hitam (AH) landfill sites to evaluate their suitability as compacted landfill liner materials through the development of a preliminary empirical hydraulic conductivity prediction model. Laboratory investigations were conducted in accordance with BS 1377:1990 to determine the physical properties, compaction characteristics and hydraulic conductivity of the investigated soils. Both soils were classified as Silty SAND, with the Tanjung Dua Belas soil exhibiting higher plasticity and moisture sensitivity, whereas the Air Hitam soil exhibited higher particle density. Standard Proctor compaction tests established the Optimum Moisture Content (OMC) and Maximum Dry Density (MDD), followed by specimen preparation at 3% below OMC, OMC and 3% above OMC to simulate field moisture tolerance. Tanjung Dua Belas achieved an MDD of 1.50 g/cm³ at an OMC of 18.56%, while Air Hitam attained an MDD of 1.88 g/cm³ at an OMC of 11.75%. Hydraulic conductivity was evaluated using a modified oedometer under incremental vertical loading from 25 kPa to 200 kPa. At 200 kPa, hydraulic conductivity ranged from 1.241 × 10⁻⁸ cm/s to 3.256 × 10⁻⁸ cm/s across t

papers.title: Integrating ecohydrological, isotopic, and numerical approaches to assess water use by montane Scots pine under varying wetness conditions
papers.summary: (English) Ecohydrology provides a critical framework for understanding interactions between vegetation and the hydrological cycle, particularly in forested ecosystems that strongly regulate water fluxes and ecosystem resilience. In Mediterranean mountain regions, increasing climate variability and recurrent droughts place forests close to their hydraulic limits. Despite these mounting pressures, key uncertainties remain regarding how trees access, store, and utilize water across contrasting wetness conditions, and how these processes can be represented in ecohydrological models. This thesis investigates tree water uptake dynamics and their representation by integrating high temporal- and spatial-resolution field observations, stable water isotopes, and process-based modeling. The study was conducted in the Vallcebre Research Catchments (NE Spain), focusing on Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris L.). Field observations combined meteorological measurements, sap flow and stem diameter variations, soil water content and potential, groundwater levels, and weekly water stable isotopes sampling of precipitation, soil water, groundwater, and xylem water. These data were analyzed using statistical approaches and numerical modeling to examine tree water uptake at the plot scale during contrasting dry and wet periods. Field-based ecohydrological and isotopic analyses revealed that Scots pine water use is strongly constrained by soil water potential during drought, with trees relying on internal stem water storage and showing limited coupling to recent precipitation inputs. Stable isotope evidence demonstrated a dominant contribution of winter-recharged soil water stored in tightly bound soil pores, even following intense summer rainfall events. Only after sustained soil rewetting did trees begin incorporating summer precipitation, ultimately sourcing water from a mixture of winter and summer inputs. papers.title: Time-Lapse 3D Electrical Resistivity Tomography to Resolve Preferential Flow Paths in a Forestry Hillslope supported by a Brilliant Blue Tracer
papers.summary: Understanding subsurface water movement, particularly preferential water flow, is critical for water resource management and predicting contaminant transport. However, traditional invasive methods like dye staining experiments are destructive and only provide static information. Consequently, this thesis investigates the effectiveness of 3D time-lapse electrical resistivity tomography (ERT) for monitoring infiltration dynamics on a forested hillslope in Lower Austria. A Brilliant Blue saline tracer was applied to a 0.8 × 0.8 m plot during a two-hour irrigation event. ERT measurements were collected at 7-minute intervals and processed using various inversion strategies to resolve resistivity changes over time. The resistivity data were then used to delineate preferential flow paths and estimate pore water velocities.The ERT monitoring successfully captured the decrease in resistivity, directly corresponding to the infiltration of the tracer.The wetting front migrated rapidly to a depth of 0.25 m within the first 45 minutes before slowing to a maximum of 0.28 m at the end of the irrigation. Pore water velocities, derived from resistivity breakthrough curves, varied from 0.0002 cm/min in the soil matrix to up to 6 cm/min in localized preferential flow paths. Comparison of the ERT inversion results with the post-excavation Brilliant Blue staining patterns confirmed that the centers of conductive anomalies align with the staining patterns, although discrete macropores and root channels could not beresolved due to the limited resolution of the method.These results demonstrate that 3D time-lapse ERT is a robust, non-invasive tool for quantifying the spatio-temporal dynamics of preferential flow, though its resolution remains constrained by the electrode array geometry and the inherent smoothing of the inversion process.

papers.title: 淡水性ラフィド藻に由来するトリクロロ酢酸前駆物質の化学構造解析と浄水処理における処理性評価
Study of methodological approaches for biodiversity monitoring in Nature-based Solutions (NBS) interventions, using Soil and Water Bioengineering (SWBE) techniques in the Mediterranean region.
papers.summary: In the context of the current climate crisis, the intensification of extreme meteoro-logical events necessitates a shift in hydrogeological risk-mitigation strategies, promoting a transition toward Nature-Based Solutions (NBS). Among these, Soil and Water Bioengineer-ing (SWBE) represent a bioinspired solution for slope stabilisation, as it combines geotech-nical safety with the restoration of ecological functionality. However, the scientific valida-tion of such techniques is often caught up in disciplinary fragmentation and by the lack of long-term monitoring protocols capable of assessing both the evolution of slope stability and the success of environmental recovery. This study aims to address this gap through the development and application of an integrated, multidisciplinary monitoring approach. The research focuses on shallow landslides in the Northwest Tuscany (Pomezzana case study, 1996 flood events), comparing sites restored using SWBE techniques and naturally evolved landslides. Subsequently, the core of the research focused on a dual-phase long-term monitoring campaign, focusing on both slope stability and ecological recovery. The first phase involved a comparative stability analysis between a landslide restored with SWBE techniques and an adjacent landslide left to natural evolution. Data acquired from the multi-approach protocol were incorporated into slope-stability modelling to quantify the temporal evolution of the Factor of Safety. The results demonstrate that, in the SWBE restored site, the physiological degradation of wooden structural elements is effectively compensated by the progressive in-crease in soil-root reinforcement. This dynamic equilibrium ensures that the Factor of Safe-ty remains stable over time, contrasting with the fluctuations observed in the natural evolu-tion scenario. Soil characteristics of flood control dikes along the Morava-Thaya River in eastern Austria : effects of environmental factors and dike management
papers.source: Epsilon Archive for Student Projects (University of Southampton)
papers.summary: This study investigates the interactions between soil physical, chemical and biological parameters as well as the influence of climatic, environmental and spatial components on them in the context of dike stability along the Morava-Thaya river system in Central Europe. Climatic variability with more frequent droughts and extreme precipitation events in the future, induced through climate change, might affect flood protection systems through changes in soil structure, hydrology and biogeochemical processes. This study aims to identify dominant environmental gradients, site-specific variability and assess the potential implications for dike stability in the mentioned region. In total, 20 dike sites, including 4 measurement points on the landside and waterside were taken into consideration together with management practices, exposition, distance to agriculture and to forest as well as location along the dam. Soil texture, bulk density, aggregate stability, organic matter fractions, nutrient availability, microbial biomass, enzyme activities, soil moisture, and temperature were analyzed together with climatic variables. The results revealed a pronounced spatial heterogeneity along the dam. Coarse-textured sandy sites with lower moisture, reduced microbial biomass, weaker macroaggregate stability and lower organic carbon content could favor piping, seepage and internal erosion. On the other hand, finer-textured sites exhibited stronger aggregation, greater nutrient availability and increased microbial biomass. There, an increase in water retention capacities could occur, but also an increase in vulnerability to shrink-swell dynamics, desiccation cracking and preferential flow formation during drought periods. Organic carbon, microbial biomass, nutrient availability and macroaggregate stability are indicators of biologically mediated aggregation processes, which can contribute to structural cohesion of dike soils. papers.summary: Agricultural water management plays a key role in sustainable crop production. Controlled drainage has been proposed as a method for mitigating the environmental impacts of drained agricultural lands and adapting to meteorological variability and climate change. However, there remains a lack of quantitative understanding of how controlled drainage influences field-scale hydrology across different soil types and climatic conditions. A process-based hydrological model was used to simulate the field-scale hydrological effects of controlled drainage in comparison to conventional free drainage in Finland. The main objective was to quantify the effects on groundwater table depths and field water balance and analyze how the effects change during the 21st century due to climate change. The simulations applied both mineral soil and peatland parameterizations. Furthermore, the dissertation addressed the following objectives: 1) to analyze the hydrology and performance of controlled drainage on a peatland field with a strong groundwater connection to an upslope forest area, 2) to couple hydrological simulations with peat subsidence under controlled drainage, and 3) to simulate the combination of controlled drainage and open ditch damming and assess the spatial distribution of the effects on groundwater table depths. The simulation results showed controlled drainage to be a viable method to reduce groundwater table depth, with even growing season groundwater table depths being reduced by 0.06–0.26 m. Especially when storing water in the field during earlier months, controlled drainage has potential to reduce growing season drought risk and the environmental impacts of deep groundwater levels. Drain discharge was reduced by 7–23%. This was reflected in increased lateral groundwater outflow, which may be beneficial in reducing substance load, but the peatland simulations showed also a strong increase in surface layer runoff. papers.title: Infiltration in a novel unsaturated multi-layered cover system for use in tailings storage facilities
papers.summary: Conventional barrier systems in tailings storage facilities often rely on thick monolithic geomaterials (1.5 m-2.5 m) or geosynthetics that fail under ex-treme precipitation or snowmelt events typical in Nordic climates. This study proposes and evaluates a novel, fully unsaturated multi-layered cover system (MLCS) constructed majorly from on-site sourced tailings and waste rock. The tailings are modified through either mixing with biochar and clay or by altering surface polarity to make them functional components of a newly conceptual-ized MLCS. The MLCS design integrates capillary barrier mechanisms with a water-entry-head-controlled hydrophobic interface to act as a final hydraulic buffer during extreme ponding conditions. Laboratory characterization of soil-water retention curves (SWRCs), unsaturated hydraulic conductivity functions (SHCFs), and hydrophobicity confirmed the enhanced water-buffering capaci-ty of the modified tailings mixtures. Especially, the threshold-based break-through resistance of the hydrophobic layer (WEH ≈ 4.71 kPa) allowed the construction of an overall thin MLCS (≤0.5-m-thick). This MLCS was physically modelled in an instrumented 1-D column subjected to a ponding head equivalent to a 500-year rainfall event. Results showed complete suppression of percolation below the MLCS for 61 days of testing period, with the hydro-phobic layer preventing breakthrough even after upper layers neared saturation. Complementary two-stage finite element simulations, incorporating WEH-triggered hydraulic switching, accurately reproduced observed suction, water-content, and percolation behaviour. The findings demonstrate that the proposed MLCS provides a climate-resilient, all-weather hydraulic barrier, reduces dependence on imported materials, and offers a feasible, low-cost closure strategy for Nordic TSFs. Further work should assess performance under field-scale slopes including lateral drainage conditions.

papers.title: Groundwater Flow and Age Tracer Modeling in the Montérégie Est Bedrock Aquifer using MODFLOW, MODPATH, and MT3D-USGS
papers.summary: Groundwater residence times and flow pathways are difficult to constrain in regional fractured bedrock aquifers because groundwater movement is controlled by heterogeneous fracture networks, variable recharge conditions, and mixing between local and regional flow systems. This study developed a numerical coupled groundwater flow, particle-tracking, and age-tracer transport model for the 9,218 km² Montérégie Est fractured bedrock aquifer system in southern Québec, Canada. The model was constructed using MODFLOW-NWT to simulate steady-state regional groundwater flow, and hydraulic head, MODPATH-7 to evaluate advective flow pathways, and MT3D-USGS to simulate the infiltration, transport and decay of tritium (³H) and radiocarbon (¹⁴C) from major recharge zones in the region. The model was developed and calibrated using hydrogeological and geochemical datasets from the 2010 PACES field campaign and was subsequently independently evaluated using groundwater samples collected during a 2025 field campaign. The 2025 sampling targeted wells located near model-derived regional flowpaths and included analyses of ³H, ¹⁴C, dissolved inorganic carbon, δ²H, δ¹⁸O, and major ions. Surface-water samples were also collected from the region's major watersheds to assess potential river influence. Simulated hydraulic heads reproduced the regional groundwater gradient well, with strong agreement between measured and modelled heads. The model also captured the main spatial patterns in groundwater age-tracer distributions. ³H simulations reproduced the overall measured–predicted relationship across the 2010 and 2025 datasets, although local deviations indicate unresolved variability in recharge, mixing, and flowpath geometry. ¹⁴C simulations showed strong agreement with measured values from 2025, supporting the model's ability to reproduce first-order regional residence-time patterns, while also highlighting the presence of water-rock interactions. papers.title: Direction-Dependent Skin Friction of Snakeskin-Inspired Surfaces, Piles, and Suction Caissons in Clay and Sand
papers.summary: The installation and performance of geotechnical structures such as piles, anchors, and suction caissons are governed by the skin friction mobilized at soil–structure interfaces. Conventional surfaces typically mobilize slightly greater skin friction in compression than tension, leading to a fundamental trade-off: a high skin friction translates to greater capacity but also leads to greater installation forces, while a low skin friction is beneficial for installation but can result in a limited ultimate capacity and excessive movements. Inspired by the ventral scales of snakes, which generate smaller friction when moving in the caudal direction (along the scales) than in the cranial direction (against the scales), this dissertation investigates the direction-dependent shear behavior of snakeskin-inspired surfaces across a broad range of soils, drainage conditions, and structural applications through interface element testing and centrifuge physical modeling.Interfaces between snakeskin-inspired surfaces and normally consolidated kaolin clay were characterized through direct interface shear tests performed under drained and undrained conditions, together with centrifuge load tests on axially loaded piles. Cranial shearing consistently mobilized greater strength than caudal shearing, and the interface strength increased as the asperity height (H) was increased and the asperity length (L) was decreased, with the L/H ratio unifying the effects of asperity geometry. Piles installed caudally and pulled cranially mobilized skin friction up to 60% greater during pullout than installation, and tensile skin friction 2.8 to 4.1 times greater than an untextured reference pile.Characterization of the interface response was also performed with compacted, unsaturated silty clay through interface shear tests that examined the coupled effects of asperity geometry, normal stress, and water content. papers.title: Application of the Material Point Method to the Stability and Runout Analysis of Vegetated Slopes
papers.summary: Slope failures cause severe human and economic losses worldwide, yet conventional stability methods describe them only up to the onset of failure. Limit equilibrium methods treat the failing mass as rigid and perfectly plastic, and the finite element method is restricted to small deformations, so neither follows the slide once it forms. The Material Point Method (MPM) avoids this limitation by discretizing soil into Lagrangian material points that move through a fixed background mesh, so no mesh distortion develops under large deformation. This dissertation applies MPM to the analysis of slope failures in two parts, the assessment of slope stability and the influence of vegetation on rainfall-induced failures. The one-phase and coupled two-phase formulations are first derived and verified against classical benchmark problems in poromechanics. Next, MPM is applied to evaluate the stability of slopes using the strength reduction technique. For dry and unsaturated slopes, slip surfaces agree with finite element solutions and factors of safety differ by less than about 10%, reflecting the different criteria by which each method identifies failure. Unlike mesh-based methods, MPM continues past the onset of failure and captures the post-failure runout. The effect of root reinforcement is then investigated. A multiple-hardening constitutive model for root-reinforced soil is implemented within the coupled formulation and validated against triaxial tests. Comparative analyses of bare and vegetated slopes under rainfall show that roots delay the initiation of failure, roughly halve the displacement, and change a retrogressive slide into the movement of a single block, although they do not prevent failure under continued rainfall. Finally, the method is validated against a documented centrifuge slope test. papers.title: Managing the effect of infiltration variability on the performance of surface irrigation
papers.source: University of Southern Queensland ePrints (University of Southern Queensland)
papers.summary: Infiltration variability is a major issue during the design phase and management for all types of irrigation systems. Infiltration is of particular significance for furrow irrigation and other forms of surface irrigation as the soil intake rate at any given position not only determines the depth applied but also governs the distribution of water to other locations in the field. Despite this, existing measurement and evaluation procedures generally assume homogeneous soil infiltration rates across the field to simplify data collection and computational requirements. This study was conducted to (a) determine whether spatial and temporal variations in soil infiltration characteristics have a significant impact on the performance of surface irrigation and (b) identify more appropriate management strategies that account for this variability and substantially improve irrigation performance. The soil infiltration rate is typically expressed as an empirical function of opportunity time. The infiltration function parameters cannot be directly measured but are commonly estimated from field hydraulic measurements using an appropriate simulation model. The volume balance model as used in the inverse solution for infiltration (e.g. Two Point Method) was modified to enable runoff data collected during the inflow period to be used in the estimation of the infiltration parameters. The resulting model, IPARM also accommodates the full (variable) inflow hydrograph rather than relying on a constant inflow assumption. Inclusion of runoff data in the inverse solution improved the accuracy of the infiltration curve during the runoff phase and hence offered the greatest benefit where the irrigation time exceeded the completion of advance. Analysis of field data collected from multiple furrows at a single site indicated that accounting for the variable inflow in IPARM both reduced the variability (e.g. reduction in the coefficient of variance (CV) of cumulative infiltrated depths of 18.6%

papers.title: Toward real-time control of surface irrigation
papers.source: University of Southern Queensland ePrints (University of Southern Queensland)
papers.summary: The performance of surface irrigation is a function of the field design, infiltration characteristic of the soil, and the irrigation management practice. However, the complexity of the interactions makes it difficult for irrigators to identify optimal design or management practices. The infiltration characteristic of the soil is the most crucial of all the factors affecting the performance of surface irrigation and both spatial and temporal variations in the infiltration characteristic are a major physical constraint to achieving higher irrigation application efficiencies. Real-time optimisation and control has the potential to overcome these spatial and temporal variations and return highly significant improvements in performance. Calculation of the infiltration parameters from irrigation advance data is now the preferred method. If the process is to be included in a real time control system it must be done accurately, reliably and rapidly, and with a minimum of field data. Substantial work has been directed towards developing methods to estimate the infiltration characteristics of soil from irrigation advance data. However, none of the existing methods are entirely suitable for use in real time control. The greatest limitation is that they are data intensive and or unreliable and provide soil infiltration properties after an irrigation event. A simple real-time control system for furrow irrigation is proposed that: predicts the infiltration characteristics of the soil in real-time using data measured during an irrigation event, simulates the irrigation, and determines the optimum time to cut-off for that irrigation. The basis of the system is a new method for the Real-time Estimation of the Infiltration Parameters (REIP) under furrow irrigation, developed during this research study, and that uses a model infiltration curve, and a scaling process to predict the infiltration characteristics for each furrow and each irrigation event. papers.title: STUDI PERENCANAAN JALAN DAN PENGAMANAN LERENG PADA TRASE JALAN UJAN MAS PADA STA 0+050 SAMPAI STA 2+550
papers.source: UMM Institutional Repository (University of Maine at Machias)
papers.summary: The development of safe and efficient road infrastructure is a crucial element in regional development. This study aims to conduct technical planning for new roads and slope protection systems on the Ujan Mas Road Trace (STA 0+050 to STA 2+550). Given the location's topography, which is dominated by steep slopes, this planning integrates geometric design of the road, pavement structure, drainage system, and retaining wall design. The study methodology includes primary and secondary data collection, hydrological analysis for the design flood discharge calculation, and soil mechanics investigation to ensure the stability of the retaining wall structure against overturning, shearing, and dynamic earthquake loads (Mononobe-Okabe method). In addition to technical aspects, this study also includes the preparation of a Cost Budget Plan (RAB) to accurately estimate construction funding requirements based on the calculated work volume. The geometric design of the road refers to the Bina Marga standard, while the pavement analysis uses the Bina Marga method. The final results of this study are expected to provide a comprehensive and economical technical solution for road infrastructure development in the area, while prioritizing safety aspects and sustainable slope stability

papers.title: Boundary Influence in Truncated Groundwater Models: Reconstructing a Local-Scale MODFLOW Model from a Consultant-Developed Regional Model in the Monterey Subbasin
papers.summary: Regional groundwater models built by consultants contain valuable calibrated frameworks but are often too large and complex for repeated local-scale analysis. Rather than rebuilding an entirely new smaller model, this study truncates the existing consultant-built regional model of the Monterey Subbasin, preserving the original grid structure and parameter framework while reducing the active domain to a manageable size for planning-level use. A key finding is that boundary-condition representation exerted a dominant influence on simulated groundwater behavior within the truncated domain, highlighting that truncation is a structural decision that meaningfully affects how the model responds. Model performance was evaluated two ways. Alternative hydraulic conductivity fields derived from AEM resistivity data were used to assess how sensitive the reconstructed model was to changes in internal parameter structure. Transient injection simulations produced cumulative groundwater mounding that grew progressively over repeated seasonal cycles, confirming realistic aquifer behavior and demonstrating the model's value as a practical and transparent planning-level tool.

papers.title: CAPILLARY-DRIVEN TRANSPORT IN POROUS MEDIA: UNSATURATED FLOW, THERMAL EFFECTS, AND VADOSE-ZONE CYCLING
papers.summary: Capillary-driven transport in porous media plays a fundamental role in a wide range of natural and engineered systems, including heat pipes, fibrous and ceramic materials, soils, contaminant transport in the vadose zone, and moisture-management technologies. Although substantial progress has been made in modeling and characterizing wicking under simplified conditions, important gaps remain in understanding how thermal gradients, partial saturation, and evaporation-driven solute cycling influence liquid transport in porous media. This dissertation addresses these gaps through a combined experimental, analytical, and numerical investigation of capillary-driven flow in porous materials across thermal, engineered, and environmental settings.The first part of this dissertation develops a Richards equation-based numerical framework to model moisture infusion in porous ceramics and other engineered materials by incorporating capillary pressure–saturation and relative permeability relationships. The model was validated against high-resolution neutron microscope imaging experiments and two independent analytical solutions. Extended simulations were then performed to investigate the role of engineered wettability — including hydrophilic surface coatings and hydrophobic inclusions — on two-dimensional moisture migration patterns. These results demonstrate how material design and local wettability modification can be used to control liquid transport pathways in porous systems. The second part of this work investigates non-isothermal wicking in porous media. Experiments were conducted using sintered polymer-bead wicks and hydrocarbon liquids under imposed temperature differences between the liquid and the wick. A sharp-front Darcy-based framework was developed to model the transient rise of liquid while accounting for temperature-dependent viscosity, surface tension, and density. papers.title: Impacts of Cover Crops, No-Tillage and Cotton-Sorghum Rotation on Soil-Water Dynamics: Environmental and Economic Implications
papers.summary: Water scarcity associated with declining groundwater levels in the Ogallala Aquifer threatens the long-term sustainability of irrigated agriculture in the semi-arid Texas High Plains. As irrigation capacity decreases, management strategies that improve soil-mediated water capture and enhance production resilience are increasingly important. This thesis integrates a regional literature synthesis with field-based evaluation of conservation practices aimed at improving water-use efficiency in cotton-based cropping systems. The literature identifies irrigation technology improvements, precision agriculture technologies, and soil health management as key pathways for reducing water demand and enhancing precipitation capture, while also emphasizing economic constraints and site-specific performance of conservation practices. A two-year field study assessed the short-term effects of cover crops and cotton–sorghum rotation under no-tillage on soil physical properties, crop productivity, and economic indicators. Soil measurements included saturated hydraulic conductivity, aggregate stability, compaction, and total organic carbon, alongside cotton and sorghum yield and fiber quality. Results showed limited short-term changes in most soil properties, although aggregate stability increased under rotational systems with cover crops. Cotton yield remained consistent across treatments, but fiber quality and associated economic returns declined in rotation-based systems. Sorghum performance was largely influenced by interannual climatic variability rather than management effects. Overall, findings suggest that while conservation practices hold potential to improve soil function and water-use efficiency, measurable agronomic and economic benefits may require long-term adoption. Extended evaluation is necessary to determine whether gradual soil health improvements can enhance system resilience and profitability under increasing water limitations.

papers.summary: Arsenic contamination in groundwater represents a critical environmental and public health challenge due to its high toxicity and widespread occurrence in natural aquifers. Chronic exposure to arsenic, even at trace levels, is associated with severe health effects, including skin lesions and increased cancer risk. Conventional treatment technologies, such as adsorption using activated carbon or metal oxides, often suffer from limited selectivity, regeneration difficulty, and reduced efficiency under varying pH conditions. Therefore, developing advanced sorbent materials with high capacity, selectivity, and structural stability is essential for addressing arsenic pollution in decentralized water systems.Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) have recently emerged as promising materials for water purification owing to their tunable pore structures, high surface areas, and functional versatility. Among them, zirconium-based MOFs such as UiO-66 are particularly attractive because of their excellent water stability and Zr–OH active sites favorable for arsenate binding. However, the powdered nature of most MOFs presents significant challenges for practical filtration applications, including clogging, high pressure drop, and regeneration difficulties. To overcome these limitations, this work first focused on integrating UiO-66 and UiO-66-NH₂ with granular activated carbon (GAC) to develop hybrid point-of-use filtration materials. The composite exhibited uniform MOF attachment on GAC surfaces, mitigating issues related to powder handling and mobility. Batch adsorption tests revealed that UiO-66–GAC outperformed UiO-66-NH₂–GAC under near-neutral pH, highlighting the influence of surface chemistry on arsenic affinity.
